items.title: otterdog
items.text: Otterdog manages GitHub organizations at scale with a configuration as code approach: the settings of an organization and of its repositories are declared in Jsonnet, reviewed as pull requests and applied to GitHub. It is developed by the Eclipse Foundation, which uses it to manage the GitHub organizations of its projects.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
Declare

A repository of the organization declares its settings, teams and repositories in Jsonnet.

Propose

Anyone proposes a change as a pull request, tried out in the Playground if needed.

Review

otterdog validates it and shows what it would change on GitHub, the configured teams approve.

Apply

Once the pull request is merged, otterdog applies the changes to the GitHub organization.

The configuration only declares what differs from a default configuration shared by many organizations, and administrators can also apply changes with the otterdog command line tool. See Workflow for changes for the steps of a change.

items.title: What otterdog manages
items.text:
• Organizations: settings, roles, teams, webhooks, secrets and variables, rulesets, custom properties and code security configurations.
  • Repositories: settings, branch protection rules and rulesets, environments, webhooks, secrets and variables.
  • Across organizations: policies enforce a behavior, and blueprints keep files and settings present in repositories by opening pull requests.

Some settings are only available in the web interface of GitHub, otterdog manages them through a browser session. Others cannot be managed at all, see Unsupported settings.

items.title: Getting started
items.text: How you start with otterdog depends on what you want to do. Most people only change the configuration of an organization through pull requests and never install anything.

items.title: Change the configuration of an organization
items.text:
For the members and contributors of a project whose GitHub organization is managed by otterdog.

  1. Find the configuration repository of the organization, e.g. .eclipsefdn for the projects of the Eclipse Foundation. The configuration of the organization is otterdog/<organization>.jsonnet, and the dashboard shows the current one of each organization of the Eclipse Foundation.
  2. Find what to change: the Configuration Guides start from a need, e.g. protecting a branch or providing a secret to a workflow, the Reference documents every property. The configuration only declares what differs from the default configuration, see Inherited and explicit values.
  3. Try it out (optional): the Playground evaluates a configuration and checks its values like otterdog does.
  4. Open a pull request on the configuration repository: otterdog validates it and shows the changes it would make on GitHub, the configured teams review it, and the changes are applied once it is merged.

Next: Workflow for changes, then adding, renaming or removing resources.

items.title: Manage organizations with the command line tool
items.text:
For the administrators of GitHub organizations, who apply configurations themselves.

  1. Install git and otterdog, see Install:

    pipx install otterdog

  2. Configure the organizations to manage in an otterdog.json file: the default configuration to use and the credentials to access each organization (a GitHub token, and a GitHub account with two-factor authentication for the settings only available in the web interface), see Setup.

  3. Import the current configuration of an organization, then review and apply changes:

    otterdog import <organization>   # writes the configuration of the organization from its live settings
otterdog plan <organization>     # shows the changes that would be applied
otterdog apply <organization>    # applies them

Next: Usage of the command line tool and the CLI Operations.

items.title: Deploy otterdog for your organizations
items.text:
For the operators who run the otterdog GitHub App, which validates the pull requests of configuration repositories, applies the merged changes and provides the dashboard and its Playground.

  1. Create a GitHub App and install it in the organizations to manage.
  2. Deploy the container image with the Helm chart on Kubernetes, and initialize otterdog.
  3. Define the policies shared by your organizations: the default configuration, validation scripts and exceptions, see Organization-wide policies.

Next: Otterdog WebApp.

items.title: Contribute to otterdog
items.text:
For the developers of otterdog itself.

  1. Set up a development environment with make init, see Development Setup.
  2. Read the Architecture and the Coding & Style Guidelines.
  3. Propose your change as described in the Contribution Workflow.

Next: Testing and the Release Process.

items.title: 1. Purpose
items.text:
This document models threats for operating GitHub organizations using otterdog in two modes:

  1. otterdog CLI used from admin laptops (plan/apply)
  2. Otterdog WebApp deployed in Kubernetes (webhooks + sync/validation + persistence)

Goal: protect GitHub organization integrity, minimize credential blast radius, ensure strong governance over configuration changes, and provide adequate auditability for all applies.

items.title: 2. System overview
items.text:
Otterdog is a stateless GitHub infrastructure-as-code tool. It reads org-level configuration (JSON/Jsonnet), builds an in-memory desired model, fetches live state from GitHub via providers, computes a diff as “LivePatch” operations, then prints (plan) or executes (apply) changes. (otterdog.readthedocs.io)

Important behavior: apply does not consume a previously generated plan; it recomputes the diff at runtime and does not keep a persistent state/plan file. (otterdog.readthedocs.io)

Otterdog fetches data via multiple provider paths, including GitHub REST API, GitHub GraphQL API, and GitHub Web UI (for settings not accessible via APIs). (otterdog.readthedocs.io)

Operational model (typical): configuration is hosted in a repository; contributors propose changes via pull requests; changes are approved and then applied manually using the CLI. (otterdog.readthedocs.io)

items.title: In scope
items.text:
• Integrity of GitHub org settings managed by otterdog configuration
  • Confidentiality and integrity of credentials used by CLI and WebApp
  • Configuration repository governance and CI validation/policy checks
  • WebApp deployment hardening (ingress, internal endpoints, persistence dependencies)
  • Auditability of “who approved what” and “who applied what”
  • Availability risks that prevent managing orgs or cause disruption

items.title: Out of scope (explicitly)
items.text:
• Exploits in GitHub itself (treated as external dependency)
  • Physical threats beyond standard enterprise endpoint controls
  • Unrelated SDLC risks not interacting with otterdog (unless you extend this model)

items.title: 4. Assumptions and constraints
items.text:
A1. Applies run from admin laptops (not a controlled CI runner). This makes endpoint compromise a primary risk driver.

A2. Some settings require GitHub Web UI access; otterdog “Quick Setup” explicitly calls for username/password and a 2FA TOTP seed to access settings not available via REST/GraphQL. (otterdog.readthedocs.io)

A3. The documented GitHub PAT scopes include delete_repo (high blast radius). (otterdog.readthedocs.io)

A4. WebApp dependencies include MongoDB and Redis/Valkey; the install guide states Redis/Valkey “must be configured without authentication” (GHProxy limitation). (otterdog.readthedocs.io)

A5. WebApp exposes internal management endpoints under /internal/, including an initialization endpoint /internal/init, and the install guide recommends restricting internal endpoints via ingress rules. (otterdog.readthedocs.io)

A6. Otterdog runs with the credentials of an organization owner (CLI) or of the GitHub App (WebApp). Whoever controls a trusted input below controls what otterdog does with these credentials.

items.title: Trusted and untrusted inputs
items.text:
Trusted inputs are provided by the operators of otterdog and are equivalent to code:

Input Why it is trusted otterdog.json Written by the operator. It selects the organizations, the credential providers and their parameters, and the default configuration (base_template). Default configuration: the repository and ref referenced by base_template Provides the inherited value of every setting of every organization that uses it. Its Python scripts (validate-org-settings.py, validate-team.py, pre-add-object-hook.py, post-add-objects-hook.py) are executed by otterdog during validate, plan, apply and the validation of pull requests, with the permissions and credentials of the process, see Organization-wide policies. Local working directory The configurations of the organizations and their vendor/ directory. With --local, the default configuration in vendor/ is used as is, without fetching it. Installation The otterdog package and its dependencies, the credential tools it calls (pass, bw, Vault). WebApp deployment Helm values and environment variables, the GitHub App private key, the token of the configuration repository.

Untrusted inputs must not lead to code execution, to file access outside the directory of the organization, or to the disclosure of credentials:

Input Handling Pull requests to the configuration repository of an organization (WebApp) Only otterdog/<github-id>.jsonnet is fetched from the pull request and written to a fixed path. It is evaluated with imports restricted to the directory of the organization. The default configuration comes from otterdog.json, never from the pull request. Webhook deliveries Rejected unless their signature matches the webhook secret. Data returned by GitHub (APIs and Web UI) Processed as data.

items.title: Not considered vulnerabilities
items.text: Issues that require control of a trusted input, e.g. a malicious otterdog.json, a compromised default configuration repository, or files placed in the local working directory, are not vulnerabilities of otterdog: controlling these inputs already gives control over the managed organizations. Their protection is part of operating otterdog, see T5 below. Report an issue anyway if an untrusted party can reach a trusted input in a documented setup. Hardening suggestions are welcome as regular issues.

items.title: A. GitHub organization integrity (highest priority)
items.text:
• Org owners/admins, custom roles, and membership
  • Teams and team permissions
  • Repository settings, branch protections/rulesets, environments
  • Organization and repository webhooks
  • Organization/repository secrets and variables (note: secret values are not retrievable from GitHub after creation; configuration must reference real values via a credential provider). (otterdog.readthedocs.io)

items.title: B. Credential material (“tier-0 secrets”)
items.text:
CLI side:

  • GitHub username/password and 2FA TOTP seed used for Web UI scraping (otterdog.readthedocs.io)
  • GitHub PAT and its scopes (notably delete_repo) (otterdog.readthedocs.io)
  • Credential provider session tokens (Bitwarden/pass)

WebApp side:

  • GitHub App private key, webhook secret, config token (base64 in example values.yaml) (otterdog.readthedocs.io)
  • DB/cache connectivity secrets (MongoDB URI, Redis URI)

items.title: C. Configuration repository integrity
items.text:
• Jsonnet/JSON files defining desired state
  • Default configuration referenced by base_template: its Jsonnet defaults, and the Python scripts that otterdog executes
  • CI policy/validation logic

items.title: D. Audit evidence
items.text: • Records linking: config commit → plan/apply output → operator identity → resulting org changes

items.title: E. Availability
items.text:
• Ability to run plan/apply when needed
  • WebApp availability (webhook handling, sync, persistence)

items.title: Key trust boundaries
items.text: TB1. Admin laptop boundary (endpoint integrity, local filesystem, credential tooling) TB2. Config repository boundary (PRs, reviews, CI checks, merge protection) TB3. Network boundary to GitHub (API + Web UI automation) TB4. Kubernetes cluster boundary (WebApp ingress, internal endpoints, service-to-service traffic) TB5. Persistence boundary (MongoDB, Redis/Valkey without auth) (otterdog.readthedocs.io) TB6. Default configuration boundary (repository referenced by base_template, its ref, who can push to it)

items.title: 7. Entry points and attack surfaces
items.text:
Admin laptop / CLI:

  • otterdog execution environment and local repo checkout
  • Local secrets handling and credential provider integrations
  • Any storage of credentials in otterdog.json (risk: “plain” provider)
  • Network access from laptop to GitHub, and potentially to WebApp internal endpoints

Config repo:

  • Pull requests and merges (governance and CI enforcement)
  • Jsonnet evaluation and imports (in the WebApp, imports of a pull request are restricted to the directory of the organization)

Default configuration repository:

  • Pushes to the ref referenced by base_template; a branch is pulled on every run
  • Python scripts executed by otterdog with its credentials

WebApp:

  • Public ingress endpoints (webhooks, UI)
  • /internal/* endpoints (must be restricted) (otterdog.readthedocs.io)
  • Redis/Valkey unauthenticated access (compensate with network isolation) (otterdog.readthedocs.io)
  • MongoDB credentials and exposure

items.title: 8. Threat analysis (STRIDE)
items.text: This section lists realistic threats for your setup and recommended controls. Severity assumes admin laptops are used for apply.

items.title: 8.1 Spoofing (impersonation)
items.text:
Threat S1: Theft of CLI credentials (PAT, password, TOTP seed) enables attacker to impersonate an org admin and apply arbitrary changes. Otterdog explicitly documents username/password/2FA seed usage for Web UI settings. (otterdog.readthedocs.io) Controls:

  • Prohibit storing credentials via provider: "plain" beyond experimentation; docs warn not to use it broadly due to leakage risk. (otterdog.readthedocs.io)
  • Store credentials only in vault-backed providers (Bitwarden/pass) and enforce vault MFA and device posture checks.
  • Treat TOTP seed as tier-0: minimize who can retrieve it, do not export to disk, rotate on any suspicion of endpoint compromise.
  • Use a dedicated service account for otterdog operations; do not reuse personal admin accounts for apply.

Threat S2: WebApp GitHub App private key compromise enables attacker to mint installation tokens and operate with app permissions. WebApp install guide instructs storing GitHub App private key in values.yaml (base64). (otterdog.readthedocs.io) Controls:

  • Store app private key in a proper secret manager / sealed secrets; never commit values containing secrets.
  • Rotate webhook secret and app private key after incidents; restrict access to the secret material to cluster operators only.

Threat S3: Forged/replayed webhooks to WebApp Controls:

  • Ensure webhook signature verification is enabled and secrets are rotated.
  • Add replay protections if you have an edge proxy (timestamp tolerance, rate limits).

items.title: 8.2 Tampering (unauthorized modification)
items.text:
Threat T1: Malicious config PR weakens org security (e.g., new webhook, reduced ruleset/branch requirements, elevated bypass actors) Controls:

  • Treat config merges as privileged production changes:

  • CODEOWNERS requiring security/admin reviews

  • required CI checks + branch protection
  • no self-approval on high-impact paths

  • Add CI “policy checks” that fail PRs which:

  • add org/repo webhooks without explicit allowlist approval

  • reduce branch protection/ruleset requirements
  • broaden bypass actor lists
  • Require “apply operator” separation for sensitive changes (approver ≠ applier).

Threat T2: Local tampering on admin laptop (malware modifies config checkout or otterdog binary) Controls:

  • Use a dedicated hardened apply environment (separate OS user / VM / laptop) with minimal software.
  • Prefer pinned versions / checksums for otterdog installation (package locking and signed releases where available).
  • Require apply to reference an explicit config commit SHA (not “whatever is in the working tree”).

Threat T3: Redis/Valkey manipulation in-cluster (queue/cache poisoning) The install guide states Redis/Valkey must be deployed without authentication. (otterdog.readthedocs.io) Controls (compensating):

  • Strict NetworkPolicies: only WebApp/GHProxy pods can reach Redis/Valkey.
  • Namespace isolation and RBAC: prevent arbitrary pod creation in the same namespace.
  • Monitor and alert on unusual Redis command patterns / spikes.

Threat T4: Abuse of /internal/* management endpoints (init/maintenance actions) Docs instruct restricting /internal/ endpoints and show ingress allowlist examples; init uses /internal/init. (otterdog.readthedocs.io) Controls:

  • Restrict /internal/* at ingress to a management CIDR/VPN only.
  • Add another auth layer (mTLS or an auth proxy) if feasible.
  • Alert on any access to /internal/*.

Threat T5: Compromised or mutable default configuration The default configuration referenced by base_template defines the inherited values of every organization using it, and otterdog executes its Python scripts with its credentials: organization owner credentials on admin laptops, the GitHub App private key in the WebApp. Whoever can push to the referenced ref controls all these organizations, and can run code at the next validate, plan or pull request validation, without any change to the configuration of an organization. A branch, e.g. @main, is pulled on every run, so every push to it takes effect immediately. Controls:

  • Reference a tag or a commit SHA in base_template, not a branch. A tag or a commit is checked out once and not updated afterwards; otterdog logs a warning when base_template references a branch.
  • Prefer a commit SHA when the repository of the default configuration is not under your control; otherwise protect its tags with a ruleset that prevents their update and deletion.
  • Protect the repository of the default configuration like code: restricted push access, required reviews, no force pushes.
  • Review the Python scripts with every new version of the default configuration, and run plan for the affected organizations before switching to it.

items.title: 8.3 Repudiation (denying actions)
items.text:
Threat R1: No reliable evidence of who ran apply from an admin laptop Controls:

  • Standardize a wrapper script for applies that logs:

  • operator identity

  • config repo and commit SHA
  • timestamp
  • command-line args
  • plan/apply output (or hash + storage location)
  • Send logs to a central, immutable store (SIEM).
  • Correlate with GitHub audit log events for key changes (admins, webhooks, rulesets).

items.title: 8.4 Information disclosure
items.text:
Threat I1: Credential leakage via plain provider in otterdog.json Docs explicitly warn: do not use plain beyond quick setup to avoid leakage if the file is shared. (otterdog.readthedocs.io) Controls:

  • Ban provider: plain in repo policy checks; enforce via CI.
  • Require vault-backed providers.

Threat I2: Leakage of TOTP seed (MFA bypass) Otterdog documents storing twofa_seed / totp for GitHub Web UI access. (otterdog.readthedocs.io) Controls:

  • Tier-0 handling: least access, audit retrieval, rotate on compromise.
  • Avoid printing or logging secrets; ensure wrapper scripts redact.

Threat I3: Secrets embedded in WebApp Helm values (configToken/webhookSecret/appPrivateKey shown in example) (otterdog.readthedocs.io) Controls:

  • Externalize secrets: do not commit them; use Kubernetes external secrets or sealed secrets.
  • Scan repos for accidental secret commits (secret scanning + pre-commit hooks).

Threat I4: Disclosure of the secrets of another organization The configuration of an organization, changed by pull requests, references secrets in the credential providers of the operator, who usually has access to the secrets of all organizations, e.g. pass:bots/<other organization>/token. Applying it copies the secret of another organization into a secret of this organization, readable by its workflows. Controls:

  • Restrict the references of each organization with a secret access policy, checked when validating pull requests and before resolving secrets during apply.
  • Review the references to secrets in configuration pull requests.

items.title: 8.5 Denial of service
items.text:
Threat D1: Broad PAT scopes allow destructive operations (delete_repo) causing org-wide disruption (otterdog.readthedocs.io) Controls:

  • Remove delete_repo scope unless you explicitly need repo deletions.

  • Split credentials:

  • “routine” token: minimal scopes needed for normal operation

  • “break-glass” token: destructive scopes; time-limited access and extra approvals

Threat D2: Webhook flooding / GitHub rate limiting affects WebApp and/or admin workflows Controls:

  • Rate-limit ingress, validate signatures early.
  • Monitor GitHub API rate usage and backoff handling.

items.title: 8.6 Elevation of privilege
items.text:
Threat E1: Anyone who can merge config effectively controls org state (because apply enforces desired state) Controls:

  • Tighten merge permissions and enforce least privilege.
  • Require security review for changes to roles/admins, webhooks, bypass settings, and rulesets.

Threat E2: Admin laptop compromise becomes org-admin compromise (because apply runs there) Controls:

  • Harden apply endpoints (dedicated system, EDR, patching, minimal apps).
  • Do not use apply endpoint for daily browsing/email.
  • Device posture requirements for vault access.

items.title: 9. Risk register (starter)
items.text: ID Risk Likelihood Impact Priority Key mitigations R-01 Admin laptop compromise steals PAT + password + TOTP seed High Critical P0 Dedicated apply endpoint, vault-only creds, tier-0 controls, EDR R-02 Malicious config PR weakens org protections Medium Critical P0 CODEOWNERS, policy checks, separation of duties R-03 /internal/* endpoint reachable beyond mgmt plane Medium High P1 Ingress allowlist + auth proxy + alerting R-04 Redis/Valkey abuse in-cluster (no auth) Medium High P1 NetworkPolicies + namespace isolation + monitoring R-05 Over-scoped PAT includes delete_repo Medium Critical P0 Remove scope, split tokens, break-glass process R-06 Lack of apply audit trail High Medium P1 Wrapper logging + immutable central store + correlation R-07 Default configuration referenced by a branch or compromised runs code with otterdog credentials Low Critical P1 Tag or commit SHA in base_template, protected repository and tags, review of scripts

items.title: 10.1 Credential handling (MUST)
items.text:
• Do not use the plain credential provider outside of ephemeral experimentation; enforce via CI/policy checks. (otterdog.readthedocs.io)
  • Vault-backed credentials only (Bitwarden/pass).
  • TOTP seed treated as tier-0 secret: least access, audited retrieval, fast rotation procedure. (otterdog.readthedocs.io)
  • Remove delete_repo scope unless required; use separate “break-glass” credentials for destructive actions. (otterdog.readthedocs.io)

items.title: 10.2 Admin laptop apply controls (MUST)
items.text:
• Applies must run on a dedicated apply environment (separate machine/VM or hardened OS profile).
  • Applies must reference an explicit config commit SHA and clean working tree.
  • Operator must run plan immediately before apply (same commit, same environment).
  • Store apply logs centrally (operator, commit SHA, output hash, timestamp).

items.title: 10.3 Config repo governance (MUST)
items.text:
• Branch protection on main:

  • required reviews (CODEOWNERS)

  • required CI status checks (syntax + policy)
  • restrict who can merge

  • CI policy rules must block:

  • new webhooks without explicit approval

  • reductions in ruleset/protection strictness
  • expansions of bypass actors and admin roles without security approval

  • Default configuration:

  • base_template references a tag or a commit SHA, never a branch

  • the repository of the default configuration and its tags are protected like the configuration repository
  • changes to its Python scripts are reviewed like code

items.title: 10.4 WebApp hardening (MUST)
items.text:
• Restrict /internal/* endpoints to management network only (ingress allowlist); document the management access path. (otterdog.readthedocs.io)
  • Treat /internal/init as a privileged operation; alert on execution. (otterdog.readthedocs.io)
  • Network isolate Redis/Valkey given “no auth” constraint; only allow access from required pods/services. (otterdog.readthedocs.io)
  • Keep secrets out of Git: use external secrets, sealed secrets, or equivalent.

items.title: 11.1 Suspected admin laptop compromise
items.text:
1. Revoke GitHub PAT(s) used by otterdog; rotate password; rotate TOTP seed. (otterdog.readthedocs.io)
  2. Rotate WebApp secrets if laptop had any access (webhook secret, app key) (otterdog.readthedocs.io)
  3. Review GitHub audit log for role/webhook/ruleset changes

  4. Re-establish known-good state:

  5. pull last approved config commit

  6. run plan and apply from a clean trusted environment

items.title: 11.2 Suspicious WebApp behavior
items.text:
1. Block ingress access to /internal/* and verify allowlists (otterdog.readthedocs.io)
  2. Inspect cluster logs for /internal/init calls and anomalous Redis traffic
  3. Rotate GitHub App private key and webhook secret if tampering suspected (otterdog.readthedocs.io)

items.title: 12. Residual risks (explicitly accepted or to be reduced)
items.text:
• Storing/using a TOTP seed as automation input is inherently high risk because it can bypass MFA if stolen. This is required for Web UI-only settings in the documented setup. (otterdog.readthedocs.io)
  • Redis/Valkey without authentication is an architectural constraint in the documented WebApp deployment; accept only with strong network isolation. (otterdog.readthedocs.io)
  • “Apply from laptops” remains higher risk than “apply from a controlled CI runner.” If requirements change, migrating apply into a hardened CI environment is the single biggest risk reducer.

items.title: 13. Appendix: Security invariants to encode in CI (examples)
items.text:
These are intentionally strict “guardrails” you can implement as CI policy checks:

  • Webhooks: no new org/repo webhooks without allowlisted destinations and security approval.

  • Rulesets/branch protections:

  • cannot reduce required checks

  • cannot add bypass actors beyond an allowlist
  • cannot enable force pushes / deletions (unless explicitly approved)

  • Admin roles:

  • cannot add org owners/admins except via an allowlisted process

  • Tokens/scopes:

  • configs must not reference provider: plain (otterdog.readthedocs.io)

  • break-glass credentials must not be used by default in daily workflows

  • Default configuration:

  • every base_template in otterdog.json ends with a tag or a commit SHA, not a branch

items.title: Otterdog Architecture
items.text:
Fair warning

This looks complex. It is complex. But reading this page a few times is better than randomly poking at the code for weeks.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
Otterdog is a stateless GitHub Infrastructure-as-Code tool.

At a high level it:

  1. Reads org-level configuration (JSON / Jsonnet)
  2. Builds a desired in-memory model
  3. Fetches the actual state from GitHub via providers
  4. Computes a structured diff in the form of LivePatch operations
  5. Either prints the diff (plan) or applies it (apply) via GitHub APIs
flowchart TB
subgraph shared
    cli_apply([otterdog plan / apply])

    cli_apply --> load_config(Load org config)
    load_config --> desired_config[Desired State]

    cli_apply --> load_live(Fetch from GitHub)
    load_live --> current_state[Current State]

    desired_config --> live_gen(Generate Live Patch)
    current_state --> live_gen

    live_gen --> live_patch[Live Patch]
end

subgraph plan
  live_patch --> print(Print Diff)
end

subgraph apply
  live_patch --> apply_changes(Apply Changes)
end

Important note:

Important note

Unlike most other infrastructure-as-code tools, apply does not apply a previously generated plan. There is no persistent plan or state file — apply recomputes the diff from the current GitHub state and the config at runtime. This stateless design is intentional. While it might seem vulnerable to race conditions, applying an outdated plan would be even more problematic.

items.title: Load Org Config & Desired State
items.text:
This phase loads the desired state purely from configuration files.

  • Entry point:
    • GitHubOrganization.load_from_file() loads the org-specific config file
  • Model construction:
    • Configuration data is deserialized via from_model_data() (inherited from ModelObject)
    • Each model class recursively deserializes itself and nested resources by default, treating all members as optional nested objects
    • Override get_mapping_from_model() in individual model classes to customize deserialization (rare)
    • The Jsonnet configuration format is designed to align closely with the ModelObject structure
  • At this point:
    • No GitHub API calls have occurred
    • The in-memory model represents what GitHub should look like

items.title: Fetch from GitHub & Current State
items.text:
This phase loads the actual (live) state purely from GitHub.

  • Entry point:
    • GitHubOrganization.load_from_provider() is called with the organization name and a JsonnetConfig for defaults
    • Multiple independent tasks are launched concurrently to retrieve all organization data
  • Provider:
    • GitHubProvider (otterdog/providers/github/__init__.py) manages API interactions
    • Three sub-components query distinct APIs:
      • REST API (rest/) — classic GitHub REST endpoints
      • GraphQL API (graphql.py) — used for complex queries
      • Web UI (web.py) — for settings only available through the web interface
    • Provides get_* methods that return raw API responses (untyped dicts/lists)
  • Model construction:
    • Each model class deserializes itself and nested resources via from_provider_data() (inherited from ModelObject)
    • By default, recursively processes all class members as optional nested objects
    • Override get_mapping_from_provider() in individual model classes to customize (typically required)
  • Result:
    • A second in-memory model mirroring GitHub's current state
    • Same class structure, different data source

items.title: Diff & LivePatch Generation
items.text:
This is the core of Otterdog — where desired and live models are compared and converted into actionable patches.

  • Entry point:

    • DiffOperation.generate_diff() (otterdog/operations/diff_operation.py)

  • Patch generation:

    • Each model inherits generate_live_patch from ModelObject (otterdog/models/__init__.py)
    • Models can override this method for custom behavior; otherwise the inherited implementation applies
    • The inherited generate_live_patch method calls get_difference_from on the model to compare fields and produce Change objects:
      • Fields marked with model_only are excluded from diff computation
      • Custom filtering logic can be implemented by overriding include_field_for_diff_computation and is_key_valid_for_diff_computation methods
    • Differences are collected and stored in the changes field within the LivePatch object
    • Model classes serialize themselves to provider format via to_provider_data() (inherited from ModelObject)
    • By default, to_provider_data() recurses into all class members as optional nested objects; override get_mapping_to_provider in individual model classes to customize this behavior (typically required)

items.title: Plan: Display Diff
items.text:
The LivePatch operations are formatted and shown to the user.

  • Entry point: otterdog/operations/plan.py (PlanOperation class)
  • Responsibilities:
    • Format LivePatch operations into human-readable output
    • Show legends and summaries
    • Warn about read-only or ignored fields
    • Models contribute via __str__ and custom formatting

This is a rendering step only — no GitHub changes happen here. The user reviews the diff and decides whether to apply it.

items.title: Apply: Execute Changes
items.text:
The user approved the changes. Time to execute them against GitHub.

  • Entry point: otterdog/operations/apply.py (ApplyOperation class)
  • Execution flow:
    • For each LivePatch, invoke apply_live_patch() on the corresponding model object
    • Each model class implements apply_live_patch() to translate the patch into the correct GitHub API operations
    • Operations are executed via the provider (REST, GraphQL, or web UI as appropriate)

items.title: Coding & Style Guidelines
items.text: This document describes the coding and documentation style guidelines for contributing to Otterdog. Please follow these guidelines to ensure consistency across the codebase.

items.title: Documentation
items.text: Documentation is written in Markdown and built using Zensical, see Write docs.

items.title: Code documentation
items.text:
When contributing to otterdog, please make sure that all code is well documented. The following should be documented using properly formatted docstrings:

  • Modules
  • Class definitions
  • Function definitions
  • Module-level variables

Otterdog uses Google-style docstrings formatted according to PEP 257 guidelines. (See Example Google Style Python Docstrings for further examples.)

Where this is a conflict between Google-style docstrings and pydocstyle linting, follow the pydocstyle linting hints.

Class attributes and function arguments should be documented in the format "name: description." When applicable, a return type should be documented with just a description. Types are inferred from the signature.

class Foo:
    """A class docstring.

    Attributes:
        bar: A description of bar. Defaults to "bar".
    """

    bar: str = 'bar'

def bar(self, baz: int) -> str:
    """A function docstring.

    Args:
        baz: A description of `baz`.

    Returns:
        A description of the return value.
    """

    return 'bar'

You may include example code in docstrings. This code should be complete, self-contained, and runnable. Docstring examples are tested using doctest, so make sure they are correct and complete.

Class and instance attributes

Class attributes should be documented in the class docstring.

Instance attributes should be documented as "Args" in the __init__ docstring.

items.title: Contribution Workflow
items.text: This document describes the typical workflow for contributing to Otterdog.

items.title: Fork the repository
items.text:
Fork the repository on GitHub and clone your fork locally.

git clone https://github.com/<your username>/otterdog.git
cd otterdog

items.title: Add a git remote
items.text:
Add a remote and regularly sync to make sure you stay up-to-date with our repository:

git remote add upstream https://github.com/eclipse-csi/otterdog
git checkout main
git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main

items.title: Prepare development environment
items.text:
Install otterdog development Python dependencies 

make init

See Development Setup for more details.

items.title: Pre-commit hooks
items.text:
The project extensively uses pre-commit hooks to ensure consistent source code formatting and type checking. To enable pre-commit run the following:

poetry run prek install

items.title: Check out a new branch and make your changes
items.text:
Create a new branch for your changes.

# Checkout a new branch and make your changes
git checkout -b my-new-feature-branch
# Make your changes...

items.title: Run tests
items.text:
Run tests locally to make sure everything is working as expected.

# Run tests
make test

Note: Code coverage HTML is also available in htmlcov/

The end-to-end tests of the Playground of the dashboard, in tests/webapp/playground/, run in Firefox with Playwright. They are skipped unless the assets of the webapp are built and Firefox is installed, which make init does:

(cd otterdog/webapp/static && npm ci && npm run build)
poetry run pytest tests/webapp/playground

The scripts of the Playground also have unit tests, run with npm test in otterdog/webapp/static.

items.title: Write docs
items.text:
Otterdog docs are built with Zensical, check out its docs for specific Markdown flavors (admonitions, content tabs, code annotations, snippets).

Relevant sources are:

  • docs/: Site contents
  • zensical.toml: Site config (navigation, theme, Markdown extensions)
  • docs-theme/ and docs/assets/theme.css: Theme overrides (Eclipse colors, hero of the home page)
  • docs_site.py: Staging of the site for Zensical (playground links, settings from the environment)
  • .github/workflows/docs.yml: Build and preview of every pull request, deployment of main to GitHub Pages
  • .github/workflows/docs-preview.yml: Removal of the preview of a pull request when it is closed

Please always review your changes locally (some things render differently, than you might be used from GitHub):

make docs-serve              # live preview on http://127.0.0.1:8000/
make docs                    # strict build into site/, broken links and anchors fail

Every pull request that changes the documentation is built strictly. When it comes from a branch of the repository, its preview is published at https://csi.eclipse.dev/otterdog-website-preview/pr-preview/pr-<number>/, and a comment on the pull request links it. The pull requests from forks are built without a preview: they have no access to the token that publishes it.

Complete jsonnet examples, i.e. examples that define an organization with orgs.newOrg without omitting content with ... or using placeholders like <github-id>, get a link that opens them in the Playground of an otterdog dashboard. The link is added by docs_playground.py when docs_site.py stages the site, the url of the dashboard is set by the environment variable OTTERDOG_URL (https://otterdog.eclipse.org by default, an empty value omits the links):

OTTERDOG_URL=https://otterdog.example.org make docs-serve

To target the webapp of your development environment, use make docs-serve-dev, make docs-serve-tunnel or make docs-serve-ngrok, see Test the Playground with the documentation.

The jsonnet examples of the Configuration Guides must be complete: the test tests/test_docs_examples.py validates each of them against the example default configuration.

The Playground of the dashboard lists these examples from a catalog generated from the guides, and describes the properties that it completes from a catalog generated from the Reference, i.e. from the property tables of its pages and from their "Jsonnet Function" sections. After changing an example or the reference, update both catalogs, otherwise tests/test_docs_playground.py fails:

make playground-examples

items.title: Commit and push your changes
items.text:
Commit your changes, push your branch to GitHub, and create a pull request.

Please follow the pull request template and fill in as much information as possible. Link to any relevant issues and include a description of your changes.

When your pull request is ready for review, add a comment with the message "please review" and we'll take a look as soon as we can.

items.title: Pull Requests
items.text:
It should be extremely simple to get started and create a Pull Request.

Unless your change is trivial (typo, docs tweak etc.), please create an issue to discuss the change before creating a pull request.

If you're looking for something to get your teeth into, check out the "help wanted" label on GitHub.

To make contributing as easy and fast as possible, you'll want to run tests and linting locally. Luckily, Otterdog has few dependencies, doesn't require compiling and tests don't need access to databases, etc. Because of this, setting up and running the tests should be very simple.

items.title: Development Setup
items.text: This document describes how to set up a development environment for Otterdog.

items.title: Basic prerequisite tools
items.text:
• Any Python version >= 3.11
  • git
  • make
  • poetry >= 2

Verify that you have Make installed We use Make to run, build, update docs, tests, formatting, etc. Verify that you have Make installed in your environment.

make --version
If you do not have Make installed, consult your operating system documentation on how to install make.

Install poetry (preferred using pipx)

pipx install poetry

or alternatively

curl -sSL https://install.python-poetry.org | python3 -

items.title: [Optional] Otterdog WebApp development prerequisites
items.text:
• Docker Engine (including Docker Compose)
  • Minikube
  • Helm
  • Skaffold

Why Docker?

Docker simplifies development environment set up.

Install Docker Engine

Why Minikube?

Minikube will provide a local kubernetes cluster and using Otterdog from helm charts

Install Minikkube

Why helm?

Helm will deploy otterdog, dependency-track and ghproxy in the minikube cluster.

Install Helm

Why Skaffold?

Skaffold will build, deploy and watch your development environment, including the infrastructure services redis, mongodb and ghproxy.

Install Skaffold

items.title: Release Process
items.text:
The release process is performed by committers following these steps:

  1. Update CHANGELOG.md: Create a PR updating the CHANGELOG.md file

    • Ensure all changes are documented

      Note

      • If new features are added: bump the semver minor version (e.g., 1.2.0 → 1.3.0)
      • If breaking compatibility changes are introduced: bump the semver major version (e.g., 1.2.0 → 2.0.0)
      • For bug fixes only: bump the patch version (e.g., 1.2.0 → 1.2.1)

    • Add the release date to the version that is currently marked as unreleased

    • [Optional] Add the new unreleased version

  2. Create and Push Tag:

    • Create a new tag (signing is recommended): 
      git tag -s v1.2.3 -m "Release version 1.2.3"
    • Push the tag to the repository: 
      git push origin v1.2.3

items.title: Testing
items.text: This document describes how to run tests for Otterdog. You should set up your development environment as described in the Development Setup guide before running tests.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• Skaffold
  • tailscale or ngrok (either can expose the dev environment for GitHub Webhooks, see below)
  • minikube
  • k9s

items.title: [Optional] Creating an Organization for development
items.text:
On your profile, create an organization

  • Organization name: otterdog-<github username> (Ex: otterdog-foobar)
  • Contact email: your@email
  • This organization belongs to: My personal account

Accept the Terms of Service (if you agree)

items.title: Fork otterdog
items.text:
Fork otterdog in your own organization. This will act as a base for modifications and contributions to the project, and will serve as the URL for the otterdog config base_template.

https://github.com/<Github Username>/otterdog

items.title: Create a user token
items.text:
Create a Personal Access Token with sufficient permissions to access the organization API.

The GitHub API token needs to have the following scopes enabled: repo, workflow, admin:org, admin:org_hook, delete_repo.

For more about credentials, see Credentials.

items.title: Credentials provider configuration
items.text:
For the purpose of this testing section, we use GitHub environment variables, but third-party providers are also supported, such as pass or bitwarden.

Add these environment variables at the GitHub org level: https://github.com/organizations/otterdog-/settings/secrets/actions/new: * OTTER_USERNAME * OTTER_PASSWORD * OTTER_TOTP_SEED * OTTER_API_TOKEN (token previously created)

NOTE: 2FA must be activated on your account.

For other credential providers, see Credentials.

items.title: Configure your otterdog (source code) to work with your development organization
items.text:
Create a new repository named otterdog-config and set up the otterdog configuration: Otterdog configuration

Go to your organization https://github.com/otterdog-<github username> > Repositories > New repository

  • Repository name: otterdog-config

Click on Create repository.

Then create the file otterdog.json in this repository with all the required settings.

{
    "defaults": {
        "jsonnet": {
            "base_template": "https://github.com/<Github Username>/otterdog#otterdog/resources/defaults/otterdog-defaults.libsonnet@main",
            "config_dir": "orgs"
        }
    },
    "organizations": [
        {
            "name": "otterdog-<Github Username>",
            "github_id": "otterdog-<Github Username>",
            "credentials": {
                "provider": "env",
                "api_token": "OTTER_API_TOKEN",
                "username": "OTTER_USERNAME",
                "password": "OTTER_PASSWORD",
                "twofa_seed": "OTTER_TOTP_SEED"
            }
        }
    ]
}

items.title: [Optional] Set up Otterdog GitHub org configuration repository
items.text:
Go to your organization https://github.com/otterdog-<github username> > Repositories > New repository

  • Repository name: .otterdog

Click on Create repository.

If the name differs from .otterdog, edit your configuration and include:

    "github": {
      "config_repo": ".<your_otterdog_github_config_repo>"
    },

items.title: [Optional] Otterdog WebApp development environment
items.text:
To run the otterdog webapp (without integration with GitHub)

Make sure you have the eclipse-csi Helm chart repository added:

helm repo add eclipse-csi https://eclipse-csi.github.io/helm-charts

make dev-webapp

Note

The make dev-webapp* targets deploy to the current kubectl context. They stop with an error if this context is not minikube, e.g. after working with another cluster, to prevent deploying the development environment to it. Switch back with kubectl config use-context minikube, or check the context with make check-kube-context.

If you want use the integration with GitHub, you can use tailscale or ngrok to expose your development environment. Pick one:

  • Setup a tailscale tunnel
  • Setup an ngrok tunnel (alternative to tailscale)

items.title: Setup a tailscale to enable GitHub Webhooks to your development environment
items.text:
1. Sign up/Login to tail tailscale

  2. Go to tailscale admin console

We use tailscale on Kubernetes (minikube), configuring it:

  1. Go to tailscale admin console -> ACL

    Include or update the tagOwners

        "tagOwners": {
        "tag:k8s-operator": [],
        "tag:k8s":          ["tag:k8s-operator"],
    },

    Add tag:k8s to the nodeAttrs:

    "nodeAttrs": [
    {

        "target": ["autogroup:member", "tag:k8s"],
        "attr":   ["funnel"],
    },
    {
        "target": ["tag:k8s"], // tag that Tailscale Operator uses to tag proxies; defaults to 'tag:k8s'
        "attr":   ["funnel"],
    },
],

  2. Create an OAuth in Settings > OAuth clients (https://login.tailscale.com/admin/settings/oauth)

    Create an OAuth client in the OAuth clients page of the admin console. Create the client with Devices Core and Auth Keys write scopes, and the tag tag:k8s-operator.

    This is well described in the official doc

    Your new OAuth client's Client ID and Client Secret will be displayed—copy these values now as you'll need them in the next step.

  3. Save your tailscale DNS

    It might look like tail<some hash>.ts.net

  4. Export them in your terminal

    export TS_CLIENT_ID=<client id>
export TS_CLIENT_SECRET=<client secret>
export TS_DNS=tail<some hash>.ts.net

    NOTE: If you close the terminal, you will need to re-export these values.

  5. Test secrets

export TS_ACCESS_TOKEN="$(
  curl -sS \
    -d "client_id=${TS_CLIENT_ID}" \
    -d "client_secret=${TS_CLIENT_SECRET}" \
    "https://api.tailscale.com/api/v2/oauth/token" \
  | jq -r '.access_token'
)"

echo "$TS_ACCESS_TOKEN"

curl -sS \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${TS_ACCESS_TOKEN}" \
  "https://api.tailscale.com/api/v2/tailnet/-/devices" \
| jq .
  1. Enabling HTTPS

Official documentation: https://tailscale.com/docs/how-to/set-up-https-certificates

Go to the dns configuration page: https://login.tailscale.com/admin/dns

HTTPS Certificates -> Click Enable HTTPS...

items.title: Create a tailscale GitHub App
items.text:
NOTES:

  • Replace <OTTERDOG-WEBAPP> by your tail<some hash>.ts.net (tailscale) or otterdog.<your reserved domain> (ngrok)
  • You can always double check the URL at https://login.tailscale.com/admin/machines as multiple instances of your development environment can generate otterdog-1, otterdog-2 ...

It is required if you are the integration with GitHub (Create a GitHub app)

  1. Go to your organization https://github.com/organizations/<ORG>
  2. Click Settings.
  3. In the left sidebar, select <> Developer settings
  4. Click GitHub Apps
  5. New GitHub App

Basic Information

  • Add GitHub App name: <choose a name>
  • Homepage URL: <OTTERDOG-WEBAPP>

Webhook

  • [X] Active
  • Webhook url: <OTTERDOG-WEBAPP>/github-webhook/receive
  • Secret: Choose the secret

Add the following permissions and events:

Repository Permissions

Permission Access Level Actions Read & Write Administration Read & Write Codespaces secrets Read & Write Commit statuses Read & Write Contents Read & Write Custom properties Read & Write Dependabot secrets Read & Write Environments Read & Write Issues Read only Metadata Read only Pages Read & Write Pull requests Read & Write Secrets Read & Write Variables Read & Write Webhooks Read & Write Workflows Read & Write

Organization Permissions

Permission Access Level Administration Read & Write Custom Organization Roles Read & Write Custom properties Admin Members Read only Organization codespaces secrets Read & Write Organization dependabot secrets Read & Write Plan Read only Secrets Read & Write Variables Read & Write Webhooks Read & Write

The permissions for Codespaces and Dependabot secrets are only used when the default configuration defines the functions that create these secrets, see Dependabot and Codespaces secrets.

Events

Event Issue comment Pull request Pull request review Push Workflow job Workflow run

Note

When permissions are added to an existing GitHub App, each installation keeps its previous permissions until an organization owner accepts the new ones in the organization settings (Settings > GitHub Apps > Configure > Review request).

The otterdog app should appear in the organization settings > Third-party Access > GitHub Apps: https://github.com/organizations/otterdog-/settings/apps

items.title: Install the GitHub App in the organization
items.text:
Once the app is created, you need to install it in your organization:

https://github.com/organizations/otterdog-/settings/apps/otterdog--org-app/installations

Click Install next to your organization and grant the required permissions.

items.title: Configure the values.yaml to setup your otterdog webapp
items.text:
This file must be set at the root level of your otterdog fork project.

config:
  configOwner: "otterdog-<github username>"  # GitHub organization hosting the otterdog.json
  configToken: ""  # GitHub token — no specific permissions required, used only for rate-limiting
  dependencyTrackToken: ""  # Dependency Track API token

github:
  webhookSecret: ""  # webhook secret as configured for the GitHub App
  appId: ""  # The App ID created in GitHub
  appPrivateKey: ""  # TApp private key

NOTE: In the dev configuration, the Otterdog webapp uses the following repositories by default:

config:
  configRepo: "otterdog-configs"
  configPath: "otterdog.json"

You can override these defaults in values.yaml

It is recommended to create the repository otterdog-configs and add the otterdog.json file.

Example of otterdog.json

{
    "defaults": {
        "jsonnet": {
            "base_template": "https://github.com/<GitHub Username>/otterdog#otterdog/resources/defaults/otterdog-defaults.libsonnet@main",
            "config_dir": "orgs"
        }
    },
    "github": {
        "config_repo": ".otterdog"
    },
    "organizations": [
        {
            "name": "otterdog-<GitHub Username>",
            "github_id": "otterdog-<GitHub Username>"
        }
    ]
}

items.title: Run otterdog with tailscale
items.text:
Make sure you have the eclipse-csi, tailscale, and dependency-track Helm chart repositories added:

helm repo add dependency-track https://dependencytrack.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo add eclipse-csi https://eclipse-csi.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo add tailscale https://pkgs.tailscale.com/helmcharts

Start the otterdog webapp with the tailscale tunnel:

make dev-webapp-tunnel

You can verify the machine is registered at https://login.tailscale.com/admin/machines.

The Otterdog WebApp is reachable at https://otterdog.tail<some hash>.ts.net

Trigger the Otterdog initialization:

curl https://otterdog.tail<some hash>.ts.net/internal/init

Dependency Track is reachable at https://sbom.tail<some hash>.ts.net (it still needs to be configured — see below)

items.title: Setup ngrok to enable GitHub Webhooks to your development environment
items.text:
Alternative to the tailscale tunnel above.

  1. Sign up/Login to ngrok

  2. Go to the ngrok dashboard

We use the ngrok Kubernetes Operator (minikube), configuring it:

  1. Get your API Key from https://dashboard.ngrok.com/api and your Authtoken from https://dashboard.ngrok.com/get-started/your-authtoken

  2. Reserve a domain in https://dashboard.ngrok.com/domains

    NOTE: Free ngrok domains (e.g. <something>.ngrok-free.dev/.ngrok-free.app) do not support subdomains — only a custom domain you own, with wildcard DNS delegated to ngrok on a paid plan, does (see ngrok custom domains). NGROK_DOMAIN below is therefore used as-is (no otterdog. prefix) for the Otterdog webapp. Dependency Track is not exposed via ngrok in this dev setup — access it with kubectl port-forward instead (see [Optional] Configure dependency track below).

  3. Export them in your terminal

    export NGROK_API_KEY=<api key>
export NGROK_AUTHTOKEN=<authtoken>
export NGROK_DOMAIN=<your reserved domain>

    NOTE: If you close the terminal, you will need to re-export these values.

items.title: Run otterdog with ngrok
items.text:
Alternative to #### Run otterdog with tailscale above.

Make sure you have the eclipse-csi, ngrok, and dependency-track Helm chart repositories added:

helm repo add dependency-track https://dependencytrack.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo add eclipse-csi https://eclipse-csi.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo add ngrok https://charts.ngrok.com

Start the otterdog webapp with the ngrok tunnel:

make dev-webapp-ngrok

The Otterdog WebApp is reachable at https://<your reserved domain>

Trigger the Otterdog initialization:

curl https://<your reserved domain>/internal/init

Dependency Track is not exposed via ngrok; reach it with:

kubectl port-forward -n otterdog svc/dependency-track-frontend 8080:8080

then open http://localhost:8080 (it still needs to be configured — see below)

items.title: Verify webhook delivery
items.text:
Once the service is running and the GitHub App is installed in your organization, verify that webhooks are correctly reaching the backend by sending a ping event from the app's advanced settings:

https://github.com/organizations/otterdog-/settings/apps/otterdog--org-app/advanced

Click Redeliver on the most recent ping delivery to trigger a test event. Check the otterdog backend logs to confirm the ping was received:

[2026-07-01 09:30:22.093  ] [9] [INFO] ping (3d5b7472-7522-11f1-9353-7f66c710a3db)

items.title: [Optional] Test the Playground with the documentation
items.text:
The Playground of the webapp is available at /playground, it lists the examples of the Configuration Guides next to the editor. It evaluates them with the default configuration of the instance, or with the example template of otterdog (otterdog/resources/defaults, /playground?template=example) which the examples are validated with. Complete examples of the documentation link to it with the example preloaded and the example template selected. To make these links target your development environment, serve the documentation with the target that matches the way you started the webapp, in a second terminal:

Webapp started with Documentation served with Playground links target make dev-webapp make docs-serve-dev $OTTERDOG_DEV_URL, http://localhost:5000 by default make dev-webapp-tunnel, make dev-webapp-tunnel-local make docs-serve-tunnel https://otterdog.$TS_DNS make dev-webapp-ngrok, make dev-webapp-ngrok-local make docs-serve-ngrok https://$NGROK_DOMAIN

The webapp started with make dev-webapp is not exposed, forward its port first:

kubectl port-forward -n otterdog deploy/otterdog 5000:5000

Then open the documentation at http://127.0.0.1:8000, e.g. the Configuration Guides, and follow the "Open in the Playground" link below an example.

The webapp started with any make dev-webapp* target links the examples of its Playground to the documentation served with make docs-serve*, at http://127.0.0.1:8000/ by default. Both take this address from the variable DOCS_DEV_ADDR of the Makefile, set it for both to serve the documentation on another port, e.g.:

make dev-webapp-ngrok DOCS_DEV_ADDR=127.0.0.1:8001
make docs-serve-ngrok DOCS_DEV_ADDR=127.0.0.1:8001

The webapp gets this address as value config.documentationUrl of the Helm chart (environment variable DOCUMENTATION_URL), supported from version 1.6.0 of the chart: with an earlier chart, use the -local targets, which deploy the chart of a helm-charts checkout. Outside of development, the Playground links to https://csi.eclipse.dev/otterdog/ unless config.documentationUrl is set.

The Playground of a project starts with the current configuration of its organization, once the webapp fetched it again, e.g. after calling /internal/init. Its button "Propose on GitHub" validates the modified configuration with otterdog, asking to confirm if it has errors, then copies it and opens it in the editor of GitHub, where the user creates the pull request from their own account. It opens the editor on the default branch of the configuration repository, which is also known once the configuration has been fetched again.

items.title: [Optional] Configure dependency track
items.text:
1. Access https://sbom.tail<some hash>.ts.net (tailscale) or http://localhost:8080 via kubectl port-forward (ngrok, see above) — default DependencyTrack credentials (First time will ask to change password and re-login)

  2. To generate the dependencyTrackToken, go to Administration > Access Management > Teams

  3. Create a Team or choose one (i.e. Automation) create and API Key.

  4. Use this API Key as dependencyTrackToken in values.yaml

It will reload automatically.

items.title: Test otterdog client
items.text: This section walks through basic end-to-end testing of the otterdog CLI against your development organization.

items.title: 1. Test GitHub web access
items.text:
Export your credentials and set the path to your local otterdog configuration project, then verify that web-based login works:

export OTTER_API_TOKEN=...
export OTTER_USERNAME=...
export OTTER_PASSWORD=...
export OTTER_TOTP_SEED=...

export OTTERDOG_CONFIG_ROOT="/path/to/your/otterdog-config"

otterdog web-login otterdog-<GitHub Username>

NOTE: These environment variables must be re-exported in every new terminal session.

items.title: 2. Import and push the organization configuration
items.text:
Import the current state of your GitHub organization and push the generated configuration to the .otterdog repository:

otterdog import otterdog-<GitHub Username>
otterdog push-config

This creates the initial jsonnet configuration file under orgs/otterdog-<GitHub Username>/ in your config project.

items.title: 3. Fetch the remote configuration
items.text:
Fetch the configuration stored in the remote .otterdog repository to ensure it is in sync with your local state:

otterdog fetch-config otterdog-<GitHub Username>

items.title: 4. Create a test repository
items.text:
Edit the organization jsonnet configuration file:

/path/to/your/otterdog-config/orgs/otterdog-<GitHub Username>/otterdog-<GitHub Username>.jsonnet

Add a new repository entry:

orgs.newRepo('test-repo') {
  description: "OtterDog test repository",
},

If the file contains org-level settings that conflict with the defaults (e.g. settings already defined in otterdog-defaults.libsonnet), remove the duplicates. For example, the following block can be trimmed down to only the settings you want to override:

orgs.newOrg('otterdog-<GitHub Username>', 'otterdog-<GitHub Username>') {
  settings+: {
    members_can_change_repo_visibility: true,
    members_can_create_private_pages: true,
    members_can_create_private_repositories: true,
    members_can_create_public_repositories: true,
    members_can_create_teams: true,
    members_can_delete_repositories: true,
  },

Apply the changes to GitHub:

otterdog apply otterdog-<GitHub Username>
otterdog push-config otterdog-<GitHub Username>

items.title: Test otterdog PR
items.text:
Clone the .otterdog repository:

git clone https://github.com/otterdog-<GitHub Username>/.otterdog

Change description of test-repo:

Edit the organization jsonnet configuration file:

/path/to/your/otterdog-config/orgs/otterdog-<GitHub Username>/otterdog-<GitHub Username>.jsonnet

Change repo-test description:

orgs.newRepo('test-repo') {
  description: "OtterDog test repository from PR",
},

Create a specific branch and commit the modification:

git checkout -b "feat/repo_desc"
git add .
git commit -s -m "feat: change repo-test description"
git push origin "feat/repo_desc"

Then open a PR from this branch: https://github.com/otterdog-<GitHub Username>/.otterdog/pull/new/feat/repo_desc

items.title: Operating Otterdog
items.text: This section is intended for infrastructure maintainers who set up, configure, and operate Otterdog in CI or automation. Most contributors and organization users can safely skip this section.

items.title: Install
items.text: Otterdog requires Python 3.11+ to run.

items.title: System requirements
items.text: A few system dependencies are required to be installed:

items.title: Mandatory system dependencies
items.text:
• python 3.11+: Python 3 + pip + pipx
apt install python3 python3-pip pipx
  • poetry: Python package manager
pipx install poetry>=2.0.1
  • git: popular distributed version control system
apt install git

items.title: Optional system dependencies
items.text:
Depending on the type of credential system you are using, install one of the following tools:

  • bitwarden cli: command line tools to access a bitwarden vault.
snap install bw
  • password manager: lightweight directory-based password manager.
apt install pass

items.title: Build instructions
items.text:
After installing the required system dependencies, a virtual python environment needs to be setup and populated with all python dependencies:

$ make init

You should be set to finally run otterdog:

$ ./otterdog.sh --version

Additionally, make init creates a symlink called otterdog in ~/.local/bin, so you can also run it like that:

$ otterdog --version

items.title: Shell integration
items.text:
To enable shell completion, add the following snippet to your shell configuration file (~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc):

bashzsh 
eval "$(_OTTERDOG_COMPLETE=bash_source otterdog)"

eval "$(_OTTERDOG_COMPLETE=zsh_source otterdog)"

When running otterdog in a directory that contains a otterdog.json file, shell completion will be able to suggest organizations found in the otterdog.json file.

items.title: Otterdog WebApp
items.text:
Otterdog WebApp is available as a container image, with releases published to the GitHub Container Registry (GHCR).

For Kubernetes environments, we also provide Helm charts to simplify deployment and configuration.

This guide covers how to deploy the Otterdog WebApp using Helm charts.

items.title: System Requirements
items.text:
Make sure the following requirements are met before deployment:

  • A running Kubernetes cluster
  • Helm installed

items.title: Create a GitHub App
items.text:
It is required if you are the integration with GitHub (Create a GitHub app)

  1. Go to your organization https://github.com/organizations/<ORG>
  2. Click Settings.
  3. In the left sidebar, select <> Developer settings
  4. Click GitHub Apps
  5. New GitHub App

Basic Information

  • Add GitHub App name: <choose a name>
  • Homepage URL: <OTTERDOG-WEBAPP>

Webhook

  • [X] Active
  • Webhook url: <OTTERDOG-WEBAPP>/github-webhook/receive
  • Secret: Choose the secret

Add the following permissions and events:

Repository Permissions

Permission Access Level Actions Read & Write Administration Read & Write Codespaces secrets Read & Write Commit statuses Read & Write Contents Read & Write Custom properties Read & Write Dependabot secrets Read & Write Environments Read & Write Issues Read only Metadata Read only Pages Read & Write Pull requests Read & Write Secrets Read & Write Variables Read & Write Webhooks Read & Write Workflows Read & Write

Organization Permissions

Permission Access Level Administration Read & Write Custom Organization Roles Read & Write Custom properties Admin Members Read only Organization codespaces secrets Read & Write Organization dependabot secrets Read & Write Plan Read only Secrets Read & Write Variables Read & Write Webhooks Read & Write

The permissions for Codespaces and Dependabot secrets are only used when the default configuration defines the functions that create these secrets, see Dependabot and Codespaces secrets.

Events

Event Issue comment Pull request Pull request review Push Workflow job Workflow run

Note

When permissions are added to an existing GitHub App, each installation keeps its previous permissions until an organization owner accepts the new ones in the organization settings (Settings > GitHub Apps > Configure > Review request).

items.title: Step 1: Planning the deployment
items.text:
Before deploying Otterdog, ensure you have the following dependencies ready:

MongoDB: Otterdog requires MongoDB for data persistence. You'll need to deploy MongoDB and have its connection string ready.

Redis or Valkey: Required for caching and message queuing.

  • Important: Valkey/Redis must be configured without authentication as this is not currently supported by GHProxy (included in the Otterdog Helm Charts).

Access controls:

Internal Endpoints Access Control: Otterdog exposes internal management endpoints at https://<address>/internal/.

  • These endpoints should be restricted to Otterdog management only.

  • This can be achieved through ingress configuration using annotations.

    Example:

    ingress:
 annotations:
   nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/configuration-snippet: |
     location ~* ^/internal/ {
       # Allow only specific IP ranges for management access
       allow 192.168.0.0/16;      # Private network example
       deny all;
     }

items.title: Step 2: Add the Helm Repository
items.text:
helm repo add eclipse-csi https://eclipse-csi.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update

items.title: Step 3: Prepare Configuration
items.text:
Create a values.yaml file to define your deployment configuration:

This is an example

config:
  configOwner: "<ORGANIZATION>"
  configToken: "<GITHUB TOKEN>"
  configRepo: "otterdog-configs"
  configPath: "otterdog.json"
  dependencyTrackUrl: "https://otterdog-dt.default.svc.cluster"
  dependencyTrackToken: "faketoken"

github:
  webhookSecret: "<WEBHOOK SECRET>"
  appId: "<GITHUB APP ID>"
  appPrivateKey: "<GITHUB APP PRIVATE KEY>"
  webhookValidationContext: "otterdog/otterdog-validation"
  webhookSyncContext: "otterdog/otterdog-sync"

items.title: Step 4: Install Otterdog WebApp
items.text: helm install eclipse-csi otterdog -f values.yaml

items.title: Step 5: Verify the Deployment
items.text:
Use the following commands to verify that the WebApp is running:

kubectl get pods
kubectl get svc
kubectl get ingress

items.title: Init Otterdog
items.text:
After deployment, Otterdog initializes itself automatically with a helm hook, but this can also be done manually by calling the initialization endpoint::

curl https://<your-otterdog-address>/internal/init

This initialization will: - Fetch the Otterdog configuration from the GitHub repository - Sync the current state from GitHub - Set up the initial data structures in MongoDB - Refresh, in the background, the per organization pull request digests backing the statistics

Note

Refreshing the pull request digests queries GitHub once per organization, so a deployment with many organizations makes the initialization consume a noticeable part of the GitHub rate limit. The refresh stops on its own once the remaining quota gets low, and the statistics then report the organizations it could not read.

The digests are cached in Redis for PULL_REQUEST_STATISTICS_CACHE_TTL seconds, one day by default. Calling /internal/init daily keeps the statistics fresh without anybody ever waiting for GitHub while browsing them.

Note

The initialization refreshes the configuration, pull requests, policies and blueprints of every organization in background tasks. At most MAX_CONCURRENT_INSTALLATION_TASKS of these tasks, 10 by default, run concurrently to bound the memory usage of the webapp and the load on GitHub, so the initialization of a deployment with many organizations takes a while.

The limit applies to each worker process of the webapp, 4 by default, set by the HYPERCORN_WORKERS environment variable. An initialization is handled by a single worker, but refreshes triggered at the same time in different workers, e.g. an initialization and a push to the otterdog configuration repository, run up to this many tasks each.

items.title: Validation in the Playground
items.text:
The Validate button of the Playground posts the evaluated configuration of an organization to /playground/validate and /projects/<project>/playground/validate, which validate it with otterdog, see Validation in the Playground. Like the Playground, these endpoints are public. They neither call GitHub nor store or apply the configuration, but each validation prepares the default configuration and validates the posted one, which takes up to a second for a large organization. They are bounded by two settings:

  • PLAYGROUND_VALIDATION_MAX_SIZE: the maximum size in bytes of a posted configuration, 5 MB by default, a larger one being rejected with the status 413. The evaluated configuration of an organization with 300 repositories takes about 800 KB.
  • PLAYGROUND_MAX_CONCURRENT_VALIDATIONS: the maximum number of validations running concurrently in each worker process of the webapp, 4 by default, the other ones being rejected at once with the status 503.

Note

These settings bound the work of each worker process, not the number of requests of a client. To limit the requests of a client, configure a rate limit for these paths in the ingress or the reverse proxy in front of the webapp.

items.title: Updating the Deployment
items.text:
To upgrade to the latest chart or image version:

helm repo update
helm upgrade eclipse-csi otterdog -f values.yaml

Note

It requires to init Otterdog to sync the PRs

curl https://<your-otterdog-address>/internal/init

items.title: Uninstalling Otterdog
items.text:
To remove the WebApp from your cluster:

helm uninstall otterdog
