items.title: Organization-wide policies
items.text:
This page is intended for administrators who maintain the default configuration and the otterdog setup for several organizations. For the configuration of a single organization, see the Configuration Guides.

Otterdog offers several mechanisms to establish common rules across organizations. They differ in whether an organization can deviate from them:

Mechanism Effect Deviation by an organization Default configuration provides the inherited value of every property override the property in the configuration Validation scripts reject configurations that do not comply not possible, unless the script allows it Blueprints open pull requests that add missing configuration or files close the pull request, which dismisses the blueprint Policies enforce a behavior, e.g. cancel workflow jobs on certain runners only with a policy of the same type on organization level

items.title: The default configuration as baseline
items.text:
The default configuration, referenced by base_template in otterdog.json, provides the inherited value of every property and defines which settings and resources otterdog manages, see Inherited and explicit values.

  • Keep the default configuration in its own repository, protect it like code and publish released versions, e.g. as tags, which base_template references.
  • Before releasing a new version, run plan for the affected organizations: every changed default applies to all resources that do not override it.
  • Adding a setting or a resource type to the default configuration makes otterdog manage it for every organization, e.g. defining team_permissions for repositories makes the team permissions of all repositories authoritative.

items.title: Enforce settings with validation scripts
items.text:
The directory of the default configuration, i.e. the root of the repository referenced by base_template, can contain Python scripts that otterdog executes during validation:

Script Executed for Available variables validate-org-settings.py the organization settings self: the organization settings, context: the validation context validate-team.py every team self: the team, context: the validation context

context.property_equals(self, '<key>', <value>) reports an error if a property does not have the required value, context.add_failure(...) reports any other failure. For example, the following validate-org-settings.py requires that members get no access to repositories by default and that two-factor authentication is required:

context.property_equals(self, "default_repository_permission", "none")
context.property_equals(self, "two_factor_requirement", True)

Similarly, scripts can run when apply creates resources:

Script Executed Available variables pre-add-object-hook.py before each resource is created model_object: the resource, org_config, self: the operation post-add-objects-hook.py after all resources have been created patches: the applied additions, org_config, self: the operation

Warning

These scripts are executed as Python code by otterdog, with the permissions and credentials of the process that runs it. Anybody who can change the default configuration can therefore run code in this context. Restrict and review changes to the repository of the default configuration accordingly, and reference a tag or a commit SHA in base_template: a branch is pulled on every run, so every push to it takes effect immediately, and otterdog logs a warning for it. See also the threat model.

items.title: Teams managed by another tool
items.text:
When teams are created and maintained by another tool, e.g. a synchronization with an identity provider, exclude them from otterdog with regular expressions that are matched against the team slugs:

{
  "defaults": {
    "github": {
      "exclude_teams": [
        ".*-committers",
        "^sync-.*"
      ]
    }
  }
}

Excluded teams are not imported, and defining them in the configuration of an organization is reported as error, unless they are defined by the default configuration. Their permissions on repositories are ignored as well, unless a repository lists the team in team_permissions, see Teams and access.

The repository that holds the configuration of each organization is set with config_repo in the same github section, .otterdog by default. It is used by the fetch-config and push-config operations.

items.title: Exceptions
items.text:
Common rules need exceptions from time to time. Make them visible and reviewable:

  • document the reason of an override in the configuration of the organization with a comment
  • require a review by the team that owns the rule for such changes, e.g. with a CODEOWNERS file in the configuration repository
  • if a validation script enforces the rule, keep the list of exceptions in the script, so that it is reviewed centrally
orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  settings+: {
    // Exception to the organization-wide default: the project publishes its documentation
    // from private repositories, which requires read access for all members.
    default_repository_permission: "read",
  },
}

Open in the Playground

items.title: Cost-related changes
items.text: Changes that may incur costs, e.g. a larger GitHub Actions cache, can require a review by a designated team, see Cost policy.

items.title: Environments managed by another tool
items.text:
Repository environments that are created and maintained by another tool can be excluded from otterdog with regular expressions that are matched against the environment names:

{
  "defaults": {
    "github": {
      "exclude_environments": [
        "^copilot$",
        "^external-.*"
      ]
    }
  }
}

Each pattern is matched independently from the start of the name, use ^name$ to match a single environment exactly.

Excluded environments, including their secrets and variables, are ignored when reading the live state of a repository, so they are not reported as differences and otterdog never deletes them.

items.title: Managing an excluded environment
items.text:
To manage an excluded environment, declare it in the configuration of the repository:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      environments+: [
        orgs.newEnvironment('external-prod') {
          deployment_branch_policy: "selected",
          branch_policies+: [
            "main",
          ],
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

The same applies to environments created automatically by GitHub, e.g. copilot, which GitHub creates for the Copilot coding agent. To manage its settings, declare it explicitly:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      environments+: [
        // created automatically by GitHub, only declared to manage its settings
        orgs.newEnvironment('copilot') {
          deployment_branch_policy: "all",
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

A declared environment is managed like any other, even if its name matches a pattern: it is compared with the live state, changed if it differs and created if it does not exist. If the declaration is removed again, the environment is ignored again and remains on GitHub unmanaged.

Note

Otterdog never deletes an environment that matches an exclusion pattern, not even after its declaration has been removed from the configuration. If such an environment is no longer needed, delete it by other means, e.g. in the repository settings on GitHub or via the GitHub API.

Note

The import operation has no configuration to compare against and therefore always skips excluded environments. When importing into an existing configuration, add the declarations of excluded environments you want to manage again afterwards.

items.title: Setup Otterdog
items.text:
After completing the installation of Otterdog, you need to perform some additional steps to configure otterdog.

To start using the cli part of otterdog right away on a specific organization you have to set up the following:

  • define a default configuration to use, or use the following default config right away
  • create a otterdog.json file that contains a list of GitHub organizations to manager and their respective credentials
  • start managing your organizations using the cli

items.title: Default configuration
items.text:
The example default config has all supported features enabled and can be used right away. However, reference a released tag or a commit SHA instead of main in base_template, the ref after @ in the example below, to avoid incompatibilities and unreviewed changes. A branch is pulled on every run: every push to it changes the inherited values of your organizations and the validation scripts that otterdog executes with your credentials. Otterdog logs a warning when base_template references a branch.

A change of the default configuration applies to all the organizations using it. Its impact can be evaluated beforehand on the Template impact page of the administration of the otterdog dashboard: the files of the default configuration are edited there, and the configurations of the projects are evaluated with the edited files. The page groups the changes by property across the projects, e.g. repositories[*].delete_branch_on_merge changed from true to false in 807 repositories of 269 projects, and lists the projects whose configuration changes, with their changes, and the ones whose configuration fails to evaluate. The configurations are the ones fetched by the dashboard, and are evaluated in the browser.

items.title: Otterdog configuration
items.text:
Create a otterdog.json file with the following content (replace bracketed values according to your setup):

{
  "defaults": {
    "jsonnet": {
      "base_template": "https://github.com/eclipse-csi/otterdog#otterdog/resources/defaults/otterdog-defaults.libsonnet@main",
      "config_dir": "orgs"
    }
  },
  "organizations": [
    {
      "name": "<project-name>",
      "github_id": "<github-id>",
      "credentials": {
        "provider": "plain",
        "api_token": "<GitHub PAT>",
        "username": "<Username>",
        "password": "<Password>",
        "twofa_seed": "<2FA TOTP seed>"
      }
    }
  ]
}

The name of the configuration file can be freely chosen (can be overridden with the -c flag). However, when named otterdog.json, the cli tool will automatically detect and use that file if it is in the current working directory.

Warning

In this example the plain provider is being used to access credentials to avoid setting up a real credential provider (see below) for a quick setup. However, the plain provider should NOT be used for anything else to avoid leakage of data in case the otterdog.json file is shared with other users.

items.title: Local base template
items.text:
Instead of a file in a GitHub repository, base_template can also be the path to a local file, e.g. to adjust the default configuration for one organization without maintaining a repository for it:

{
  "defaults": {
    "jsonnet": {
      "base_template": "defaults/otterdog-defaults.libsonnet"
    }
  },
  "organizations": [
    {
      "name": "<project-name>",
      "github_id": "<github-id>",
      "base_template": "/path/to/other/otterdog-defaults.libsonnet"
    }
  ]
}
  • A relative path is relative to the directory of the otterdog.json file. ~ is expanded.
  • The directory of the file is linked as vendor/<directory-name> of the organization, so the configuration of the organization imports it like a template from a repository, e.g. import 'vendor/defaults/otterdog-defaults.libsonnet'. The template can import the other files in its directory, and its hooks are looked up there.
  • The link is recreated on every run, changes of the template are picked up right away. It is also done with --local, as there is nothing to fetch.
  • The directory of the template must not contain the configuration of the organization, so it cannot be the directory of otterdog.json itself. Keep the template in a directory of its own.
  • A value without :// is a path, everything else is the url of a GitHub repository, see above.

items.title: Skipping the web UI
items.text:
Some settings can only be read and changed via the GitHub web interface, which requires the username, password and twofa_seed of the credentials. The operations plan, apply, import, show-live, check-status and local-apply skip these settings when called with -n / --no-web-ui.

To skip them by default, e.g. if you only use an access token, set no_web_ui in the defaults of the otterdog.json file:

{
  "defaults": {
    "github": {
      "no_web_ui": true
    }
  }
}

The default can be overridden per call: --web-ui uses the web interface although no_web_ui is set, --no-web-ui skips it although it is not.

items.title: Cost policy
items.text:
Pull requests that may incur costs cannot be auto-merged and require a review by the designated team. The thresholds used for this check can be adjusted in the defaults of the otterdog.json file:

{
  "defaults": {
    "cost_policy": {
      "free_max_cache_size_gb": 10
    }
  }
}
Key Default Description free_max_cache_size_gb 10 GitHub Actions cache size limit (in GB) included free of charge, adding a repository with a max_cache_size_gb above this value is considered cost-related

Any change of max_cache_size_gb on an existing repository or organization is always considered cost-related.

items.title: Credentials
items.text:
Otterdog needs certain credentials to access information from an organization and its repositories on GitHub:

  • username / password / 2FA seed
  • API token

The login / username / 2FA seed are required to access the web interface of GitHub in order to retrieve certain settings that are not accessible via its rest / graphql API.

The GitHub api token needs to have the following scopes enabled:

  • repo
  • workflow
  • admin:org
  • admin:org_hook
  • delete_repo

The credentials can be stored in different providers (bitwarden, pass, vault, env).

items.title: Bitwarden
items.text:
When using bitwarden to store the credentials, you need to enter a valid item id as additional credential data:

{
  "organizations": [
    {
      "name": "<org name>",
      "github_id": "<github org id>",
      "credentials": {
        "provider": "bitwarden",
        "item_id" : "<bitwarden item id>"
      }
    }
  ]
}

The item stored in bitwarden needs to contain the following information (a sample json output of such an item):

{
  "object": "item",
  "id": "<bitwarden item id>",
  "name": "<item name>",
  "fields": [
    {
      "name": "api_token_admin",
      "value": "<github API token>"
    }
  ],
  "login": {
    "username": "<github username>",
    "password": "<github password>",
    "totp": "<github 2FA TOTP seed>"
  }
}

Mandatory items:

  • Field with name "api_token_admin" and as value the GitHub token to access the organization
  • login.username of a user that can access the organization with enabled 2FA
  • login.password the password of that user
  • login.totp the 2FA TOTP seed

items.title: Pass
items.text:
When using pass to store the credentials, you need to enter fully qualified pass names to access the various required credential data:

{
  "organizations": [
    {
      "name": "<org name>",
      "github_id": "<github org id>",
      "credentials": {
        "provider": "pass",
        "api_token": "<path/to/api_token>",
        "username": "<path/to/username>",
        "password": "<path/to/password>",
        "twofa_seed": "<path/to/2fa_seed>"
      }
    }
  ]
}

In case your password storage dir is not located at the default location, you can configurate that in the defaults:

{
  "defaults": {
    "pass": {
      "password_store_dir": "path/to/storage/dir"
    }
  }
}

As the password_store_dir might be different on different machines, you can also customize that in a separate .otterdog-defaults.json file:

{
  "pass": {
    "password_store_dir": "path/to/storage/dir"
  }
}

items.title: HashiCorp Vault
items.text:
When using a HashiCorp Vault to store the credentials, the secrets are read from a KV version 2 secrets engine. Each credential is referenced as <path/to/secret>/<field>, the last component being the name of the field:

{
  "organizations": [
    {
      "name": "<org name>",
      "github_id": "<github org id>",
      "credentials": {
        "provider": "vault",
        "api_token": "<path/to/secret>/<field>",
        "username": "<path/to/secret>/<field>",
        "password": "<path/to/secret>/<field>",
        "twofa_seed": "<path/to/secret>/<field>"
      }
    }
  ]
}

The connection to the Vault is configured in the defaults:

{
  "defaults": {
    "vault": {
      "vault_addr": "https://vault.example.org",
      "mount_point": "<kv mount point>",
      "verify_ssl": true
    }
  }
}
Key Description vault_addr the address of the Vault, defaults to the environment variable VAULT_ADDR vault_token the token to use, defaults to the environment variable VAULT_TOKEN, then to the file ~/.vault-token; if no valid token is found, otterdog asks to log in interactively mount_point the mount point of the KV secrets engine, it is recommended to always set it verify_ssl whether to verify the TLS certificate of the Vault, disabled by default; enable it, or set ca_cert ca_cert path to a CA certificate bundle used to verify the TLS certificate of the Vault client_cert path to a client certificate for mutual TLS batch_mode if true, fail instead of asking to log in interactively, e.g. in automation api_token_pattern, username_pattern, password_pattern, twofa_seed_pattern patterns of the credential paths used when an organization does not specify them, {0} is replaced by the name of the organization

items.title: Environment based credentials
items.text:
When using environment variables to store the credentials, you need to set the following environment variables:

{
  "organizations": [
    {
      "name": "<org name>",
      "github_id": "<github org id>",
      "credentials": {
        "provider": "env",
        "api_token": "<env_var_which_contains_api_token>",
        "username": "<env_var_which_contains_username>",
        "password": "<env_var_which_contains_password>",
        "twofa_seed": "<env_var_which_contains_2fa_seed>"
      }
    }
  ]
}

The environment variables need to be set in the system where otterdog is executed. They can also be set in a .env file in the current working directory, which will be automatically loaded by otterdog.

If you want to keep the same environment variable pattern across organizations, you can set defaults and use placeholders in the defaults.env section. The env provider normalizes placeholder values by converting them to uppercase and replacing spaces and hyphens with underscores. You can use {org_name} and {github_id}.

{
  "defaults": {
    "credentials": {
      "provider": "env"
    },
    "env": {
      "api_token": "OTTER_{org_name}_API_TOKEN",
      "username": "OTTER_{org_name}_USERNAME",
      "password": "OTTER_{github_id}_PASSWORD",
      "twofa_seed": "OTTER_{github_id}_TOTP_SEED"
    }
  }
}

Hint: You can combine this provider with GitHub Actions secrets to securely store the credentials in a GitHub repository and use them in a GitHub action that runs otterdog:

  env:
    OTTER_USERNAME: ${{ vars.OTTER_USERNAME }}
    OTTER_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.OTTER_PASSWORD }}
    OTTER_TOTP_SEED: ${{ secrets.OTTER_TOTP_SEED }}
    OTTER_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.OTTER_API_TOKEN }}

items.title: Secret access policy
items.text:
The configuration of an organization references secrets in a credential provider, see Secret Value. This configuration can be changed with pull requests, and otterdog resolves the references with the credentials of the operator, who usually has access to the secrets of all organizations. To prevent an organization from using the secrets of another one, the secrets that an organization can reference can be restricted in the defaults of the otterdog.json file:

{
  "defaults": {
    "secrets": {
      "mode": "enforce",
      "allowed_references": {
        "pass": ["bots/{org_name}/**"],
        "vault": ["{org_name}/**"]
      }
    }
  }
}

Additional references can be allowed for an organization, e.g. secrets shared by several organizations:

{
  "organizations": [
    {
      "name": "<org name>",
      "github_id": "<github org id>",
      "secrets": {
        "allowed_references": {
          "pass": ["bots/shared/sonatype/**"],
          "bitwarden": ["<bitwarden item id>"]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
Key Default Description mode enforce enforce: a reference that is not allowed is a validation error, and apply aborts before reading it from the credential provider; warn: it is a validation warning and apply resolves it, e.g. to find such references before enforcing the policy allowed_references {} the patterns of the allowed references of each credential provider (pass, vault, bitwarden), the secrets of a provider without patterns can not be referenced

The mode can only be set in the defaults. Without defaults.secrets, only the organizations with secrets have their references restricted, in enforce mode.

The patterns are matched against the path of a reference, segment by segment:

  • * matches any part of a segment, e.g. bots/{org_name}/*-token
  • ** matches any number of segments, at least one at the end of a pattern: bots/{org_name}/** does not match bots/{org_name} itself

The patterns can use the following placeholders, the examples are given for an organization with the name technology.apoapsis and the github_id eclipse-apoapsis:

Placeholder Replaced by Example pattern Example of an allowed reference {org_name} the name of the organization in otterdog.json bots/{org_name}/** pass:bots/technology.apoapsis/gpg/key_id {github_id} the github_id of the organization in otterdog.json {github_id}/** vault:eclipse-apoapsis/oss.sonatype.org/password

The placeholders are replaced by the values of otterdog.json, never by the names in the configuration of the organization, which a pull request can change. Their values are matched literally, e.g. the . of technology.apoapsis is not a wildcard. Any other placeholder is rejected when loading otterdog.json.

A Bitwarden reference <item id>@<field> is matched against its item id, each item has to be allowed explicitly.

A reference must consist of segments separated by / that only contain letters, digits, ., _, @, + and -. Segments . and .. are not allowed, so that a reference can not leave the allowed paths.

The policy is checked when validating a configuration, including the validation of pull requests and the playground of a project in the WebApp, and before resolving each secret during apply.

items.title: Environment variables
items.text:
The cli of otterdog reads the following environment variables:

Variable Description OTTERDOG_CONFIG_ROOT directory in which otterdog looks for otterdog.jsonnet or otterdog.json when no file is given with --config, and base directory of the config_dir; defaults to the current directory OTTERDOG_WEB_TIMEOUT timeout in milliseconds to load a page of the GitHub web interface or to wait for one of its elements, defaults to 10000; increase it on a slow connection VAULT_ADDR address of the Vault when vault_addr is not set, see HashiCorp Vault VAULT_TOKEN token to access the Vault when vault_token is not set, see HashiCorp Vault VAULT_USERNAME username used to log in to the Vault interactively, asked for if not set

The names of the environment variables that contain the credentials of an organization are defined in the configuration, see Environment based credentials.

items.title: Usage cli tool
items.text:
In general, all operations act on the local configuration stored in <cwd>/<config-dir>/<organization>/<organization>.jsonnet.

A typical workflow to handle changes to an organization are as follows:

  1. (first time) run an initial import of the organization
  2. (first time) run an apply operation to create all resources already inherited from the default config (e.g. config repo)
  3. (regular) fetch the latest config from the config repo using fetch-config
  4. (optional) make any local changes to the configuration
  5. (optional) run the validate operation to see if the configuration is syntactically and semantically correct
  6. (optional) run the plan operation to see which changes would be applied taking the current live configuration into account
  7. (regular) run the apply operation to actually apply the changes (also runs validate and plan, so steps 6 & 7 are redundant)
  8. (regular) push the local configuration to the config repo using the push-config operation

Note

It is not mandatory to store the configuration in the remote config repository (<org>/.otterdog by default). It could be stored anywhere else, however the operations fetch-config and push-config expect this repository to exist to function properly.

items.text:
• Resources: Format

items.title: Format
items.text: The infrastructure configuration of a GitHub organization is stored in jsonnet format.

items.title: Jsonnet content
items.text:
The following example illustrates the basic structure used by otterdog:

local orgs = import 'vendor/otterdog-defaults/otterdog-defaults.libsonnet'; // (1)!

orgs.newOrg('adoptium') { // (2)!
  settings+: {
    blog: "https://adoptium.net", // (3)!
    ...
  },
  webhooks+: [ // (4)!
    orgs.newOrgWebhook('https://app.codacy.com/2.0/events/gh/organization') {
      content_type: "json",
      ...
    },
  ],
  ...
  _repositories+:: [ // (5)!
    orgs.newRepo('.github') {
      allow_auto_merge: true,
      ...
      branch_protection_rules: [ // (6)!
        orgs.newBranchProtectionRule('main'),
      ],
    }
  ]
}
  1. Import of the default configuration
  2. Calling a function to create a specific resource (e.g. a GitHub organization) with default values as defined in the default config
  3. Overriding properties for a specific resource as defined in the default configuration, e.g. organization settings
  4. Extending an array of objects, e.g. webhooks defined on organization level
  5. Extending an array of objects that supports overriding objects already defined in the default configuration
  6. Nested resources, e.g. branch protection rules

Let's take a closer look at the definition of a function that is defined in the default configuration, e.g. orgs.newOrg:

local newOrg(id) = {
  github_id: id,
  settings: {
    name: null,
    plan: "free",
    billing_email: "webmaster@eclipse-foundation.org",
    ...
  },
  ...
}

It defines a json object with various properties and their respective values, e.g. .settings.name = null.

items.title: Concatenation
items.text:
In order to concatenate json objects, jsonnet offers the + operator, which we can use to override specific properties that are already defined by a function while inheriting every other object or value:

orgs.newOrg('adoptium') {
  settings+: {
    name: "Eclipse Adoptium",
  }
}

Open in the Playground

The resulting json object will inherit all properties defined by the function orgs.newOrg, but will override the specific property .settings.name to the value Eclipse Adoptium.

{
  github_id: "adoptium",
  settings: {
    name: "Eclipse Adoptium",
    plan: "free",
    billing_email: "webmaster@eclipse-foundation.org",
    ...
  },
  ...
}

items.title: Replacement
items.text:
On the contrary, if we would not use the + operator but instead use the function like that:

orgs.newOrg('adoptium') {
  settings: {
    name: "Eclipse Adoptium",
  }
}

Open in the Playground

the resulting json object would not include any properties in .settings as the whole nested structure was replaced:

{
  github_id: "adoptium",
  settings: {
    name: "Eclipse Adoptium",
  },
  ...
}

Warning

Otterdog will use the + operator by default when importing the current live configuration of a GitHub organization. In general it is strongly discouraged to remove the + operator as it might lead to incomplete configurations due to missing properties.

items.title: Blueprints
items.text:
Blueprints are a mechanism to help project to ensure that certain settings / files are present. They can be defined on global or organization level. Any configured blueprint is also displayed in the dashboard.

Blueprints are defined in an additive manner (contrary to policies), i.e. multiple blueprints of the same type might be active for a single organization. To distinguish blueprints of the same type, an additional id setting must be defined. If multiple blueprints use the same id value, only the first encountered blueprint will be taken into account.

If a blueprint is defined for an organization, otterdog will check if the matching repositories of the organization comply to the configuration of that blueprint. If this is not the case, a PR will be created to remediate the situation, e.g. by adding a file or updating its contents. The committers of an organization still need to manually merge the PR but are able to edit it prior to merging.

If such a remediation PR gets closed without being merged, the associated blueprint for that repository is put into state DISMISSED, and not further checks will be performed for that pair of blueprint / repository. In order to reinstate the checks, the PR needs to be reopened. Before remediating, otterdog also checks the latest PR of the blueprint branch (otterdog/blueprint/<id>) on GitHub: if it was closed without being merged, the blueprint is put into state DISMISSED again, so a dismissed remediation PR is never recreated, even if the stored status got lost.

items.title: Check frequency
items.text:
Blueprints are evaluated when /internal/check is called, every 5 minutes by default (policies.schedule in the Helm chart). A blueprint is evaluated at most once per BLUEPRINT_CHECK_INTERVAL seconds for a given organization, one hour by default (config.blueprintCheckInterval in the Helm chart). Calls within that interval skip the blueprint, which is logged at debug level:

skipping blueprint with id '<id>' for org '<org>', last checked at '<date>'

A change to a blueprint definition is therefore picked up at the next evaluation, at most BLUEPRINT_CHECK_INTERVAL seconds later.

items.title: Configuration
items.text: Blueprints are defined using a yaml syntax and placed in the otterdog/blueprints folder of the config repository using either a .yml or .yaml extension.

items.title: Example
items.text:
id: default-security-policy
name: Adds a default SECURITY.md file
description: |-
  This blueprint will create a PR that will add a default SECURITY.md file to the `.github` repo of your GitHub organization if it does not yet exist.
  You can adjust the PR as needed to fit it to your needs. If a repo defines a more specific SECURITY.md file it will take precedence of the one present in the `.github` repo.
type: required_file
config:
  repo_selector:
    name_pattern: .github
  files:
    - path: SECURITY.md
      content: |
        # Security Policy
        This Eclipse Foundation Project adheres to the [Eclipse Foundation Vulnerability Reporting Policy](https://www.eclipse.org/security/policy/).
        ...

items.title: Settings
items.text: Setting Necessity Description id mandatory unique identification of the blueprint name optional Name of the blueprint as displayed in the dashboard description optional Description of the blueprint as displayed in the dashboard type mandatory Type of the blueprint config mandatory Custom configuration dependent on the type of blueprint

items.title: Append Configuration
items.text: This blueprint type will append a configuration snippet to the configuration of an organization depending on a condition that is evaluated against the current configuration.

items.title: Configuration
items.text: • type - append_configuration

items.title: Settings
items.text:
Setting Necessity Value type Description condition mandatory string a JSONata expression that is evaluated against the current configuration content mandatory string the configuration snippet to add if the condition evaluates to true reviewers optional list[string] the list of teams for which a review shall be requested upon pull request creation

Note

Team names will be implicitly slugified, i.e. a team name defined with a template like technology.csi-project-leads will be converted to technology-csi-project-leads.

items.title: Templating
items.text:
It is possible to use Mustache logic-less templates within the content / reviewers parameters of this blueprint.

To use a context variable, simply enclose its name in curly braces:

  This is an example to use mustache template for repo: {{repo_name}}

In this example, {{repo_name}} will be replaced with the actual name of the repository being processed. For more complex examples please refer to the mustache documentation.

items.title: Template Context
items.text:
The following context is injected during template evaluation when a specific repository is being processed:

Variable Type Description project_name string the project name of the associated GitHub organization, e.g. technology.csi github_id string the name of the associated GitHub organization repo_name string the name of the repository being processed org dict the organization settings for the associated GitHub organization repo dict the repository settings for the repository being processed repo_url string the url of the repository being processed, e.g. https://github.com/eclipse-csi/otterdog blueprint_id string the id of the associated blueprint, e.g. require-dependabot-auto-merge blueprint_url string the url of the associated blueprint, e.g. https://github.com/eclipse-csi/.eclipsefdn/blob/main/otterdog/blueprints/test.yml

items.title: References
items.text:
• JSONata playground
  • JSONata documentation

items.title: Example
items.text:
The following example adds an Organization Ruleset to the configuration to prevent force-pushes on the default branch of any repository if one does not exist yet:

id: prevent-force-pushes
name: Prevents force-pushes for the default branch
type: append_configuration
config:
  condition: >-
    $count($.rulesets[allows_force_pushes = false and
    "~DEFAULT_BRANCH" in include_refs and
    "~ALL" in include_repo_names and target = "branch"]) = 0
  content: |-
    {
      # snippet added due to '{{blueprint_url}}'
      rulesets+: [
        orgs.newOrgRuleset('{{blueprint_id}}') {
          allows_creations: true,
          include_repo_names: [
            "~ALL"
          ],
          include_refs: [
            "~DEFAULT_BRANCH"
          ],
          required_pull_request: null,
          required_status_checks: null,
        },
      ],
    }

items.title: Pin Workflow
items.text:
This blueprint type will pin any encountered GitHub action or reusable workflow in any used workflow of matching repositories to the commit hash of the latest released version that corresponds to the currently used reference.

Furthermore, if actions are already pinned but the corresponding version in the comment does not matchup, this blueprint will also correct the comment to the tag / branch that matches the used commit hash.

items.title: Example
items.text:
A workflow uses the actions/checkout action with reference v3. This action will be pinned to the commit hash of the latest corresponding release v3.6.0.

     steps:
     - name: Checkout code
-      uses: actions/checkout@v3
+      uses: actions/checkout@f43a0e5ff2bd294095638e18286ca9a3d1956744 # v3.6.0

items.title: Configuration
items.text: • type - pin_workflow

items.title: Settings
items.text: Setting Necessity Value type Description repo_selector optional RepoSelector If omitted, all repos are matched

items.title: Repo Selector
items.text:
Allows to define a list of repositories that this blueprint should apply to. The pattern is expected to be in python regular expression format.

Setting Necessity Value type name_pattern mandatory list[string] | string

items.title: Skipping pinning
items.text:
By default, any action using main or master as reference will be skipped. In case an action can not be pinned as it is required to be used with a specific tag or branch (e.g. slsa-github-generator) you can add a comment to the action:

    uses: slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator/.github/workflows/generator_generic_slsa3.yml@v2.0.0 # ignore: pin

items.title: Example
items.text:
id: pin-workflows
name: Pin GitHub actions in workflows
description: |-
  This blueprint pins GitHub actions used in workflows to their corresponding commit hash.
type: pin_workflow
config:

items.title: Required File
items.text: This blueprint type ensures that one or more files are present in the repositories that match this blueprint. Depending on the strict setting, it will be checked whether the file already exists or if it exactly matches the configured content.

items.title: Configuration
items.text: • type - required_file

items.title: Settings
items.text: Setting Necessity Value type Description repo_selector optional RepoSelector If omitted, all repos are matched files mandatory list[FileSetting]

items.title: Repo Selector
items.text:
Allows to define a list of repositories that this blueprint should apply to. The pattern is expected to be in python regular expression format.

Setting Necessity Value type name_pattern mandatory list[string] | string

items.title: File setting
items.text: Setting Necessity Value type Description path mandatory string the path of the file within the repository without leading slash content mandatory string the content of the file strict optional boolean if false (default), the file will be only checked for existence, otherwise the content will be compared

items.title: Templating
items.text:
It is possible to use Mustache logic-less templates within the content of a blueprint.

To use a context variable, simply enclose its name in curly braces:

  This is an example to use mustache template for repo: {{repo_name}}

In this example, {{repo_name}} will be replaced with the actual name of the repository being processed. For more complex examples please refer to the mustache documentation.

items.title: Template Context
items.text:
The following context is injected during template evaluation when a specific repository is being processed:

Variable Type Description project_name string the project name of the associated GitHub organization, e.g. technology.csi github_id string the name of the associated GitHub organization repo_name string the name of the repository being processed org dict the organization settings for the associated GitHub organization repo dict the repository settings for the repository being processed repo_url string the url of the repository being processed, e.g. https://github.com/eclipse-csi/otterdog blueprint_id string the id of the associated blueprint, e.g. require-dependabot-auto-merge blueprint_url string the url of the associated blueprint, e.g. https://github.com/eclipse-csi/.eclipsefdn/blob/main/otterdog/blueprints/test.yml

items.title: Example
items.text:
In this example a workflow file .github/workflows/dependabot-auto-merge.yml should be present in a set of repositories matching the configured content.

id: require-dependabot-auto-merge
name: Require dependabot-auto-merge.yml
type: required_file
config:
  repo_selector:
    name_pattern:
      - temurin-build
      - containers
  files:
    - path: .github/workflows/dependabot-auto-merge.yml
      content: |
        # This is a templated file from {{blueprint_url}} for {{repo_name}}
        name: Dependabot auto-merge
        on: pull_request_target

        permissions: read-all

        jobs:
          dependabot:
            permissions:
              contents: write
              pull-requests: write
            uses: {{github_id}}/.github/.github/workflows/dependabot-auto-merge.yml@main
      # ensure that changes to the template are propagated
      strict: true

items.title: Scorecard Integration
items.text:
This blueprint type ensures that matching repositories run an OpenSSF Scorecard analysis.

If none of the workflows of a repository uses the configured scorecard action, this blueprint creates a pull request that adds a workflow with the configured content.

items.title: Configuration
items.text: • type - scorecard_integration

items.title: Settings
items.text: Setting Necessity Value type Description repo_selector optional RepoSelector If omitted, all repos are matched scorecard_action optional string the name of scorecard action to search for, default: 'ossf/scorecard-action' workflow_name optional string the name of the workflow to be added, default: 'scorecard-analysis.yml' workflow_content mandatory string the workflow content to be added if no scorecard action can be found

items.title: Repo Selector
items.text:
Allows to define a list of repositories that this blueprint should apply to. The pattern is expected to be in python regular expression format.

Setting Necessity Value type name_pattern mandatory list[string] | string

items.title: Templating
items.text:
It is possible to use Mustache logic-less templates within the workflow content of this blueprint.

To use a context variable, simply enclose its name in curly braces:

  This is an example to use mustache template for repo: {{repo_name}}

In this example, {{repo_name}} will be replaced with the actual name of the repository being processed. For more complex examples please refer to the mustache documentation.

items.title: Template Context
items.text:
The following context is injected during template evaluation when a specific repository is being processed:

Variable Type Description project_name string the project name of the associated GitHub organization, e.g. technology.csi github_id string the name of the associated GitHub organization repo_name string the name of the repository being processed org dict the organization settings for the associated GitHub organization repo dict the repository settings for the repository being processed repo_url string the url of the repository being processed, e.g. https://github.com/eclipse-csi/otterdog blueprint_id string the id of the associated blueprint, e.g. require-dependabot-auto-merge blueprint_url string the url of the associated blueprint, e.g. https://github.com/eclipse-csi/.eclipsefdn/blob/main/otterdog/blueprints/test.yml

items.title: Example
items.text:
id: scorecard-integration
name: Integrate OSSF Scorecard anaylsis
description: |-
  Integrate OSSF Scorecard analysis.
type: scorecard_integration
config:
  repo_selector:
    name_pattern:
      - repoA
      - repoB
  workflow_name: scorecard-analysis.yml
  workflow_content: |
    name: Scorecard analysis workflow
    on:
      push:
        branches:
        - main
      schedule:
        # Weekly on Saturdays.
        - cron:  '30 1 * * 6'

    permissions: read-all

    jobs:
      analysis:
        if: github.repository_owner == '{{github_id}}'
        name: Scorecard analysis
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        permissions:
          security-events: write
          id-token: write

        steps:
          - name: "Checkout code"
            uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2
            with:
              persist-credentials: false

          - name: "Run analysis"
            uses: ossf/scorecard-action@62b2cac7ed8198b15735ed49ab1e5cf35480ba46 # v2.4.0
            with:
              results_file: results.sarif
              results_format: sarif
              publish_results: true

items.title: CLI Operations
items.text:
The CLI has support for various operations to operate on individual organizations. In general, if no organization is specified, the selected operation runs on all organizations defined in the used configuration file (otterdog.json).

Usage: otterdog [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

  Managing GitHub organizations at scale.

Options:
  --version   Show the version and exit.
  -h, --help  Show this message and exit.

Commands:
  apply              Apply changes based on the current configuration to the live configuration at GitHub.
  canonical-diff     Displays a diff of the current configuration to a canonical version.
  delete-file        Deletes a specified file in a repository.
  dispatch-workflow  Dispatches a specified workflow in a repository.
  fetch-config       Fetches the configuration from the corresponding config repo of an organization.
  import             Imports existing resources for a GitHub organization.
  list-apps          Lists all installed GitHub apps for an organization.
  list-members       Displays the 2FA status of members of an organization.
  local-plan         Show changes to another local configuration.
  plan               Show changes to live configuration on GitHub.
  push-config        Pushes the local configuration to the corresponding config repo of an organization.
  show               Displays the full configuration for an organization.
  show-default       Displays the default configuration for an organization.
  show-live          Displays the live configuration for organizations.
  sync-template      Sync contents of repositories created from a template repository.
  validate           Validates the configuration for organizations.
  web-login          Open a browser window logged in to the GitHub organization.

items.title: Working directory
items.text: When running otterdog, all used data is stored and accessed locally. The configuration files for each organization are expected to be at location $CWD/<config-dir>/<github-id>/, where <config-dir> can be configured in otterdog.json and defaults to orgs.

items.title: GitHub API usage statistics
items.text:
Every operation that processes organizations can report the requests it has sent to GitHub, to understand the cost of an operation and to find room for optimization:

  • --stats (or OTTERDOG_STATS=1) prints a summary to stderr once the operation has finished, failed or been interrupted, including the 10 organizations that sent the most requests. Any output of the operation on stdout, e.g. list-apps --json, stays untouched.
  • --stats-file <file> (or OTTERDOG_STATS_FILE=<file>) writes the statistics as JSON to the given file, including the requests per organization and per endpoint.
  • with -v, a one-line summary is logged for each organization, and --stats lists all organizations as well as the top endpoints.

 eclipse-bar       1,318         2       30      834   ~436 core · 52 points
 eclipse-baz         541         0       11      350   ~171 core · 24 points

Every HTTP request that is actually sent counts as one request, including every page of a paginated result, every retried attempt, every followed redirect and every request resent by the HTTP client on a new connection. Retries, errors and cached responses are subsets of the requests, the quota cost is measured apart:

Column Description Retries requests that repeat a failed attempt Errors requests that failed with an HTTP status >= 400, or a network error or timeout once sent; for GraphQL also responses reporting errors in their body Cached requests answered with 304 Not Modified or served by a caching proxy Quota cost points deducted from the GitHub rate limits, see Quota cost and rate limits

A response that is served from the local cache without contacting GitHub is not a request. Neither is an attempt that fails before being sent, e.g. as no connection to GitHub could be established, or as it timed out or was interrupted while waiting for a free connection of the connection pool: such attempts are listed apart as Not sent. Many 404 errors are expected, as some settings are only available depending on the plan of an organization.

Page loads of the GitHub web interface, used for settings that are not available via the api, are listed as Web UI and do not count against any api quota. Cloning the default configuration with git is not accounted.

items.title: Quota cost and rate limits
items.text:
GitHub limits the use of its apis per hour, with a separate quota for each resource. Each response tells which resource it has been accounted to, and the statistics use that name:

Resource Covers core almost every REST endpoint graphql the GraphQL api, accounted in points others specific endpoints with their own, often smaller quota, e.g. webhook_deliveries

A REST cost may thus be split across several resources, e.g. ~54 core, 4 webhook_deliveries.

The quota cost of a run is the number of points it has deducted from these quotas:

  • REST (~1,308 core): GitHub does not report the cost of a REST request, so it is estimated from its documented rules, hence the ~. Every response costs one point, including errors and retries, except responses with 304 Not Modified: otterdog revalidates its cached responses with conditional requests, which GitHub answers for free if nothing has changed. The estimate is thus close to the number of requests minus the cached ones.
  • GraphQL (171 points): every query asks GitHub for its cost, so the value is exact. A query costs at least one point, more if it requests many nested items; as otterdog fetches results in pages of 100 items, most queries cost a single point. Mutations and failed requests do not report their cost and are listed as + N unpriced.

The Rate limit lines show, for each resource used during the run, the points left (3,402), the size of the quota for the used credentials (5,000) and when the quota is reset. The size depends on the credentials, e.g. 5,000 requests per hour for a personal access token, see rate limits for the REST API and rate limits for the GraphQL API. The points left are the lowest value GitHub reported during the current window. They only decrease with requests that are accounted: a run answered mostly with 304 Not Modified hardly changes them. Responses served by a caching proxy are ignored, as they carry the rate limit of the original request. As the quota is shared with any other client using the same credentials, it can not be used to derive the consumption of a single run.

GitHub also enforces secondary rate limits, e.g. on concurrent requests, which are not measured.

items.title: Apply
items.text:
The apply operation will apply changes of the local configuration to the current live settings on GitHub.

When the apply operation is executed, the following happens:

  • the local configuration is validated
  • the current live configuration is retrieved
  • the current changes are planned
  • if approved, the changes are applied

Note

In general, resources that are present on GitHub but not contained in the local configuration are marked for deletion, however, by default otterdog will not remove any resources unless the option --delete-resources has been specified.

items.title: Options
items.text:
--stats                 print the GitHub API usage statistics to stderr at the end  [env var: OTTERDOG_STATS]
  --stats-file FILE       write the GitHub API usage statistics as JSON to the given file  [env var:
                          OTTERDOG_STATS_FILE]
  --local                 work in local mode, not updating the referenced default config
  -c, --config FILE       configuration file to use  [default: otterdog.json]
  -v, --verbose           enable verbose output (-vvv for more verbose output)
  -f, --force             skips interactive approvals
  -n, --no-web-ui / --web-ui  skip settings retrieved via web ui, defaults to the
                              'no_web_ui' setting of the otterdog configuration
  --repo-filter TEXT      a valid shell pattern to match repository names to be included  [default: *]
  --update-webhooks       updates webhook with secrets regardless of changes
  --update-secrets        updates secrets regardless of changes
  --update-filter TEXT    a valid shell pattern to match webhook urls / secret names to be included for update
                          [default: *]
  -d, --delete-resources  enables deletion of resources if they are missing in the definition
  --delete-filter SELECTOR  only applies the deletions of the resources selected by their type, optionally
                            followed by their key as displayed by plan, using shell patterns, e.g.
                            'org_code_security_configuration' or 'org_code_security_configuration[name="Legacy*"]',
                            requires '--delete-resources', can be repeated
  -h, --help              Show this message and exit.

Note

As otterdog does not maintain any local state, it can not determine if secret values need to be updated as GitHub will not disclose secret values via their APIs anymore after they have been set. As a consequence, otterdog will not update secret values by default unless --update-secrets or --update-webhooks has been specified.

items.title: Deleting selected resources
items.text:
--delete-filter turns apply into a targeted deletion: only the deletions of the resources it selects are planned and applied. All the other changes, i.e. the additions, the modifications and the other deletions, are skipped. They are neither displayed nor applied, only counted. The option requires --delete-resources, and can be repeated to select more resources.

otterdog apply my-org --delete-resources --delete-filter org_code_security_configuration

  - remove org_code_security_configuration[name="Legacy - private/internal repositories"] {
    ...
  - }

  2 other change(s) are skipped, only the deletions selected by '--delete-filter' are applied.

  Do you want to perform these actions? (Only 'yes' or 'y' will be accepted to approve)
  ...
  Executed plan: 0 added, 0 changed, 1 deleted, 2 skipped.

items.title: Selectors
items.text:
A selector is written like the header of a resource in the output of plan and apply, so that a header can be copied as is, e.g. org_code_security_configuration[name="Legacy - private/internal repositories"]:

  • the type of the resource, e.g. org_code_security_configuration, team_sync or repo_variable, selects all the resources of this type
  • optionally followed by conditions between brackets, separated by commas, each one naming either the key of the resource, e.g. name or pattern, or the type of its parent, e.g. repository

The type and the values are shell patterns, e.g. org_* or name="Legacy*", matched with their case. A value is quoted when it contains spaces, commas or brackets. Quote the whole selector in the shell:

Selector Deletes org_code_security_configuration all the code security configurations missing in the definition 'org_code_security_configuration[name="Legacy*"]' the ones whose name starts with Legacy 'org_code_security_configuration[name="Legacy - private/internal repositories"]' only this configuration 'repo_variable[repository=my-repo]' the variables of the repository my-repo 'branch_protection_rule[pattern="master", repository=jiro]' the rule for master of the repository jiro 'org_*' the resources of the organization, e.g. its variables and secrets

A selector that matches none of the resources to delete is reported with a warning, e.g. for a misspelled type or a condition that names neither the key of the resource nor its parent. The planning takes the selection into account, e.g. a team stays connected to an IdP group whose removal from team_sync is not selected.

items.title: Deleting resources in all organizations
items.text:
Without organization, apply processes all the organizations of the otterdog configuration, one after the other, and asks for approval for each organization that has a selected deletion:

otterdog apply --delete-resources --delete-filter 'org_code_security_configuration[name="Legacy*"]'

The organizations without a selected deletion report No changes required., together with the warning above. --force applies the deletions without asking for approval. Run the command without it first to review the deletions of each organization, and answer anything but yes to cancel them.

items.title: Plan
items.text:
The plan operation shows the changes that an apply operation would perform, without changing anything on GitHub.

When the plan operation is executed, the following happens:

  • the local configuration is validated, planning is aborted if validation errors are found
  • the current live configuration is retrieved
  • the differences between the local and the live configuration are displayed

Resources that exist on GitHub but are missing in the local configuration are displayed as deletions. Whether they are actually deleted depends on how the changes are applied, see Apply.

items.title: GitHub Organization
items.text:
This resource represents a GitHub organization with all supported settings and nested resources.

jsonnet 
orgs.newOrg('<project-name>', '<github-id>') {
    settings+: { ... }, // (1)!
    webhooks+: [ ... ], // (2)!
    secrets+: [ ... ], // (3)!
    dependabot_secrets+: [ ... ], // (4)!
    codespaces_secrets+: [ ... ], // (5)!
    variables+: [ ... ], // (6)!
    rulesets+: [ ... ], // (7)!
    code_security_configurations+: [ ... ], // (8)!
    _repositories+:: [ ... ], // (9)!
}
  1. see Organization Settings
  2. see Organization Webhook
  3. see Organization Secret
  4. see Organization Dependabot Secret
  5. see Organization Codespaces Secret
  6. see Organization Variable
  7. see Organization Ruleset
  8. see Organization Code Security Configuration
  9. see Repository

Note

Repositories use a slightly different property name (_repositories+::) which has mainly technical reasons. This syntax allows to override properties for repositories that are already defined in the default configuration. See the Repository reference for more details.

Organization Code Security Configuration
items.text:
Definition of a Code Security Configuration on organization level, the following properties are supported:

The enablement status of code scanning default setup enabled, disabled or not_set code_scanning_default_setup_runner_type string or null The type of runners code scanning default setup uses standard, labeled, not_set or null if not managed code_scanning_default_setup_runner_label string or null The label of the runners code scanning default setup uses Only taken into account if code_scanning_default_setup_runner_type is labeled code_scanning_allow_advanced boolean or null If repositories using code scanning advanced setup are allowed null if not managed code_scanning_delegated_alert_dismissal string or null The enablement status of code scanning delegated alert dismissal enabled, disabled, not_set or null if not managed secret_scanning string The enablement status of secret scanning enabled, disabled or not_set secret_scanning_push_protection string The enablement status of secret scanning push protection enabled, disabled or not_set secret_scanning_delegated_bypass string The enablement status of delegated bypass for push protection enabled, disabled or not_set secret_scanning_delegated_bypass_reviewers list[string] or null List of teams or roles that review requests to bypass push protection see Bypass Reviewers, null if not managed secret_scanning_validity_checks string The enablement status of secret scanning validity checks enabled, disabled or not_set secret_scanning_non_provider_patterns string The enablement status of secret scanning of non-provider patterns enabled, disabled or not_set secret_scanning_generic_secrets string or null The enablement status of Copilot secret scanning enabled, disabled, not_set or null if not managed secret_scanning_generic_secrets_push_protection string or null The enablement status of push protection for generic secrets enabled, disabled, not_set or null if not managed secret_scanning_delegated_alert_dismissal string or null The enablement status of secret scanning delegated alert dismissal enabled, disabled, not_set or null if not managed secret_scanning_extended_metadata string or null The enablement status of secret scanning extended metadata enabled, disabled, not_set or null if not managed private_vulnerability_reporting string The enablement status of private vulnerability reporting enabled, disabled or not_set enforcement string If repositories the configuration is attached to can change its settings enforced or unenforced default_for_new_repos string The visibility of new repositories the configuration is attached to by default none, all, public or private_and_internal

A feature set to not_set is not changed on the repositories the configuration is attached to, while properties set to null are not managed by otterdog, e.g. because the feature is not available to every organization.

Only configurations of the organization are managed, the predefined configurations of GitHub (e.g. GitHub recommended) and configurations of an enterprise are neither created, updated nor deleted. The name identifies a configuration: renaming a configuration deletes it and creates a new one, which is not attached to the repositories of the previous configuration anymore.

A configuration is attached to a repository with the code_security_configuration property of the Repository, and to new repositories with the default_for_new_repos property. The configuration is attached before the other settings of the repository are applied, and otterdog waits until GitHub completed the attachment, as well as until an updated configuration is applied to its repositories. The patches of the repositories that an update is not applied to, as it failed or is still pending after 30 seconds, are skipped and reported as errors, as they might depend on the updated settings, as well as the patches of the repositories attached to a configuration whose update or deletion failed, or of all repositories if the attached ones can not be retrieved. Archived repositories support code security configurations, only secret scanning runs while they are archived.

The settings of a repository that the configuration attached to it sets are not managed on the repository, as the configuration takes precedence, and changing them on the repository might detach it from its configuration. This applies to the configuration the repository specifies, otherwise the one currently attached to it, even if it is not managed (e.g. GitHub recommended) or not deleted as --delete-resources is not used, or for a new repository, the default configuration for its visibility, unless default_code_security_configurations_disabled is enabled:

Feature of the configuration Settings of the repository dependabot_alerts dependabot_alerts_enabled dependabot_security_updates dependabot_security_updates_enabled code_scanning_default_setup code_scanning_default_setup_enabled, code_scanning_default_query_suite, code_scanning_default_languages secret_scanning secret_scanning secret_scanning_push_protection secret_scanning_push_protection private_vulnerability_reporting private_vulnerability_reporting_enabled

Features set to not_set leave the settings of the repository unchanged, they are still managed on the repository. GitHub supports private vulnerability reporting only on public repositories, a configuration does not enable it on private repositories. For a feature that the configuration does not specify, its current value on GitHub applies. When the current settings of repositories are not retrieved from GitHub, e.g. for the local apply of the dashboard, the settings that their configuration stops setting are applied again, as the configuration might have changed them on GitHub.

Note

To use a code security configuration as default for new repositories, the setting default_code_security_configurations_disabled of the Organization Settings must be disabled, as it removes any default code security configuration otherwise.

items.title: Bypass Reviewers
items.text:
The entries of secret_scanning_delegated_bypass_reviewers reference teams and roles like the bypass actors of rulesets:

Reviewer Format Example Team @<organization>/<team> @OtterdogTest/security-team Role #<role> #OrganizationAdmin, #RepositoryAdmin, #Maintain, #Write Custom role #<role-id> #4711

By default, a reviewer reviews the requests to bypass push protection. With the suffix :exempt, e.g. @OtterdogTest/release-bots:exempt, the reviewer is exempt from push protection instead.

items.text:

  secret_protection: "disabled",

  dependabot_alerts: "disabled",
  dependabot_security_updates: "disabled",
  dependabot_reachability: null,
  dependabot_delegated_alert_dismissal: null,

  # code scanning
  code_scanning_default_setup: "disabled",
  code_scanning_default_setup_runner_type: null,
  code_scanning_default_setup_runner_label: null,
  code_scanning_allow_advanced: null,
  code_scanning_delegated_alert_dismissal: null,

  # secret scanning
  secret_scanning: "disabled",
  secret_scanning_push_protection: "disabled",
  secret_scanning_delegated_bypass: "disabled",
  secret_scanning_delegated_bypass_reviewers: null,
  secret_scanning_validity_checks: "disabled",
  secret_scanning_non_provider_patterns: "disabled",
  secret_scanning_generic_secrets: null,
  secret_scanning_generic_secrets_push_protection: null,
  secret_scanning_delegated_alert_dismissal: null,
  secret_scanning_extended_metadata: null,

The default configuration of an instance of otterdog, set by base_template, might define other values, see otterdog show-default or the Defaults page of a project in the dashboard.

items.title: Validation rules
items.text:
• specifying a value that is not allowed for a property triggers an error
  • specifying a description longer than 255 characters triggers an error
  • setting code_scanning_default_setup_runner_type to labeled without a code_scanning_default_setup_runner_label triggers an error
  • specifying a bypass reviewer that is neither a team nor a role, or with a mode other than always or exempt, triggers an error
  • setting the same visibility of new repositories in default_for_new_repos of several configurations triggers an error
  • setting default_for_new_repos while default_code_security_configurations_disabled of the organization settings is enabled triggers an error
  • enabling a feature of secret scanning while secret_protection is disabled triggers an error
  • enabling code_scanning_default_setup or code_scanning_delegated_alert_dismissal while code_security is disabled triggers an error
  • setting code_security and secret_protection to a different status for an organization with free plan triggers an error
  • enabling secret_scanning_delegated_bypass without any secret_scanning_delegated_bypass_reviewers triggers a warning
  • enabling a feature of secret scanning while secret_scanning is disabled triggers a warning
  • enabling secret_scanning_delegated_bypass while secret_scanning_push_protection is disabled triggers a warning
  • enabling dependabot_security_updates while dependabot_alerts is disabled triggers a warning

Note

Enabling code_security or secret_protection can consume GitHub Advanced Security licenses for the private and internal repositories the configuration is attached to. Such changes are considered to be cost-related if private repositories are attached to the configuration or it is the default for new private repositories, and so is attaching a private repository to a configuration that enables them. This does not apply to an organization with free plan, for which these products cannot be purchased. If the configurations attached to repositories are not retrieved from GitHub, e.g. to validate a pull request, a private repository that does not specify a configuration might be attached to any existing one. Setting code_security and secret_protection to a different status requires an unbundled GitHub Advanced Security plan, i.e. GitHub Code Security and GitHub Secret Protection, which is not available for an organization with free plan. GitHub rejects it otherwise.

Key Value Description Notes name string The name of the custom property value_type string The type of this property, see Notes about allowed values string, single_select, multi_select or true_false required boolean If this property is required for any repository default_value string or list[string] or null The default value to assign to a repository if the property is required description string or null A description of this property allowed_values list[string] or null The list of allowed values if either single_select or multi_select is used values_editable_by string Who can edit the values of this property on a repository org_actors (default) or org_and_repo_actors

Note

Due to a limitation of the GitHub Api, it is not possible to change the value_type of a Custom Property after its creation. Trying to change the property will result in an error in the plan / apply operation after validation as the change can only be determined after the live settings have been analyzed.

items.title: Validation rules
items.text:

items.title: Organization Ruleset
items.text:
Definition of an Organization Ruleset, the following properties are supported:

Key Value Description Notes include_repo_names list[RepoNameMatcher] List of names or patterns to include matching repositories exclude_repo_names list[RepoNameMatcher] List of names or patterns to exclude matching repositories protect_repo_names boolean If enabled, target repositories can only be renamed by those with bypass permission name string The name of this repository ruleset target string The target of this ruleset Possible values are branch, tag or push enforcement string The enforcement status of this ruleset Possible values are active, disabled or evaluate (evaluate only available when enterprise billing is enabled) bypass_actors list[BypassActor] List of actors able to bypass this ruleset include_refs list[RefMatcher] List of refs or patterns to include matching branches exclude_refs list[RefMatcher] List of refs or patterns to exclude matching branches allows_creations boolean If disabled, only allows users with bypass permission to create matching refs allows_deletions boolean If disabled, only allows users with bypass permission to delete matching refs allows_updates boolean If disabled, only allows users with bypass permission to push matching refs allows_force_pushes boolean If disabled, only allows users with bypass permission to force push matching refs required_status_checks StatusCheckSettings or null If specified, status checks must pass before branches can be merged into a matching branch requires_commit_signatures boolean If enabled, commits pushed to matching branches must have verified signatures requires_linear_history boolean If enabled, prevent merge commits from being pushed to matching branches requires_deployments boolean If enabled, environments must be successfully deployed to before branches can be merged into a matching branch required_deployment_environments list[string] List of environments that must be successfully deployed to before branches can be merged Only taken into account when requires_deployments is enabled required_pull_request PullRequestSettings or null If specified, requires a pull request before merging. All commits must be made to a non-protected branch and submitted via a pull request before they can be merged into matching branches required_merge_queue MergeQueueSettings or null If specified, merges must be performed via a merge queue copilot_code_review CopilotCodeReviewSettings or null If specified, request a review from Copilot automatically for new pull requests, if their author has access to Copilot code review Only supported by rulesets with target branch commit_message_pattern PatternSettings or null If specified, the message of the commits pushed to matching refs must match a pattern Not supported by rulesets with target push commit_author_email_pattern PatternSettings or null If specified, the email of the author of the commits pushed to matching refs must match a pattern Not supported by rulesets with target push committer_email_pattern PatternSettings or null If specified, the email of the committer of the commits pushed to matching refs must match a pattern Not supported by rulesets with target push branch_name_pattern PatternSettings or null If specified, the names of matching branches must match a pattern Only supported by rulesets with target branch tag_name_pattern PatternSettings or null If specified, the names of matching tags must match a pattern Only supported by rulesets with target tag restricted_file_paths list[string] List of file paths that can not be pushed, using fnmatch syntax, e.g. secrets/** Only supported by rulesets with target push, at most 200 entries of up to 200 characters restricted_file_paths_exceptions list[string] List of file paths that can be pushed even if they match restricted_file_paths Only taken into account when restricted_file_paths is not empty max_file_path_length integer The maximum number of characters of the paths of the files that can be pushed Only supported by rulesets with target push, allowed values in the range [0, 32767], 0 disables the rule restricted_file_extensions list[string] List of file extensions that can not be pushed, e.g. *.exe Only supported by rulesets with target push, at most 200 entries of up to 200 characters max_file_size integer The maximum size in megabytes of the files that can be pushed, files stored with Git LFS are not limited Only supported by rulesets with target push, allowed values in the range [0, 100], 0 disables the rule max_file_size_exceptions list[string] List of file paths that can exceed max_file_size Only taken into account when max_file_size is not 0 required_code_scanning CodeScanningSettings or null If specified, code scanning tools must provide results before branches can be merged into a matching branch Only supported by rulesets with target branch required_workflows WorkflowsSettings or null If specified, workflows must pass before branches can be merged into a matching branch Only supported by rulesets with target branch

Rulesets support use-cases that can not be modelled with Branch Protection Rules, e.g. bypass actors that are exempted from all rules of a ruleset, while the bypass allowances of a Branch Protection Rule only lift the pull request requirement and required status checks still apply. See Rulesets or branch protection rules for a comparison and the features of rulesets that are not supported, and Protecting branches for examples, e.g. restricting the files that can be pushed with a ruleset with target push.

A ruleset with target push checks the content of every push, to any ref of the matching repositories: GitHub only supports the push rules in it, restricted_file_paths, max_file_path_length, restricted_file_extensions and max_file_size. The rules protecting branches or blocking the merge of pull requests, e.g. requires_linear_history or required_workflows, have to be defined in a separate ruleset with target branch.

A rule missing from a ruleset, e.g. because the default template predates it, is not managed: plan reports no difference for it and apply keeps its current setting on GitHub, including its exceptions, e.g. restricted_file_paths_exceptions, while a rule set to its disabled value, e.g. null, is removed.

items.text: Key Value Description Notes do_not_enforce_on_create boolean If enabled, allow repositories and branches to be created if a check would otherwise prohibit it strict boolean If enabled, pull requests targeting a matching branch must have been tested with the latest code This setting will not take effect unless at least one status check is enabled status_checks list[StatusCheck] List of status checks that must succeed before branches can be merged

items.text: Key Value Description Notes merge_method string Method to use when merging changes from queued pull requests Possible values are MERGE, SQUASH or REBASE build_concurrency integer Limit the number of queued pull requests requesting checks and workflow runs at the same time Must be in non-negative number min_group_size integer The minimum number of PRs that will be merged together in a group Must be in non-negative number max_group_size integer The maximum number of PRs that will be merged together in a group Must be in non-negative number wait_time_for_minimum_group_size integer The time in minutes the merge queue should wait after the first PR is added to the queue for the minimum group size to be met.After this time has elapsed, the minimum group size will be ignored and a smaller group will be merged Must be in non-negative number status_check_timeout integer Maximum time in minutes for a required status check to report a conclusion.After this much time has elapsed, checks that have not reported a conclusion will be assumed to have failed Must be in non-negative number requires_all_group_entries_to_pass_required_checks boolean When this setting is disabled, only the commit at the head of the merge group, i.e. the commit containing changes from all of the PRs in the group, must pass its required checks to merge

The ref is a branch or a tag, the sha a commit, the repository is case-insensitive. %, @ and # are written %25, %40 and %23 in a path or a ref
