          reviewers+: [
            "@my-org/release-managers",
          ],
          prevent_self_review: true,
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}
  1. Patterns for tags start with tag:, see Branch or Tag.

Open in the Playground

The publishing job of the workflow then references the environment:

jobs:
  publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: release
    steps:
      ...

Warning

An environment with deployment_branch_policy: "all" and no reviewers does not protect its secrets: a workflow running on any branch, e.g. a branch pushed by any user with write access, can use them. This also applies to environments used for publishing with OpenID Connect, as the trust configuration of the target system often identifies the repository, the workflow or the environment, but not the branch.

Recommendation

Restrict every environment that holds credentials or is trusted by an external system to the branches or tags that are allowed to deploy, and protect these branches and tags as well, see Protecting branches and Protecting tags and releases.

items.title: Require a manual approval
items.text:
An environment without secrets can serve as a manual approval step, e.g. before an expensive workflow runs or before a workflow runs with elevated permissions:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      environments+: [
        orgs.newEnvironment('manual-approval') {
          reviewers+: [
            "@my-org/maintainers",
          ],
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

Up to 6 users or teams can be listed as reviewers, and the approval of one of them is sufficient.

items.title: GitHub Pages
items.text:
When GitHub Pages is enabled for a repository, GitHub automatically creates an environment named github-pages. Declare it in the configuration, otherwise plan reports it as a resource to delete:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-website') {
      gh_pages_build_type: "workflow",
      environments+: [
        orgs.newEnvironment('github-pages') {
          deployment_branch_policy: "selected",
          branch_policies+: [
            "main",
          ],
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

See Common repository patterns for the other GitHub Pages settings.

items.title: Require a successful deployment before merging
items.text:
A ruleset or a branch protection rule can require that changes were successfully deployed to an environment before they are merged. The required environments must be defined in the same repository:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-service') {
      environments+: [
        orgs.newEnvironment('staging'),
      ],
      rulesets: [
        orgs.newRepoRuleset('default-branch') {
          include_refs+: [
            "~DEFAULT_BRANCH",
          ],
          required_pull_request+: {
            required_approving_review_count: 1,
          },
          required_status_checks: null,
          requires_deployments: true,
          required_deployment_environments+: [
            "staging",
          ],
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

items.title: Environments created by GitHub features
items.text: Besides github-pages, some GitHub features create or use environments with a specific name. Before removing such an environment from the configuration, check whether it is still used. For example, GitHub moved the secrets of the Copilot cloud agent from an environment named copilot to dedicated agent secrets, see the GitHub changelog.

items.title: Securing GitHub Actions
items.text: GitHub Actions settings exist on organization level (settings.workflows) and on repository level (workflows). When the organization setting is more restrictive, the repository setting is ignored, see Organization settings take precedence. This guide covers the settings that limit what workflows can do.

items.title: Restrict the permissions of the GITHUB_TOKEN
items.text:
Every workflow run receives a GITHUB_TOKEN. The setting default_workflow_permissions defines its default permissions:

  • read: read access to the repository contents and packages only
  • write: read and write access for all permission scopes

Workflows that need more permissions declare them explicitly with the permissions key, e.g. a release job:

jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write # create the release
    steps:
      ...

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  settings+: {
    workflows+: {
      default_workflow_permissions: "read",
    },
  },
}

Open in the Playground

Recommendation

Use read as default and grant additional permissions per workflow or job. A compromised step, e.g. a dependency of the build, can then not modify the repository. Since February 2023, GitHub uses read for new organizations, but older organizations and repositories may still use write, see the GitHub changelog. A configuration imported from such an organization contains default_workflow_permissions: "write".

To switch an existing organization from write to read:

  1. Identify the workflows that need write access, e.g. workflows that push commits or tags, create releases, publish packages or comment on pull requests, and add the required permissions to them.
  2. Switch the repositories with such workflows first, e.g. one repository at a time, with workflows+: { default_workflow_permissions: "read" }.
  3. Switch the organization setting. From then on, a repository setting write is ignored.
  4. Watch for failing workflow runs with errors like Resource not accessible by integration.

items.title: Prevent workflows from approving pull requests
items.text:
The setting actions_can_approve_pull_request_reviews controls whether workflows can create and approve pull requests with the GITHUB_TOKEN.

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  settings+: {
    workflows+: {
      actions_can_approve_pull_request_reviews: false,
    },
  },
}

Open in the Playground

Organization policy

An approval by a workflow is not a human review: disable this setting if pull requests require reviews. Some automation, e.g. tools that open release or update pull requests with the GITHUB_TOKEN, needs this setting; in that case, consider a GitHub App token for this automation instead. GitHub disables the setting by default for new organizations, see Preventing GitHub Actions from creating or approving pull requests.

items.title: Control which actions can run
items.text:
The setting allowed_actions controls which actions and reusable workflows can run:

  • all: any action
  • local_only: only actions and reusable workflows defined in the organization
  • selected: actions created by GitHub (allow_github_owned_actions), by verified creators (allow_verified_creator_actions) and actions that match allow_action_patterns
orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  settings+: {
    workflows+: {
      allowed_actions: "selected",
      allow_github_owned_actions: true,
      allow_verified_creator_actions: false,
      allow_action_patterns+: [
        "my-org/*",
        "example-owner/example-action@*",
      ],
    },
  },
}

Open in the Playground

Organization policy

An allow-list reduces the risk of running untrusted code, but every new action requires a configuration change. It suits organizations with a central review of dependencies. Otherwise, pinning actions to a commit SHA, e.g. with the Pin Workflow blueprint, and keeping them up to date with Dependabot provides a good level of control with less maintenance.

Patterns are described in Allowing select actions and reusable workflows to run. The GitHub policy that requires actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA cannot be configured with otterdog.

items.title: Approve workflows from forks
items.text:
Pull requests from forks can run workflows. The setting fork_pr_approval_policy defines when a maintainer has to approve such runs:

Value Approval required for first_time_contributors_new_to_github users who are new to GitHub and never had a contribution merged in the repository first_time_contributors users who never had a contribution merged in the repository all_external_contributors all users who are not members of the organization 
orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  settings+: {
    workflows+: {
      fork_pr_approval_policy: "all_external_contributors",
    },
  },
}

Open in the Playground

Organization policy

Requiring an approval for all external contributors gives maintainers a chance to review the changes before any workflow runs, at the cost of an additional step for every external pull request. It is especially relevant for repositories that use self-hosted runners, see Approving workflow runs from forks.

items.title: Disable GitHub Actions where it is not needed
items.text:
Repositories that do not use workflows, e.g. mirrors, can disable GitHub Actions entirely:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-mirror') {
      workflows+: {
        enabled: false,
      },
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

On organization level, enabled_repositories set to selected only enables GitHub Actions for the repositories listed in selected_repositories.

items.title: Cache size and costs
items.text:
The setting max_cache_size_gb limits the total size of the GitHub Actions caches of a repository. Increasing it may incur costs: depending on the setup of your otterdog installation, such changes require a review by a designated team, see Cost policy.

Policies can enforce further restrictions on GitHub Actions, e.g. the usage of macOS large runners.

items.title: Summary
items.text: Setting Suggested value Reason default_workflow_permissions read least privilege, grant more per workflow actions_can_approve_pull_request_reviews false approvals should come from people fork_pr_approval_policy first_time_contributors or stricter review unknown code before it runs allowed_actions depends on your organization policy trade-off between control and maintenance

items.title: Inherited and explicit values
items.text: Every value that otterdog applies to GitHub comes either from the configuration file of your organization or from the default configuration that this file imports. Knowing where a value comes from explains most surprises when reviewing the output of a plan operation.

items.title: Where values come from
items.text:
A value of a resource is determined in the following order:

  1. The default configuration defines a function for each resource type, e.g. orgs.newRepo or orgs.newBranchProtectionRule. Each function returns an object with a default value for every supported property. The default configuration to use is set by base_template in the otterdog.json file, see Default configuration.
  2. The configuration of your organization overrides the properties that should differ from the defaults. These are the explicit values, all other values are inherited.
  3. Organization settings can take precedence over repository settings, see Organization settings take precedence.

In the following example, has_wiki is explicit, while all other properties of the repository, e.g. delete_branch_on_merge or secret_scanning, are inherited from orgs.newRepo:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      has_wiki: false,
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

To see the values that actually apply, use the following operations:

  • show-default displays the default configuration for an organization
  • show displays the complete configuration of an organization, with all inherited values resolved
  • canonical-diff compares a configuration with the canonical form that import would write, which reveals for example explicit values that are identical to the inherited ones

The Playground of the otterdog dashboard can also be used to evaluate a snippet against the default configuration, e.g. with the link below each example of these guides. It highlights the explicit values that are identical to the values of the default configuration, e.g. has_wiki: true while orgs.newRepo already returns has_wiki: true: these lines can be removed, the values are inherited. Only literal values are compared, e.g. true or "main", not values computed from variables or functions.

Note

The values are compared with the default configuration of otterdog, i.e. the base_template of the organization, not with the defaults of GitHub. Otterdog applies the values of its default configuration: a value that equals the default of GitHub but differs from the default configuration is required, e.g. allow_merge_commit: true when the default configuration disables merge commits.

items.title: The default configuration also defines what is managed
items.text:
The default configuration does not only provide default values. Otterdog only retrieves, compares and applies the resource types and organization settings that the default configuration defines:

  • an organization setting is only managed if its key is present in the default organization settings
  • a resource type, e.g. teams, custom roles or repositories, is only managed if the default configuration provides the corresponding function
  • team permissions of repositories are only managed if the default repository defines team_permissions, see Team Permissions

As a consequence, adding a key or a function to the default configuration makes otterdog start managing it for every organization that uses this default configuration. Run a plan for all affected organizations before updating the default configuration.

items.title: Imported configurations only contain differences
items.text:
The import operation only writes the properties whose live value differs from the default configuration. For an organization that already existed before using otterdog, the imported file usually contains many explicit values, e.g. allow_update_branch: false or delete_branch_on_merge: false. Such values describe the state of the repository at the time of the import, not necessarily a deliberate choice.

Recommendation

Before copying a setting from an existing configuration to another repository, check whether it is still intended. Removing an explicit value that matches the needs of the repository makes it inherit future improvements of the default configuration.

items.title: Extending or replacing values
items.text:
As explained in Resource Format, the + operator extends the inherited value, while omitting it replaces the inherited value. For nested objects like settings or workflows, always use +:, otherwise all other inherited properties of the object are lost.

For lists, both forms are valid but have different effects:

  • <key>+: [...] appends entries to the inherited list
  • <key>: [...] replaces the inherited list

This matters for lists that are not empty in your default configuration, e.g. required status checks, bypass actors, security managers or webhook events. In the following example, the function newRule stands for a branch protection rule as it could be defined by the default configuration of your organization:

// a rule as it could be defined by the default configuration of your organization
local newRule(pattern) = orgs.newBranchProtectionRule(pattern) {
  required_approving_review_count: 1,
  required_status_checks: [
    "license-check",
  ],
};

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('extended-repo') {
      branch_protection_rules: [
        newRule('main') {
          required_status_checks+: [ // (1)!
            "build",
          ],
        },
      ],
    },
    orgs.newRepo('replaced-repo') {
      branch_protection_rules: [
        newRule('main') {
          required_status_checks: [ // (2)!
            "build",
          ],
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}
  1. Required status checks: license-check and build.
  2. Required status checks: only build, the inherited license-check is no longer required.

Open in the Playground

Recommendation

Use +: unless you deliberately want to drop inherited entries. If you do, add a comment that explains why, as reviewers cannot see the inherited entries in the diff of a pull request.

items.title: Always use the functions of the default configuration
items.text:
Create resources with the functions of the default configuration, e.g. orgs.newBranchProtectionRule, instead of writing plain objects. A plain object only contains the properties that are written in it: all other properties are not set, so otterdog does not manage them and the configuration no longer describes the actual protection.

 branch_protection_rules: [
-  {
-    pattern: "main",
-    requires_pull_request: true,
-    required_approving_review_count: 1,
-  },
+  orgs.newBranchProtectionRule('main') {
+    required_approving_review_count: 1,
+  },
 ],

Similarly, use orgs.extendRepo('<name>') instead of orgs.newRepo('<name>') to change a repository that is already defined by the default configuration, see Repository. Using orgs.newRepo would reset all properties that the default configuration customized for this repository.

items.title: Organization settings take precedence
items.text:
Some organization settings restrict what repositories can configure, as GitHub does. When an organization setting is more restrictive, otterdog ignores the repository setting and reports it during validation:

Organization setting Ignored repository setting web_commit_signoff_required: true web_commit_signoff_required workflows.default_workflow_permissions: "read" workflows.default_workflow_permissions workflows.actions_can_approve_pull_request_reviews: false workflows.actions_can_approve_pull_request_reviews workflows.allowed_actions more restrictive than the repository setting workflows.allowed_actions and related settings workflows.enabled_repositories: "none", or "selected" without the repository workflows.enabled has_organization_projects: false has_projects immutable_releases_enforced_repositories includes the repository immutable_releases_enabled

See Organization Settings and Repository for a description of these settings.

Note

A repository setting that is ignored remains in the configuration and takes effect as soon as the organization setting allows it. Remove such settings if they are not intended anymore, otherwise relaxing the organization setting later might have unexpected effects.

items.title: Updating the default configuration
items.text:
Changing a default value affects every resource that does not override it, in every organization that uses the default configuration.

Recommendation

Reference a released version of the default configuration in base_template, e.g. ...@v1.2.0, or a commit SHA instead of ...@main. Before switching to a newer version, review its changes and run a plan operation for the affected organizations to see their impact.

items.title: Migrating to rulesets
items.text:
This guide describes how to replace branch protection rules with rulesets in an otterdog configuration, without leaving a branch unprotected. Read Rulesets or branch protection rules first to check that rulesets cover your needs.

Warning

Do not use the "Convert to ruleset" button of the GitHub web interface on repositories managed by otterdog. The created rulesets are not part of the configuration and are removed the next time the configuration is applied with deletions enabled, see Otterdog specifics.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
1. Map each branch protection rule to one or more rulesets.
  2. Add the rulesets while keeping the branch protection rules.
  3. Verify that the rulesets behave as expected.
  4. Remove the branch protection rules in a separate change.

As GitHub enforces branch protection rules and rulesets together, adding the rulesets first never weakens the protection: the most restrictive setting applies while both exist.

items.title: Step 1: Map the properties
items.text:
Branch protection rule Ruleset pattern include_refs: refs/heads/<pattern>, or ~DEFAULT_BRANCH for the default branch requires_pull_request: true, required_approving_review_count required_pull_request+: { required_approving_review_count: ... } requires_pull_request: false required_pull_request: null dismisses_stale_reviews required_pull_request.dismisses_stale_reviews requires_code_owner_reviews required_pull_request.requires_code_owner_review require_last_push_approval required_pull_request.requires_last_push_approval requires_conversation_resolution required_pull_request.requires_review_thread_resolution requires_status_checks, required_status_checks required_status_checks+: { status_checks: [...] }, or null if no check is required requires_strict_status_checks required_status_checks.strict requires_linear_history, requires_commit_signatures same names requires_deployments, required_deployment_environments same names allows_force_pushes, allows_deletions same names lock_branch allows_updates: false restricts_pushes, push_restrictions allows_updates: false, with the allowed actors as bypass_actors blocks_creations allows_creations: false (default), with the allowed actors as bypass_actors bypass_pull_request_allowances, bypass_force_push_allowances bypass_actors, see Exceptions is_admin_enforced: false #RepositoryAdmin in bypass_actors, see Exceptions restricts_review_dismissals, review_dismissal_allowances no equivalent lock_allows_fetch_and_merge no equivalent

Formats of status checks and actors are described in Status Check, Actor and Bypass Actor.

Note

By default, a ruleset restricts the creation of matching branches to its bypass actors (allows_creations is false). This has no effect on the default branch, but set allows_creations: true for patterns like refs/heads/release/* if contributors could create such branches before.

items.title: Exceptions
items.text:
Exceptions work differently in both mechanisms:

  • a branch protection rule exempts administrators unless is_admin_enforced is enabled, while a ruleset only exempts its bypass actors
  • an allowance of a branch protection rule lifts a single requirement, e.g. the pull request requirement, while a bypass actor of a ruleset bypasses all rules of the ruleset

To keep an exception limited to a single requirement, put this requirement in a separate ruleset and add the bypass actor only to this ruleset, as shown in the example below.

items.title: Step 2: Add the rulesets
items.text:
The following example migrates a typical rule of the default branch. The release app may push without a pull request, and administrators are exempted, as with the original rule.

BeforeDuring the migrationAfter 
orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      branch_protection_rules: [
        orgs.newBranchProtectionRule('main') {
          required_approving_review_count: 1,
          dismisses_stale_reviews: true,
          requires_strict_status_checks: true,
          required_status_checks+: [
            "build",
          ],
          requires_linear_history: true,
          bypass_pull_request_allowances+: [
            "my-release-app",
          ],
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      branch_protection_rules: [
        orgs.newBranchProtectionRule('main') {
          required_approving_review_count: 1,
          dismisses_stale_reviews: true,
          requires_strict_status_checks: true,
          required_status_checks+: [
            "build",
          ],
          requires_linear_history: true,
          bypass_pull_request_allowances+: [
            "my-release-app",
          ],
        },
      ],
      rulesets: [
        orgs.newRepoRuleset('default-branch') {
          include_refs+: [
            "~DEFAULT_BRANCH",
          ],
          bypass_actors+: [
            "#RepositoryAdmin",
          ],
          required_pull_request: null,
          required_status_checks+: {
            strict: true,
            status_checks+: [
              "build",
            ],
          },
          requires_linear_history: true,
        },
        orgs.newRepoRuleset('default-branch-reviews') {
          include_refs+: [
            "~DEFAULT_BRANCH",
          ],
          bypass_actors+: [
            "#RepositoryAdmin",
            "my-release-app",
          ],
          required_pull_request+: {
            required_approving_review_count: 1,
            dismisses_stale_reviews: true,
          },
          required_status_checks: null,
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      rulesets: [
        orgs.newRepoRuleset('default-branch') {
          include_refs+: [
            "~DEFAULT_BRANCH",
          ],
          bypass_actors+: [
            "#RepositoryAdmin", // (1)!
          ],
          required_pull_request: null,
          required_status_checks+: {
            strict: true,
            status_checks+: [
              "build",
            ],
          },
          requires_linear_history: true,
        },
        orgs.newRepoRuleset('default-branch-reviews') {
          include_refs+: [
            "~DEFAULT_BRANCH",
          ],
          bypass_actors+: [
            "#RepositoryAdmin",
            "my-release-app", // (2)!
          ],
          required_pull_request+: {
            required_approving_review_count: 1,
            dismisses_stale_reviews: true,
          },
          required_status_checks: null,
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}
  1. Keeps the exemption of administrators of the original rule (is_admin_enforced: false). Remove it to enforce the rules for administrators as well.
  2. The release app may push without a pull request, but the rules of the first ruleset still apply to it.

Open in the Playground

Apply the change and check with plan that the only remaining differences are the new rulesets.

items.title: Step 3: Verify
items.text:
While the branch protection rule is still in place, check that the rulesets behave as expected:

  • the rulesets are listed in the repository under Settings > Rules > Rulesets
  • pull requests show the expected required reviews and checks, and automation can still push where intended
  • for organizations on GitHub Enterprise, a ruleset can first be added with enforcement: "evaluate": GitHub then only reports what the ruleset would block in the rule insights, see Managing rulesets for a repository, while the branch protection rule still protects the branch

items.title: Step 4: Remove the branch protection rules
items.text:
Remove the branch protection rules from the configuration in a separate change, once the rulesets have been verified. The plan operation reports the removal as a deletion:

  • when changes are applied after merging a pull request, deletions are applied automatically
  • with the command line, apply only removes resources when --delete-resources is specified, see Apply

items.title: Common pitfalls
items.text:
• Status checks reported by apps: keep the <app-slug>:<check-name> format of the original rule, otherwise any source can satisfy the check.
  • Renaming a ruleset: the name identifies a ruleset, renaming it in the configuration deletes it and creates a new one.
  • Limits: a repository can have up to 75 rulesets, see About rulesets.
  • Organization-wide protections: if many repositories share the same protection, consider an organization ruleset for the common part instead of repeating it in every repository.

items.title: Organization-wide rulesets
items.text:
A repository ruleset protects the branches of a single repository. An organization ruleset applies the same rules to several repositories, selected by their name, and is maintained in a single place: administrators of a repository can see it, but not change or remove it. This guide shows how to define a baseline for all repositories and how to target some of them.

Note

GitHub provides organization rulesets with GitHub Team and GitHub Enterprise, see Availability by GitHub plan. Otterdog currently only accepts them for organizations on the enterprise plan, validate reports them as error for other plans. The rules that otterdog supports are the same as for repository rulesets, except the code quality, code coverage and license compliance rules that GitHub only supports for repository rulesets, see Otterdog specifics.

items.title: Protect the default branch of all repositories
items.text:
The following ruleset blocks force pushes and deletions of the default branch in all repositories of the organization, except sandboxes:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  settings+: {
    plan: "enterprise", // (1)!
  },
  rulesets+: [
    orgs.newOrgRuleset('default-branch-baseline') {
      include_repo_names+: [
        "~ALL",
      ],
      exclude_repo_names+: [
        "sandbox-*", // (2)!
      ],
      include_refs+: [
        "~DEFAULT_BRANCH",
      ],
      required_pull_request: null, // (3)!
      required_status_checks: null,
    },
  ],
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo'),
    orgs.newRepo('sandbox-experiments'),
  ],
}
  1. Read-only property that reflects the billing plan of the organization, see the note above.
  2. Repository names are matched with the fnmatch syntax, ~ALL matches all repositories, including the ones created later. validate warns about patterns that do not match any repository, e.g. after a repository has been renamed.
  3. The baseline only blocks force pushes and deletions, which orgs.newOrgRuleset() blocks by default. Requiring pull requests and status checks is left to the rulesets of the repositories, as they differ between repositories.

Open in the Playground

Recommendation

Start with a baseline that every repository can follow, e.g. blocking force pushes and deletions of the default branch, and add stricter rules in the rulesets of the repositories that need them.

items.title: Target repositories by name
items.text:
To apply stricter rules to a group of repositories, select them by a naming convention, e.g. all libraries:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  settings+: {
    plan: "enterprise",
  },
  rulesets+: [
    orgs.newOrgRuleset('libraries') {
      include_repo_names+: [
        "lib-*",
      ],
      protect_repo_names: true, // (1)!
      include_refs+: [
        "~DEFAULT_BRANCH",
      ],
      required_pull_request+: {
        required_approving_review_count: 1,
      },
      required_status_checks: null,
    },
  ],
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('lib-core'),
    orgs.newRepo('lib-cli'),
  ],
}
  1. A repository could otherwise leave the ruleset by being renamed. With protect_repo_names, only the bypass actors of the ruleset can rename the targeted repositories.

Open in the Playground

Otterdog only selects repositories by name: targeting repositories by custom properties, which GitHub supports, cannot be configured with otterdog.

items.title: Require workflows in all repositories
items.text:
An organization ruleset can require workflows maintained in a single repository to pass before pull requests are merged into the default branch of all repositories:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  settings+: {
    plan: "enterprise",
  },
  rulesets+: [
    orgs.newOrgRuleset('required-workflows') {
      include_repo_names+: [
        "~ALL",
      ],
      include_refs+: [
        "~DEFAULT_BRANCH",
      ],
      required_pull_request: null,
      required_status_checks: null,
      required_workflows: orgs.newWorkflows() {
        workflows+: [
          "my-org/.github:.github/workflows/license-check.yml@refs/heads/main", // (1)!
        ],
      },
    },
  ],
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('.github'),
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo'),
  ],
}
  1. A workflow is written as <owner>/<repository>:<path>[@<ref>][#<sha>], the ref being a branch or a tag and the sha a commit, e.g. @refs/heads/main#<sha> to pin the workflow to a commit of the branch, and %, @ and # are written %25, %40 and %23 in a path or a ref. GitHub identifies the repository by its id, otterdog shows it by its full name.

Open in the Playground

items.title: Combine organization and repository rulesets
items.text:
All rulesets that target a branch apply together, whether they are defined by the organization or by the repository: when several rulesets configure the same rule, the most restrictive one applies, see About rulesets. A repository ruleset can therefore add rules to an organization ruleset, but not relax it. An example combining both is shown in Rulesets or branch protection rules.

Bypass actors of a ruleset are only exempted from the rules of this ruleset: a release app that must push to the default branch of all repositories has to be a bypass actor of every ruleset that blocks it.

items.title: Prepare a ruleset before enforcing it
items.text:
enforcement controls whether the rules of a ruleset are enforced:

  • active: the rules are enforced
  • disabled: the ruleset exists but is not enforced, e.g. while it is being prepared
  • evaluate: the rules are not enforced, but GitHub reports which pushes and merges would violate them, see Managing rulesets. Only available with GitHub Enterprise.
orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  settings+: {
    plan: "enterprise",
  },
  rulesets+: [
    orgs.newOrgRuleset('linear-history') {
      enforcement: "disabled",
      include_repo_names+: [
        "~ALL",
      ],
      include_refs+: [
        "~DEFAULT_BRANCH",
      ],
      requires_linear_history: true,
      required_pull_request: null,
      required_status_checks: null,
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

Organization policy

An organization ruleset immediately applies to many repositories. Announce new rules to the maintainers of the repositories before enforcing them, and check that their workflows, e.g. release workflows pushing to protected branches, still work.

items.title: Organization settings and member privileges
items.text: The organization settings define what members can do in the organization and the policies that apply to all repositories. This guide covers the settings related to the security and the governance of the organization. The base permission of members is covered in Teams and access, the security managers in Repository security features.

items.title: Require two-factor authentication
items.text:
Requiring two-factor authentication protects the organization against compromised passwords: members and outside collaborators without two-factor authentication are removed from the organization when it is enabled, see Requiring two-factor authentication in your organization.

two_factor_requirement is a read-only setting in otterdog: GitHub does not allow changing it through its API, it is enabled in the GitHub web interface by an owner of the organization. The configuration shows its current value after an import.

Recommendation

Require two-factor authentication in every organization, and check the members who did not enable it before enabling the requirement, as they lose their access.

items.title: Restrict what members can do
items.text:
The following settings define which actions are reserved to the owners of the organization:

Setting When enabled, members ... members_can_create_public_repositories can create public repositories members_can_create_private_repositories can create private repositories members_can_fork_private_repositories can fork the private repositories of the organization members_can_change_repo_visibility with admin permission on a repository can change its visibility members_can_delete_repositories with admin permission on a repository can delete or transfer it members_can_delete_issues with admin permission on a repository can delete its issues members_can_create_teams can create teams

The example default configuration disables all of them, so that repositories are only created, deleted or made public through the configuration. An organization that lets its members create teams and delete spam issues enables these settings:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  settings+: {
    members_can_create_teams: true,
    members_can_delete_issues: true,
  },
}

Open in the Playground

Organization policy

When repositories are managed with otterdog, the configuration declares all the repositories of the organization:

  • a repository created in the GitHub web interface is not declared: plan reports it as a deletion, and applying the configuration with deletions enabled (--delete-resources) deletes it;
  • a repository deleted in the GitHub web interface is still declared: plan reports it as an addition, and applying the configuration creates it again, without its content, whether deletions are enabled or not.

Keeping repository creation and deletion reserved to owners makes the configuration the single place where repositories are added and removed, see Adding a repository.

Note

Some settings, e.g. members_can_create_teams, members_can_delete_issues, members_can_delete_repositories and members_can_change_repo_visibility, can only be read and changed through the GitHub web interface. Otterdog applies them with the credentials of a user that can log in to GitHub, see Setup. Changes to these settings that are merged in a pull request of the configuration repository have to be applied manually.

items.title: Require a sign-off for commits made in the web interface
items.text:
Some projects require contributors to sign off their commits, e.g. to confirm a developer certificate of origin. web_commit_signoff_required makes GitHub add the sign-off to the commits that are made in its web interface, e.g. when editing a file or applying a suggestion, see Managing the commit signoff policy for your organization.

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  settings+: {
    web_commit_signoff_required: true, // (1)!
  },
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo'),
  ],
}
  1. When enabled on the organization, it applies to all repositories: a repository that disables it is reported as warning by validate, and its setting is ignored.

Open in the Playground

The sign-off of commits pushed from a local clone is added by the contributor, e.g. with git commit -s. It is not checked by this setting, but by a status check of a service or a workflow, which can be required with a ruleset, see Require status checks.

items.title: Classify repositories with custom properties
items.text:
Custom properties add structured metadata to repositories, e.g. their category or their maturity. The organization defines the properties and their allowed values, each repository sets its values:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  settings+: {
    custom_properties+: [
      orgs.newCustomProperty('category') {
        description: "Category used to group repositories",
        value_type: "single_select",
        allowed_values: [
          "library",
          "tool",
          "website",
          "other",
        ],
        required: true,
        default_value: "other", // (1)!
      },
    ],
  },
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-library') {
      custom_properties: {
        category: "library",
      },
    },
  ],
}
  1. A required property needs a default value, which GitHub assigns to the repositories that do not set the property.

Open in the Playground

Custom properties can be used to filter the repositories of the organization on GitHub, and by tools that read them through the GitHub API, e.g. to generate an overview of the repositories, see Managing custom properties for repositories in your organization.

Warning

The value_type of a custom property cannot be changed once the property exists: GitHub rejects the change, which is only detected when the configuration is applied. Remove the property and create a new one instead.

Organization rulesets can target repositories by custom properties on GitHub, but otterdog only supports targeting them by name, see Organization-wide rulesets.

items.title: Pull requests and merging
items.text:
How pull requests are merged shapes the history of a repository: which commits it contains, which messages they carry and whether it stays linear. These repository settings complement the protection of branches, which defines whether a pull request is required, see Protecting branches.

Need Settings Choose how pull requests are merged allow_merge_commit, allow_squash_merge, allow_rebase_merge Restrict the merge methods of protected branches allowed_merge_methods of a ruleset Control the messages of merge and squash commits merge_commit_title, merge_commit_message, squash_merge_commit_title, squash_merge_commit_message Merge pull requests once their requirements are met allow_auto_merge Keep pull requests up to date with their base branch allow_update_branch Delete the branch of a merged pull request delete_branch_on_merge Merge pull requests through a queue required_merge_queue of a ruleset

These settings are not available for archived repositories, otterdog ignores them for these repositories.

items.title: Choose the merge methods
items.text:
GitHub offers three ways to merge a pull request, each one can be allowed or not per repository, see About merge methods on GitHub:

Method Setting History of the base branch Merge commit allow_merge_commit all commits of the pull request, joined by a merge commit Squash allow_squash_merge a single commit for the whole pull request Rebase allow_rebase_merge all commits of the pull request, rewritten on top of the base

The following repository only allows squash merges, so that each pull request results in a single commit:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      allow_merge_commit: false,
      allow_rebase_merge: false,
      allow_squash_merge: true,
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

A protection that requires a linear history (requires_linear_history) rejects merge commits: allow squash or rebase merges in repositories that require it.

Organization policy

Squash merges keep the history of the base branch readable, one commit per change, but lose the individual commits of a pull request. Merge commits and rebase merges keep them, which helps to review the history of large changes. Allowing a single method makes the history predictable, allowing several leaves the choice to whoever merges.

items.title: Restrict the merge methods of protected branches
items.text:
The repository settings apply to all branches. A ruleset can further restrict the merge methods of the branches it protects with allowed_merge_methods, e.g. to require squash merges into the default branch while maintenance branches also accept merge commits:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      allow_merge_commit: true,
      allow_squash_merge: true,
      rulesets: [
        orgs.newRepoRuleset('main') {
          include_refs+: [
            "~DEFAULT_BRANCH",
          ],
          required_pull_request+: {
            allowed_merge_methods: [
              "squash", // (1)!
            ],
          },
          required_status_checks: null,
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}
  1. Allowed values are merge, squash and rebase. A method that the repository does not allow cannot be used, whatever the ruleset allows.

Open in the Playground

items.title: Control the messages of merge and squash commits
items.text:
By default, GitHub builds the message of a squash commit from the commits of the pull request. To use the title and description of the pull request instead, e.g. when pull request titles follow a convention:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      squash_merge_commit_title: "PR_TITLE",
      squash_merge_commit_message: "PR_BODY",
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

GitHub only accepts some combinations of title and message, validate reports the others as error:

Commit Title Message Squash PR_TITLE PR_BODY, BLANK or COMMIT_MESSAGES Squash COMMIT_OR_PR_TITLE COMMIT_MESSAGES Merge commit PR_TITLE PR_BODY or BLANK Merge commit MERGE_MESSAGE PR_TITLE

COMMIT_OR_PR_TITLE uses the title of the commit if the pull request has a single commit, the title of the pull request otherwise.

items.title: Merge pull requests once their requirements are met
items.text:
With allow_auto_merge, the author of a pull request can enable auto-merge, so that GitHub merges the pull request as soon as the required reviews and status checks are satisfied, see Automatically merging a pull request. Auto-merge is only useful for branches whose protection requires reviews or status checks:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      allow_auto_merge: true,
      allow_update_branch: true, // (1)!
      rulesets: [
        orgs.newRepoRuleset('main') {
          include_refs+: [
            "~DEFAULT_BRANCH",
          ],
          required_status_checks+: {
            strict: true, // (2)!
            status_checks+: [
              "build",
            ],
          },
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}
  1. Shows the "Update branch" button on pull requests whose branch is behind the base branch.
  2. Requires the branch of a pull request to be up to date with the base branch before merging. Combined with auto-merge, an outdated pull request waits until its branch is updated.

Open in the Playground

Auto-merge is available for public repositories, and for private repositories with a paid GitHub plan.

items.title: Delete the branch of a merged pull request
items.text: delete_branch_on_merge deletes the head branch of a pull request once it is merged, which keeps the list of branches short. A deleted branch can be restored from the pull request. The example default configuration enables it for all repositories.

items.title: Merge pull requests through a queue
items.text:
A merge queue merges pull requests one after the other, or in groups, after running the required status checks on the result of the merge, see Managing a merge queue. It is configured with required_merge_queue in a ruleset, branch protection rules do not support it in otterdog:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      rulesets: [
        orgs.newRepoRuleset('main') {
          include_refs+: [
            "~DEFAULT_BRANCH",
          ],
          required_status_checks+: {
            status_checks+: [
              "build",
            ],
          },
          required_merge_queue: orgs.newMergeQueue() {
            merge_method: "SQUASH", // (1)!
            max_group_size: 3,
          },
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}
  1. MERGE, SQUASH or REBASE. The other settings of orgs.newMergeQueue(), e.g. build_concurrency and status_check_timeout, come from the default configuration.

Open in the Playground

Warning

The required status checks must also run for the merge queue: the workflows that report them need the merge_group event as trigger, otherwise the queued pull requests wait for checks that never run and are removed from the queue after status_check_timeout minutes.

The merge queue is available for public repositories owned by an organization, and for private repositories with GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

items.title: Repository features and metadata
items.text: Repositories come with features that a project may or may not use, e.g. issues, a wiki, projects or discussions, and with metadata that help to find them, e.g. a description and topics. This guide shows how to enable the features that a project uses, how to set up discussions for the whole organization and how to describe repositories.

items.title: Enable only the features that are used
items.text:
A feature that nobody looks at, e.g. a wiki that is not maintained or issues that are tracked elsewhere, misleads users. The following repository tracks its issues and discussions on GitHub, but keeps its documentation in the repository itself:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      has_issues: true,
      has_discussions: true,
      has_wiki: false,
      has_projects: false,
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

Setting Feature Notes has_issues issues has_discussions discussions the repository used for the discussions of the organization keeps them has_wiki wiki private repositories require a paid GitHub plan has_projects projects of the repository ignored if the organization disables has_organization_projects

Disabling a feature hides it but does not delete its content: issues, wiki pages and discussions come back when the feature is enabled again.

items.title: Discussions for the whole organization
items.text:
Organization discussions are hosted in a repository of the organization, usually the .github repository, see Enabling GitHub Discussions for your organization:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  settings+: {
    has_discussions: true,
    discussion_source_repository: "my-org/.github", // (1)!
  },
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('.github') {
      has_discussions: true, // (2)!
    },
  ],
}
  1. The repository in the format <organization>/<repository>. Enabling has_discussions without it is reported as error by validate.
  2. The source repository must keep discussions enabled, disabling them is reported as error.

Open in the Playground

readers_can_create_discussions controls whether users with read access can start discussions in the repositories of the organization, otherwise only users with at least triage permission can. Users with read access can comment on discussions in both cases.

Note

The discussion settings of the organization can only be read and changed through the GitHub web interface, otterdog applies them with the credentials of a user that can log in to GitHub, see Organization settings and member privileges.

items.title: Describe repositories
items.text:
A description, a homepage and topics help users to find a repository and to understand its purpose. Topics are also used by the search of GitHub:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-library') {
      description: "A library to parse configuration files",
      homepage: "https://my-library.example.org",
      topics+: [
        "configuration",
        "parser",
        "java",
      ],
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

GitHub limits these metadata, validate reports the following as error:

  • a description longer than 350 characters
  • more than 20 topics
  • a topic with other characters than lower-case letters, numbers and -, e.g. GitHub Actions instead of github-actions

Recommendation

Describe every active repository, and agree on a set of topics in the organization, e.g. the technologies and the components, so that topics group related repositories.

Templates, mirrors, forks and websites are covered in Common repository patterns.

items.title: Common repository patterns
items.text: This guide collects the settings of recurring kinds of repositories. All properties are described in Repository.

items.title: Websites with GitHub Pages
items.text:
GitHub Pages can be built from a branch (gh_pages_build_type: "legacy") or by a workflow (gh_pages_build_type: "workflow"). In both cases, GitHub creates an environment named github-pages, which should be declared in the configuration, see Deployment environments.

The repository named <organization>.github.io hosts the website of the organization. GitHub enables Pages for it automatically, so otterdog requires it to be configured:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-org.github.io') {
      gh_pages_build_type: "legacy",
      gh_pages_source_branch: "main",
      gh_pages_source_path: "/",
      environments+: [
        orgs.newEnvironment('github-pages') {
          deployment_branch_policy: "selected",
          branch_policies+: [
            "main",
          ],
        },
      ],
    },
    orgs.newRepo('my-project') {
      gh_pages_build_type: "workflow",
      gh_pages_cname: "docs.example.org", // (1)!
      environments+: [
        orgs.newEnvironment('github-pages') {
          deployment_branch_policy: "selected",
          branch_policies+: [
            "main",
          ],
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}
  1. A custom domain requires DNS records that are configured outside otterdog.

Open in the Playground

Recommendation

When using a custom domain, verify the domain for the organization to prevent domain takeovers, and keep gh_pages_https_enforced enabled.

The organization setting members_can_create_public_pages must be enabled for sites to be published.

items.title: The .github repository
items.text:
A repository named .github provides default community health files, e.g. SECURITY.md or CONTRIBUTING.md, for all repositories of the organization that do not define their own. It is also the usual place for shared workflow templates.

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('.github') {
      description: "Default community health files",
      has_wiki: false,
      has_projects: false,
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

Blueprints can ensure that such a repository and its files exist in every organization, e.g. with the Append Configuration and Required File types.

items.title: Read-only mirrors
items.text:
A mirror of a repository hosted elsewhere should not receive contributions on GitHub:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-mirror') {
      description: "Read-only mirror, contributions are accepted at https://git.example.org/my-project",
      has_issues: false,
      has_projects: false,
      has_wiki: false,
      workflows+: {
        enabled: false,
      },
      rulesets: [
        orgs.newRepoRuleset('read-only') {
          include_refs+: [
            "~ALL",
          ],
          allows_creations: false,
          allows_updates: false,
          allows_deletions: false,
          bypass_actors+: [
            "my-mirror-app",
          ],
          required_pull_request: null,
          required_status_checks: null,
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

Only the app that synchronizes the mirror can push, see Protecting branches.

items.title: Templates and repositories created from a template
items.text:
• is_template: true marks a repository as template.
  • template_repository creates a new repository from a template. post_process_template_content lists files of the new repository in which the Mustache variables {{org}} and {{repo}} are replaced after creation.
orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('project-template') {
      is_template: true,
    },
    orgs.newRepo('my-new-project') {
      template_repository: "my-org/project-template",
      post_process_template_content+: [
        "README.md",
      ],
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

Both template_repository and post_process_template_content are only taken into account when the repository is created. The sync-template operation of the CLI synchronizes the content of repositories created from a template.

items.title: Forks
items.text:
forked_repository creates the repository as a fork of another repository, fork_default_branch_only limits the fork to the default branch. Both are only taken into account during creation, and a repository cannot be created from a template and as a fork at the same time.

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('upstream-library') {
      forked_repository: "example-owner/upstream-library",
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

items.title: Renaming, archiving and deleting
items.text:
• Renaming: list the previous name in aliases, otherwise the repository is deleted and a new one is created, see Renaming of Resources.
  • Archiving: archived: true makes the repository read-only. Many settings cannot be changed on archived repositories, and otterdog ignores them until the repository is unarchived, as well as its branch protection rules.
  • Deleting: removing a repository from the configuration deletes it on GitHub, including its issues, pull requests and wiki, when the configuration is applied with deletions enabled. Pull requests that delete resources are not merged automatically, but the deletion is applied once they are merged.

Warning

Prefer archiving over deleting: a deleted repository cannot be restored by otterdog, and its URL can be taken by a new repository. Transferring a repository to another organization is not supported by otterdog.

items.title: Repository security features
items.text:
GitHub provides several security features per repository. With otterdog, they are configured as repository settings, so that a common baseline can be defined in the default configuration and exceptions are visible in the configuration of the organization.

Need Repository settings Detect leaked credentials and block them on push secret_scanning, secret_scanning_push_protection Get alerts and fixes for vulnerable dependencies dependabot_alerts_enabled, dependabot_security_updates_enabled Let researchers report vulnerabilities privately private_vulnerability_reporting_enabled Analyze the code for vulnerabilities code_scanning_default_setup_enabled and related settings Apply the same features to many repositories code_security_configuration, see Code security configurations

The following example enables all of them for a public repository. Secret scanning, push protection and Dependabot alerts are already enabled by the example default configuration:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      dependabot_security_updates_enabled: true,
      private_vulnerability_reporting_enabled: true,
      code_scanning_default_setup_enabled: true,
      code_scanning_default_languages+: [
        "actions",
        "python",
      ],
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

Note

These features are free for public repositories. For private and internal repositories, secret scanning and code scanning require GitHub Secret Protection and GitHub Code Security, and otterdog does not manage secret scanning, push protection, Dependabot security updates and private vulnerability reporting, see About secret scanning and Configuring default setup for code scanning.

items.title: Secret scanning and push protection
items.text:
Secret scanning detects credentials committed to the repository, push protection rejects pushes that contain them. Push protection requires secret scanning: disabling secret_scanning while secret_scanning_push_protection is enabled is reported as an error, so both settings must be disabled together.

Recommendation

Keep both enabled for all repositories. If a repository contains test data that looks like credentials, prefer excluding the paths in a secret_scanning.yml file over disabling the feature, see Excluding folders and files from secret scanning.

items.title: Dependabot
items.text: dependabot_alerts_enabled reports dependencies with known vulnerabilities, dependabot_security_updates_enabled additionally opens pull requests that update them. Version updates, which keep dependencies up to date regardless of vulnerabilities, are configured in a .github/dependabot.yml file of the repository, not in otterdog. The Required File blueprint can ensure that such a file exists.

items.title: Private vulnerability reporting
items.text:
private_vulnerability_reporting_enabled lets security researchers report vulnerabilities through a private form of a public repository, see Configuring private vulnerability reporting.

Organization policy

Enable private reporting only if someone triages the reports. Document how to report vulnerabilities in a SECURITY.md file, which a Required File blueprint can add to the .github repository of the organization.

items.title: Code scanning
items.text:
Default setup lets GitHub configure and run CodeQL. It is configured with:

  • code_scanning_default_setup_enabled: enables default setup
  • code_scanning_default_languages: the languages to analyze
  • code_scanning_default_query_suite: default or extended

The languages and the query suite are only taken into account when default setup is enabled.

items.title: Supported languages
items.text:
code_scanning_default_languages only accepts the language identifiers of CodeQL, not the names of the languages that GitHub shows for a repository. Some identifiers cover several languages, which cannot be selected separately:

Value Analyzes Languages detected by GitHub actions GitHub Actions workflows always accepted c-cpp C and C++ C, C++ csharp C# C# go Go Go java-kotlin Java and Kotlin Java, Kotlin javascript JavaScript JavaScript python Python Python ruby Ruby Ruby swift Swift Swift rust Rust Rust typescript TypeScript TypeScript

Deprecated: javascript-typescript

GitHub no longer reports javascript-typescript, it returns javascript and typescript separately. Existing configurations that still list javascript-typescript keep working: otterdog translates it to javascript and typescript when loading the configuration. Replace it with the two values to get rid of the deprecated one. If both are configured, validate only requires one of them to be detected in the repository, as CodeQL analyzes them together.

Any other value is rejected as soon as the configuration is loaded, e.g. by validate or plan: java, kotlin, c or cpp, as well as languages that CodeQL does not analyze, e.g. PHP, Scala, Shell or Jsonnet. These values follow the REST API for default setup, which documents all of them except rust: CodeQL analyzes Rust in default setup since its general availability in October 2025, see the GitHub changelog. The languages supported by CodeQL are listed in Supported languages and frameworks.

items.title: Languages must be detected in the repository
items.text:
validate also checks each configured language against the languages that GitHub detects in the repository, which are shown in the sidebar of the repository: a language that is not detected, e.g. python for a repository without Python code, is reported as error, with the list of detected languages. Only actions is always accepted.

As a consequence, languages can only be configured for repositories that already exist and contain code: create the repository first, then configure the languages in a second change. A new repository can enable default setup without languages:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-new-repo') {
      code_scanning_default_setup_enabled: true, // (1)!
    },
  ],
}
  1. Without configured languages, the languages to analyze are left to GitHub. Once the repository contains code, configure the languages explicitly, so that the configuration shows what is analyzed.

Open in the Playground

Once the repository contains code, e.g. Java, Kotlin and TypeScript code as well as workflows, the languages are configured with their CodeQL identifiers:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      code_scanning_default_setup_enabled: true,
      code_scanning_default_languages+: [
        "actions",
        "java-kotlin", // (1)!
        "javascript",
        "typescript",
      ],
      code_scanning_default_query_suite: "extended", // (2)!
    },
  ],
}
  1. A single identifier for Java and Kotlin, listing java or kotlin is rejected.
  2. The extended suite runs additional queries, which find more problems but also report more false positives.

Open in the Playground

Warning

Default setup and advanced setup (a custom CodeQL workflow) exclude each other: enabling default setup disables the existing CodeQL workflow and blocks its uploads. If a repository uses a custom workflow, keep code_scanning_default_setup_enabled disabled.

items.title: Code security configurations
items.text:
A code security configuration groups the security features of the organization, and GitHub applies them to the repositories the configuration is attached to. A configuration is attached to a repository with its code_security_configuration property:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  code_security_configurations+: [
    orgs.newOrgCodeSecurityConfiguration('baseline') {
      description: "Secret scanning and Dependabot for all repositories",
      code_security: "enabled", // (1)!
      secret_protection: "enabled",
      dependabot_alerts: "enabled",
      dependabot_security_updates: "enabled",
      secret_scanning: "enabled",
      secret_scanning_push_protection: "enabled",
      private_vulnerability_reporting: "enabled",
    },
  ],
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      code_security_configuration: "baseline", // (2)!
    },
  ],
}
  1. GitHub requires secret_protection for the secret scanning features, and code_security for the code scanning ones. Without an unbundled GitHub Advanced Security plan, which is not available for an organization with free plan, both products must have the same status.
  2. The settings of the repository that the configuration sets, e.g. dependabot_alerts_enabled, are not managed on the repository anymore, the configuration takes precedence. A repository without code_security_configuration keeps the configuration attached to it on GitHub.

Open in the Playground

Warning

The features of newOrgCodeSecurityConfiguration are disabled by default, except the dependency graph: attaching a configuration disables the features it does not enable on the repository, e.g. code scanning default setup. Set a feature to not_set to leave it to the repositories.

items.title: Default configuration for new repositories
items.text:
default_for_new_repos attaches a configuration to the new repositories of a visibility, all, public or private_and_internal, when GitHub creates them. The organization setting default_code_security_configurations_disabled removes any default configuration, it has to be disabled:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  settings+: {
    default_code_security_configurations_disabled: false, // (1)!
  },
  code_security_configurations+: [
    orgs.newOrgCodeSecurityConfiguration('public-baseline') {
      code_security: "enabled",
      secret_protection: "enabled",
      dependabot_alerts: "enabled",
      secret_scanning: "enabled",
      secret_scanning_push_protection: "enabled",
      default_for_new_repos: "public", // (2)!
    },
  ],
}
  1. Otherwise, the validation reports an error, as the setting would remove the default configuration again.
  2. A visibility can have one default configuration only, all covers both public and private_and_internal.

Open in the Playground

items.title: Delegated bypass of push protection
items.text:
With delegated bypass, pushing a secret requires the approval of a reviewer, a team or a role referenced like the bypass actors of rulesets. The suffix :exempt exempts a reviewer from push protection instead, e.g. for automation:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  code_security_configurations+: [
    orgs.newOrgCodeSecurityConfiguration('baseline') {
      code_security: "enabled",
      secret_protection: "enabled",
      secret_scanning: "enabled",
      secret_scanning_push_protection: "enabled",
      secret_scanning_delegated_bypass: "enabled",
      secret_scanning_delegated_bypass_reviewers: [
        "@my-org/security-team",
        "#OrganizationAdmin",
        "@my-org/release-bots:exempt",
      ],
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

Warning

The configurations of the organization that are not defined in the otterdog configuration are deleted with --delete-resources, and listed as deletions by plan otherwise. GitHub created such configurations for the organizations that existed in March 2024, e.g. Legacy - public repositories, from their former settings for new repositories. Delete them if no repository is attached to them, or import them to keep them. The predefined configurations of GitHub, e.g. GitHub recommended, are not managed.

To only delete these configurations, without applying any other change, select them with --delete-filter, e.g. in all organizations:

otterdog apply --delete-resources --delete-filter 'org_code_security_configuration[name="Legacy*"]'

See deleting selected resources.

Note

For private and internal repositories, code_security and secret_protection enable GitHub Code Security and GitHub Secret Protection, which are licensed per active committer, they are free for public repositories. Enabling them in a configuration attached to private repositories, or attaching a private repository to a configuration enabling them, is thus considered to be cost-related, except for an organization with free plan, for which they cannot be purchased. A configuration enabling them for public repositories only can be auto-merged, if it is new or the private repositories of the organization specify their configuration, as the configuration attached on GitHub to the other ones is not known when validating a pull request.

items.title: Organization settings related to security
items.text:
• security_managers lists the teams that get the security manager role, which grants access to the security alerts and settings of all repositories, see Managing security managers.
  • default_code_security_configurations_disabled: true removes the default code security configurations of the organization, including the predefined ones of GitHub. Set it to false to use a default configuration for new repositories, it does not create one by itself.
orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  settings+: {
    security_managers+: [
      "security-team",
    ],
  },
  teams+: [
    orgs.newTeam('security-team') {
      description: "Triages security alerts and vulnerability reports",
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

items.title: Reusing configuration with Jsonnet
items.text: When many repositories share the same settings, repeating them makes the configuration long and lets the repositories drift apart over time. As the configuration is written in Jsonnet, common settings can be defined once and reused.

items.title: Functions for families of repositories
items.text:
A local function can define the settings of a family of repositories. Each repository can still override them:

local newLibraryRepo(name) = orgs.newRepo(name) {
  dependabot_security_updates_enabled: true,
  private_vulnerability_reporting_enabled: true,
  rulesets: [
    orgs.newRepoRuleset('default-branch') {
      include_refs+: [
        "~DEFAULT_BRANCH",
      ],
      required_pull_request+: {
        required_approving_review_count: 1,
      },
      required_status_checks: null,
    },
  ],
};

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    newLibraryRepo('library-a'),
    newLibraryRepo('library-b') {
      description: "Library B", // (1)!
    },
  ],
}
  1. Settings can be added or overridden as for any other repository.

Open in the Playground

items.title: Parameterized protections
items.text:
Functions can take parameters, and Jsonnet supports conditions and list comprehensions to compute values:

local defaultBranchRuleset(checks=[]) = orgs.newRepoRuleset('default-branch') {
  include_refs+: [
    "~DEFAULT_BRANCH",
  ],
  required_pull_request+: {
    required_approving_review_count: 1,
  },
  required_status_checks:
    if std.length(checks) > 0
    then orgs.newStatusChecks() { status_checks: checks }
    else null,
};

local maintenanceBranches = ["1.x", "2.x"];

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      rulesets: [
        defaultBranchRuleset(["build", "test"]),
        orgs.newRepoRuleset('maintenance-branches') {
          include_refs+: [
            "refs/heads/maintenance/%s" % branch
            for branch in maintenanceBranches
          ],
          required_pull_request+: {
            required_approving_review_count: 1,
          },
          required_status_checks: null,
        },
      ],
    },
    orgs.newRepo('my-docs') {
      rulesets: [
        defaultBranchRuleset(),
      ],
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

See the Jsonnet standard library for the available functions.

items.title: Organization-specific defaults
items.text:
If most repositories of an organization deviate from the default configuration in the same way, the functions of the default configuration can be overridden at the top of the configuration file:

local defaults = import 'vendor/otterdog-defaults/otterdog-defaults.libsonnet'; // (1)!

local orgs = defaults + {
  newRepo(name):: defaults.newRepo(name) {
    dependabot_security_updates_enabled: true,
  },
};

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo'),
  ],
}
  1. Keep the import statement of your configuration file, which depends on the default configuration in use.

Open in the Playground

Note

The override only applies to the calls in your configuration file. Resources that the default configuration itself creates, e.g. repositories defined by orgs.newOrg, still use the original functions. If the same deviation applies to several organizations, change the default configuration instead.

items.title: Trade-offs
items.text:
Warning

The import operation writes the configuration in its canonical form: local functions, variables and comments are lost, and only the previous file is kept as backup with the .bak extension. Once a configuration uses functions, update it by editing it rather than by importing it again.

  • Review: the diff of a pull request shows the change of a function, not its effect on every repository. Review the output of plan, or the automated comment on the pull request, to see the actual changes.
  • Canonical form: canonical-diff reports the differences between the configuration and its canonical form, which includes every use of a function.
  • Readability: a few well-named functions make a large configuration easier to read, deeply nested functions make it harder. Prefer simple functions with a clear purpose, and document their parameters with a comment.
  • Default branch: to protect the default branch, prefer ~DEFAULT_BRANCH in a ruleset over referring to the default_branch property of the repository with self.

items.title: Rulesets or branch protection rules
items.text:
GitHub offers two mechanisms to protect branches: branch protection rules and rulesets. Both are supported by GitHub and by otterdog. GitHub describes rulesets as a more flexible way to manage protections and provides a tool to convert branch protection rules to rulesets, but branch protection rules are not deprecated. Tag protection rules, on the other hand, have been retired by GitHub and replaced by tag rulesets, see Protecting tags and releases.

This guide compares both mechanisms and lists what otterdog supports. To migrate existing rules, see Migrating to rulesets.

items.title: Comparison
Availability by GitHub plan
items.text:
Feature Availability on GitHub Branch protection rules and rulesets public repositories with GitHub Free, public and private repositories with GitHub Pro, Team and Enterprise Organization rulesets GitHub Team and GitHub Enterprise Push rulesets private and internal repositories with GitHub Team and GitHub Enterprise Metadata restrictions (commit message, emails, branch and tag names) GitHub Enterprise Code quality and code coverage rules GitHub Team and GitHub Enterprise, repository rulesets only License compliance rule GitHub Enterprise, repository rulesets only Required workflows rule organization rulesets only Enforcement evaluate GitHub Enterprise Merge queue public repositories owned by an organization, private repositories with GitHub Enterprise Cloud

validate warns about the rules of a ruleset that require a higher plan than the plan of the organization in its configuration, it does not warn if neither the configuration nor its default configuration sets plan, see Organization Settings. validate reports push rules for a public repository as an error, whatever the plan. Plans change over time, check the GitHub documentation before relying on a feature: About rulesets, Organization rulesets for GitHub Team, Managing a merge queue.

items.title: Otterdog specifics
items.text:
Otterdog does not support all features of rulesets. The following table lists the rules that can be configured:

Rule on GitHub Ruleset property in otterdog Restrict creations, updates and deletions allows_creations, allows_updates, allows_deletions Block force pushes allows_force_pushes Require linear history requires_linear_history Require signed commits requires_commit_signatures Require deployments to succeed requires_deployments, required_deployment_environments Require a pull request before merging required_pull_request Require status checks to pass required_status_checks Require merge queue required_merge_queue Automatically request Copilot code review copilot_code_review Restrict commit metadata commit_message_pattern, commit_author_email_pattern, committer_email_pattern Restrict branch names, restrict tag names branch_name_pattern, tag_name_pattern Require code scanning results required_code_scanning Require code quality results required_code_quality Restrict code coverage required_code_coverage Require license compliance results requires_license_compliance_scanning Require workflows to pass before merging (organization rulesets) required_workflows Restrict file paths (push rulesets) restricted_file_paths, restricted_file_paths_exceptions Restrict file path length (push rulesets) max_file_path_length Restrict file extensions (push rulesets) restricted_file_extensions Restrict file size (push rulesets) max_file_size, max_file_size_exceptions

The following features cannot be configured with otterdog:

  • the parameter update_allows_fetch_and_merge of the rule restricting updates and the required reviewers of the rule requiring a pull request
  • targeting the repositories of an organization ruleset by custom properties, only repository names are supported
  • deploy keys as bypass actors

Warning

Otterdog manages all rulesets and branch protection rules of the repositories and the organization:

  • a protection created in the GitHub web interface, including with the "Convert to ruleset" button, is not part of the configuration: plan reports it as a deletion, and it is removed when the configuration is applied with deletions enabled (--delete-resources for the command line, always for changes applied after merging a pull request)
  • otterdog updates a ruleset by sending its complete definition, so rules that otterdog does not support and that were added to a managed ruleset in the web interface are removed when the ruleset is updated

Make all changes to protections through the configuration.

items.title: When to prefer rulesets
items.text:
Rulesets are the better fit when:

  • several protections must apply to the same branch, e.g. an organization baseline and repository specifics
  • tags must be protected
  • pull requests should go through a merge queue
  • exceptions must be explicit and visible, e.g. a release app or a team that may only bypass through pull requests
  • a protection should be tested before it is enforced, with the evaluate enforcement
  • the protection should follow the default branch, even if it is renamed

items.title: When branch protection rules remain a good choice
items.text:
• Existing rules that meet the needs of the project: there is no deprecation that requires migrating them.
