  • Otterdog has no ruleset equivalent for restricting who can dismiss reviews (restricts_review_dismissals) and for allowing fork syncing on a locked branch (lock_allows_fetch_and_merge).

Recommendation

For new protections, prefer rulesets when your GitHub plan supports them. Avoid protecting the same branch with both mechanisms in the long term: GitHub enforces both, but the effective protection becomes harder to review. Combining them is useful during a migration.

items.title: Secrets and variables
items.text:
Workflows often need credentials, e.g. to publish packages or sign artifacts, and configuration values. GitHub Actions provides secrets for sensitive values and variables for other values. Otterdog manages both on organization, repository and environment level.

Scope Properties Available to Organization secrets, variables the repositories selected by visibility Repository secrets, variables all workflows of the repository Environment secrets, variables jobs that use the environment, once its protection rules pass

The visibility of organization secrets and variables can be:

  • public: all repositories of the organization
  • private: private and internal repositories, not available for organizations on the free plan
  • selected: only the repositories listed in selected_repositories

items.title: Reference secret values, never write them
items.text:
Secret values must not be written in the configuration, which is stored in a repository. Instead, reference them in a credential provider with the format <provider>:<data>, e.g. pass:path/to/secret. Otterdog resolves the reference when it applies the configuration. The supported providers and their formats are listed in SecretValue, and validate reports secret values that do not use a credential provider as warning.

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  secrets+: [
    orgs.newOrgSecret('SIGNING_KEY') {
      value: "pass:path/to/signing-key",
      visibility: "selected",
      selected_repositories+: [
        "my-library",
      ],
    },
  ],
  variables+: [
    orgs.newOrgVariable('REGISTRY_URL') {
      value: "https://registry.example.org",
    },
  ],
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-library') {
      secrets+: [
        orgs.newRepoSecret('DOCS_DEPLOY_TOKEN') {
          value: "pass:path/to/docs-deploy-token",
        },
      ],
      environments+: [
        orgs.newEnvironment('publish') {
          deployment_branch_policy: "selected",
          branch_policies+: [
            "tag:v*",
          ],
          secrets+: [
            orgs.newEnvSecret('REGISTRY_TOKEN') {
              value: "pass:path/to/registry-token",
            },
          ],
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

Recommendation

Give each secret the narrowest scope that works: an environment secret for deployment credentials, protected by the rules of the environment (see Deployment environments), a repository secret for a single repository, and an organization secret with selected visibility for credentials that several repositories share. A secret with public visibility is available to every repository, including repositories created later.

items.title: Override a value for a repository or an environment
items.text:
When secrets or variables with the same name are defined on several levels, the most specific one is used: an environment value takes precedence over a repository value, which takes precedence over an organization value, see Using secrets in GitHub Actions. This allows defining a value for most repositories and overriding it where needed:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  variables+: [
    orgs.newOrgVariable('REGISTRY_URL') {
      value: "https://registry.example.org", // (1)!
    },
  ],
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-library') {
      variables+: [
        orgs.newRepoVariable('REGISTRY_URL') {
          value: "https://staging.registry.example.org", // (2)!
        },
      ],
      environments+: [
        orgs.newEnvironment('release') {
          variables+: [
            orgs.newEnvVariable('REGISTRY_URL') {
              value: "https://registry.example.org", // (3)!
            },
          ],
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}
  1. Used by all repositories, public being the default visibility of organization variables in the example default configuration.
  2. Used by the workflows of my-library, e.g. to publish snapshots to a staging registry.
  3. Used by the jobs of my-library that run in the release environment.

Open in the Playground

Recommendation

Overriding a secret hides which value a workflow actually uses. Prefer distinct names, e.g. STAGING_TOKEN and RELEASE_TOKEN, for secrets that grant different permissions, and keep overrides for configuration values.

items.title: Dependabot and Codespaces secrets
items.text:
Dependabot and Codespaces use their own secrets, which GitHub manages independently of the secrets of GitHub Actions:

  • Dependabot secrets are used by Dependabot, e.g. to access private registries, and are the only secrets available to workflows triggered by Dependabot, e.g. a workflow running for a pull request opened by Dependabot.
  • Codespaces secrets are available as environment variables in the codespaces created for a repository.

They are defined in the dependabot_secrets and codespaces_secrets properties of an organization or a repository, see Organization Dependabot Secret, Organization Codespaces Secret, Repository Dependabot Secret and Repository Codespaces Secret. A secret with the same name can be defined for GitHub Actions and for Dependabot, e.g. when a workflow needs the same credential whether it is triggered by Dependabot or not:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  secrets+: [
    orgs.newOrgSecret('REGISTRY_TOKEN') {
      value: "pass:path/to/registry-token",
    },
  ],
  dependabot_secrets+: [
    orgs.newOrgDependabotSecret('REGISTRY_TOKEN') {
      value: "pass:path/to/registry-token",
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

Note

Otterdog only reads the Dependabot and Codespaces secrets when the default configuration defines the corresponding function, e.g. newOrgDependabotSecret for the Dependabot secrets of an organization and newRepoDependabotSecret for those of its repositories. The credentials used by otterdog then need access to these secrets, see Create a GitHub App.

items.title: Secrets managed outside otterdog
items.text:
A secret with the redacted value ********, which import writes as GitHub never discloses secret values, is skipped by otterdog, see Redacted values. Such a secret can be maintained in the GitHub web interface.

Organization policy

Managing secrets with otterdog makes them visible in the configuration and centralizes their rotation, but only people with access to the credential provider can change them. Keeping a secret as ******** lets maintainers of a repository manage it themselves, but it is not visible which value is used and when it was rotated.

items.title: Updating secret values
items.text: Otterdog cannot detect that the value of a secret changed in the credential provider. After rotating a credential, update the secret explicitly, see Updating values.

items.title: Avoid long-lived secrets
items.text: Many cloud providers and package registries accept short-lived tokens that a workflow obtains with OpenID Connect, without storing any secret in GitHub, see OpenID Connect. Combined with a protected environment, this is usually safer than a long-lived token stored as secret.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
• Secret names must not start with GITHUB_, and must be uppercase as GitHub normalizes them to uppercase.
  • Secrets and variables of Copilot agents cannot be managed with otterdog, see Unsupported Features. GitHub moved the secrets of the Copilot cloud agent from an environment named copilot to dedicated agent secrets, see the GitHub changelog.

items.title: Protecting tags and releases
items.text:
Release tags identify the code that was released. If a tag can be moved or deleted, users who download a release later might get different code than what was reviewed, tested or signed. This guide shows how to protect tags with rulesets and how to make releases immutable.

Note

GitHub retired tag protection rules and migrated them to tag rulesets, see the GitHub changelog. Otterdog does not support tag protection rules, use rulesets with target: "tag" instead.

items.title: Prevent tags from being moved or deleted
items.text:
The following ruleset allows users with write access to create tags, but nobody can move or delete them afterwards:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      rulesets: [
        orgs.newRepoRuleset('tags') {
          target: "tag",
          include_refs+: [
            "~ALL",
          ],
          allows_creations: true,
          allows_updates: false, // (1)!
          required_pull_request: null, // (2)!
          required_status_checks: null,
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}
  1. Deletions and force pushes are blocked by default (allows_deletions and allows_force_pushes are false).
  2. Pull requests do not apply to tags, and this ruleset does not require status checks.

Open in the Playground

For tag rulesets, include_refs accepts ~ALL or patterns of the form refs/tags/<pattern>, see Ref Matcher.

items.title: Restrict who can create release tags
items.text:
To ensure that releases are only created by the release process, restrict the creation of release tags to a release app or a team of release managers:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      rulesets: [
        orgs.newRepoRuleset('release-tags') {
          target: "tag",
          include_refs+: [
            "refs/tags/v*",
          ],
          allows_creations: false,
          allows_updates: false,
          bypass_actors+: [
            "my-release-app",
            "@my-org/release-managers",
          ],
          required_pull_request: null,
          required_status_checks: null,
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

Warning

With allows_creations: false and no bypass actor, nobody can create matching tags, which blocks every release. If tags are created by a workflow, make sure that the identity used by the workflow is allowed to create them, e.g. by using a token of a GitHub App that is listed as bypass actor.

Bypass actors can also move or delete the matching tags. Combine both rulesets if tags must stay unchanged for everybody: since all matching rulesets apply, the first ruleset still blocks updates and deletions for the bypass actors of the second one.

items.title: Restrict the names of tags
items.text:
A pattern can enforce a naming scheme for tags, e.g. semantic versions:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  settings+: {
    plan: "enterprise", // (1)!
  },
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      rulesets: [
        orgs.newRepoRuleset('tag-names') {
          target: "tag",
          include_refs+: [
            "~ALL",
          ],
          allows_creations: true,
          required_pull_request: null,
          required_status_checks: null,
          tag_name_pattern: orgs.newPattern() {
            name: "Semantic version",
            operator: "regex", // (2)!
            pattern: "^v[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+$",
          },
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}
  1. Read-only property that reflects the billing plan of the organization. Restricting the names of tags requires GitHub Enterprise, validate warns otherwise.
  2. The operator is one of starts_with, ends_with, contains or regex, set negate: true to reject the tags that match the pattern instead, see Pattern Settings.

Open in the Playground

Only tags like v1.2.3 can be pushed. A tag name pattern is only supported by rulesets with target: "tag".

items.title: Make releases immutable
items.text:
When a release is immutable, its tag cannot be moved or deleted while the release exists, and its assets cannot be modified or deleted. Immutability only applies to releases published after it has been enabled, see Immutable releases.

Immutable releases can be enforced for some or all repositories of an organization, or enabled per repository:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  settings+: {
    immutable_releases_enforced_repositories: "selected",
    immutable_releases_selected_repositories+: [
      "my-library",
    ],
  },
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-library'),
    orgs.newRepo('my-tool') {
      immutable_releases_enabled: true,
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

When the organization enforces immutable releases for a repository, the repository setting is ignored, see Organization settings take precedence. These settings are only managed if the default configuration of your organization defines them, see The default configuration also defines what is managed.

Recommendation

Protect release tags with a ruleset in every repository that publishes releases. Immutable releases additionally protect the release assets, but only for releases published after enabling them, while a tag ruleset protects all matching tags, with or without a release.

items.title: Deploy only from tags
items.text: To ensure that deployment credentials are only available to workflows that run for a release tag, restrict the environment used for publishing to tags, see Deployment environments.

items.title: Teams and access
items.text: Access to the repositories of an organization results from the base permission of the organization, the teams and their permissions on repositories, and individual collaborators. Otterdog manages the first two; individual collaborators cannot be managed with otterdog.

items.title: Base permission
items.text:
The organization setting default_repository_permission grants a permission on all repositories to every member of the organization: none, read, write or admin, see Setting base permissions for an organization. Members keep higher permissions that they get from a team.

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  settings+: {
    default_repository_permission: "none",
  },
}

Open in the Playground

Organization policy

With none, every access must be granted explicitly through a team, which makes access reviewable in the configuration. With read, all members can read private repositories, which eases collaboration in organizations whose members all work on the same projects. A base permission of write or admin is rarely appropriate, as it grants access to every new repository.

Related settings restrict what members can do on organization level, e.g. members_can_create_public_repositories, members_can_create_teams or members_can_delete_repositories, see Organization Settings.

items.title: Teams
items.text:
Teams are defined with orgs.newTeam. Their members can be managed in the configuration or elsewhere:

Members managed ... Configuration in the configuration members lists the GitHub logins elsewhere, e.g. in the GitHub web interface skip_members: true, otterdog manages the team but ignores its members by an external tool, including the team itself the team is excluded with exclude_teams, see Organization-wide policies by an identity provider (IdP), with GitHub Enterprise Cloud team_sync or external_group_id connects the team to IdP groups, see Teams managed by an identity provider 
orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  teams+: [
    orgs.newTeam('maintainers') {
      description: "Maintainers of the project",
      members+: [
        "alice",
        "bob",
      ],
    },
    orgs.newTeam('contributors') {
      description: "Contributors, managed in the GitHub web interface",
      skip_members: true,
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

Note

Adding a user who is not yet a member of the organization to a team invites this user to the organization. With skip_non_organization_members: true, validate instead reports such users as an error, so that invitations stay under the control of another process.

Teams with privacy: "secret" are only visible to their members and organization owners. Secret teams cannot be used as bypass actors of rulesets, see Creating rulesets for a repository.

items.title: Teams managed by an identity provider
items.text:
On GitHub Enterprise Cloud, the members of a team can be provisioned by groups of an identity provider (IdP), depending on how the organization authenticates its members:

  • with team synchronization, up to five IdP groups, identified by their id, are connected to a team with team_sync
  • with Enterprise Managed Users (EMU), a single external group is connected to a team with external_group_id

The members of such a team are provisioned by the IdP, so members is not set and the current members of the team are ignored, see Identity provider integration.

Team synchronizationExternal group (EMU) 
orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  teams+: [
    orgs.newTeam('admins') {
      description: "Admins, provisioned by the IdP groups",
      team_sync: [
        orgs.newTeamSync('5d4b0a8e-2c19-4b5f-8d6c-1f2e3a4b5c6d') {
          name: "git-admins",
          description: "Admin access via the IdP",
        },
        orgs.newTeamSync('9f8e7d6c-5b4a-4321-8fed-cba987654321') {
          name: "git-release-managers",
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  teams+: [
    orgs.newTeam('admins') {
      description: "Admins, provisioned by an external group",
      external_group_id: 1234,
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

The ids of the available groups can be listed with the GitHub REST API, see List IdP groups for an organization and List external groups available to an organization.

items.title: Grant teams access to repositories
items.text:
The repository property team_permissions maps the slug of a team to its permission on the repository:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  teams+: [
    orgs.newTeam('maintainers'),
    orgs.newTeam('documentation'),
  ],
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      team_permissions+: {
        maintainers: "maintain",
        documentation: "triage",
      },
    },
  ],
}

Open in the Playground

The permissions and their GitHub roles are listed in Team Permissions, see also Repository roles for an organization.

Warning

When the default configuration defines team_permissions, as the example default configuration does, the team permissions of every repository are managed: a team that has access to a repository on GitHub but is not listed in its configuration loses its access the next time the configuration is applied. As the removal is a modification of the repository, it is applied even without --delete-resources. This also applies to teams whose members are managed outside otterdog. Review such removals with plan before applying.

The permissions of teams excluded with exclude_teams are ignored, unless the repository lists the team in team_permissions, see Organization-wide policies.

Recommendation

Grant the lowest permission that fits the role of a team, e.g. maintain instead of admin for maintainers, and grant access through teams rather than to individual users, so that access can be reviewed in one place.

items.title: Security managers and custom roles
items.text:
• The organization setting security_managers assigns the security manager role to teams, see Repository security features.
  • Custom organization roles can be defined with orgs.newOrgRole. They require the enterprise plan.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
This page lists frequent messages of validate and frequent surprises of plan and apply, with their cause and how to address them. validate reports three levels of messages:

  • Error: the configuration cannot be applied, it must be fixed.
  • Warning: the configuration can be applied, but a setting will not be applied as specified.
  • Info: a remark, only shown with -v, e.g. a resource that will be skipped.

In the messages below, <repository> stands for the resource reported by validate, e.g. repository[name="my-repo"].

items.title: Values of the configuration
items.text:
invalid value at '<path>': <value> is not of type '<type>'

A value does not have the type that otterdog expects, e.g. "0" instead of 0 for required_approving_review_count. Otterdog checks the configuration against its JSON schemas before any other validation, and stops at such an error. Other messages of the same form report a missing property, or a property that is not allowed at this place.

invalid value at '<path>': '<value>' is not one of [...]

The property only accepts the listed values, e.g. 'TITLE' instead of 'PR_TITLE' for merge_commit_title. The reference of the property lists the same values.

ignoring unknown properties found while validating organization config: Additional properties are not allowed ('<property>' was unexpected) (Warning)

The property is unknown to otterdog, usually because of a typo, e.g. has_wikki instead of has_wiki, and has no effect. Fix its name or remove it.

The Playground of the otterdog dashboard checks the same schemas while a configuration is edited: it underlines the invalid values and the unknown properties in the editor, and lists them when their number is clicked in its status. Its Validate button also has the configuration of an organization validated by otterdog, with limitations, see Validation in the Playground.

items.title: Code scanning
items.text:
invalid value at '<path>.code_scanning_default_languages[<index>]': '<language>' is not one of [...]

The value is not a CodeQL identifier, e.g. java or kotlin instead of java-kotlin. Use one of the values listed in Supported languages.

<repository> has 'code_scanning_default_languages' configured while the repository does not yet exist.

Languages are checked against the languages detected in the repository, which requires the repository to exist. Create the repository first, with default setup enabled but without languages, then configure the languages in a second change, see Languages must be detected in the repository.

<repository> has 'code_scanning_default_languages' configured with '<language>' but this language is not detected in the repository. Detected languages: ...

GitHub does not detect any code of this language in the repository, e.g. python for a repository without Python code. Remove the language, or configure it once the code has been pushed. The detected languages are listed in the message.

items.title: Secrets and webhooks
items.text:
<organization_codespaces|repository_codespaces> secrets of '<org>' are not available (GitHub answers 404 for '<path>'), they are skipped (Warning)

GitHub answers the Codespaces secrets endpoint with 404, e.g. because Codespaces is not available for the organization. Otterdog skips these secrets, other secrets are not affected. If the configuration declares Codespaces secrets, the operation fails instead with declares ... secrets which cannot be managed, as they cannot be compared with the live state: remove them, or make the endpoint available. To not read Codespaces secrets at all, use a default configuration without newOrgCodespacesSecret and newRepoCodespacesSecret.

<secret> only has a dummy value, resource will be skipped. (Info) <webhook> has a secret set, but only a dummy secret '********' is provided in the configuration, will be skipped. (Info)

The value is redacted, usually after an import, as GitHub never discloses secret values. The resource is not changed by otterdog. Replace the value with a reference to a credential provider to manage it, see Secrets managed outside otterdog.

<secret> has a value '<value>' that does not use a credential provider. (Warning)

The value is written in the configuration, which is stored in a repository. Store it in a credential provider and reference it, see Reference secret values, never write them.

<secret> has 'visibility' of value 'private', which is not available for an organization with free plan.

Organizations on the free plan cannot restrict organization secrets and variables to private repositories. Use selected with the list of repositories instead.

items.title: Repositories
items.text:
public <repository> has 'allow_forking' disabled which is not permitted. (Warning)

Public repositories can always be forked. Remove allow_forking: false from public repositories.

private <repository> has 'allow_forking' enabled, while the organization disables 'members_can_fork_private_repositories'.

The organization does not allow forking private repositories. Disable allow_forking for the repository, or allow forks in the settings of the organization.

private <repository> has 'has_wiki' enabled, which requires at least GitHub Team billing, currently using 'free' plan. (Warning)

Wikis of private repositories require a paid GitHub plan. Disable has_wiki for private repositories, see Enable only the features that are used.

<repository> has 'has_projects' enabled, while the organization disables 'has_organization_projects', setting will be ignored. (Warning)

Projects are disabled for the whole organization. Disable has_projects for the repository, or enable has_organization_projects for the organization.

<repository> has 'web_commit_signoff_required' disabled, while the organization requires it, setting will be ignored. (Warning)

The setting of the organization applies to all repositories, see Require a sign-off for commits made in the web interface. Remove the setting from the repository.

<repository> has defined an invalid topic '<topic>'. Only lower-case, numbers and '-' are allowed characters.

Topics follow the format of GitHub, e.g. github-actions instead of GitHub Actions, see Describe repositories.

<repository> has ('squash_merge_commit_title', 'squash_merge_commit_message') of value (...), while only combinations (...) are allowed.

GitHub only accepts some combinations of the title and the message of squash and merge commits, see Control the messages of merge and squash commits.

items.title: Rulesets and branch protection rules
items.text:
<ruleset> has an invalid 'include_refs' pattern '<pattern>', while only values ('refs/heads/*', '~DEFAULT_BRANCH', '~ALL') are allowed

The branches of a ruleset are matched by their full ref, e.g. refs/heads/1.2.x rather than 1.2.x, or refs/heads/release/* for a pattern, see RefMatcher. The same applies to exclude_refs, and the tags of a ruleset with target: 'tag' start with refs/tags/.

use of organization rulesets requires an 'enterprise' plan, while this organization is currently on a '<plan>' plan.

Otterdog only accepts organization rulesets for organizations on the enterprise plan, although GitHub also provides them with GitHub Team. Use repository rulesets instead, see Organization-wide rulesets.

<ruleset> has 'enforcement' of value 'evaluate' which is only available for an 'enterprise' plan.

Use disabled to prepare a ruleset without enforcing it, see Prepare a ruleset before enforcing it.

<ruleset> has 'restricted_file_paths' set, while push rules are only supported by private and internal repositories.

GitHub rejects the push rules, e.g. restricted_file_paths or max_file_size, of a ruleset of a public repository when the ruleset is applied, whatever the plan of the organization. Push rulesets also require at least GitHub Team. Remove the push ruleset or make the repository private, see Restrict the files that can be pushed.

<ruleset> requires deployment environment '<environment>' which is not defined in the repository itself.

A ruleset or branch protection rule that requires a successful deployment can only reference an environment of the same repository. Define the environment in the repository, see Require a successful deployment before merging.

items.title: Plan and apply
items.text:
plan shows changes that nobody made in the configuration

The configuration of the organization only contains the differences to its default configuration. A change of the default configuration, or a setting changed in the GitHub web interface, shows up in plan, see Inherited and explicit values.

A ruleset or branch protection rule created in the GitHub web interface is deleted

Otterdog manages all protections of the configured repositories, a protection that is not part of the configuration is removed when deletions are applied. Add it to the configuration instead, see the warning in Otterdog specifics.

A rotated secret is not updated on GitHub

Otterdog cannot detect that the value of a credential changed in the credential provider. Update the secret explicitly, see Updating secret values.

Changes to some organization settings are not applied automatically

Some settings, e.g. members_can_create_teams or the discussions of the organization, can only be changed through the GitHub web interface, which requires the credentials of a user that can log in to GitHub. plan and apply skip them with --no-web-ui, and such changes merged in a pull request of the configuration repository have to be applied manually, see Restrict what members can do.

Loading a page of the GitHub web interface times out

Settings that are only available through the GitHub web interface are retrieved with a headless browser, which waits up to 10 seconds for a page to load. On a slow connection this fails with an error like Page.goto: Timeout 10000ms exceeded. Increase the timeout, in milliseconds, with the environment variable OTTERDOG_WEB_TIMEOUT, e.g. export OTTERDOG_WEB_TIMEOUT=60000, or skip these settings with --no-web-ui, see Environment variables.

items.title: Validation in the Playground
items.text:
The Validate button of the Playground of the otterdog dashboard has the configuration of an organization, created by orgs.newOrg(...), validated by otterdog on the server, with the default configuration of the Playground. It reports the messages of validate listed on this page, the infos included, at the property they are about, e.g. at the invalid value of include_refs, if it is set in the configuration, otherwise at the repository or the organization they are about. The evaluated configuration is only sent to the server when the button is clicked, it is neither stored nor applied.

The Propose on GitHub button of the Playground of a project validates the configuration the same way first. If otterdog finds errors, which would fail the validation of the pull request, or if the configuration cannot be validated, e.g. because of schema errors, it asks to confirm before proposing it.

A configuration without problem in the Playground can still be rejected by the validation of its pull request, or fail to be applied:

  • The validations depending on the organization on GitHub are skipped: the members of a team with skip_non_organization_members being members of the organization, and the languages of code_scanning_default_languages being detected in the repository, which must exist.
  • The checks only done when applying are not done, by validate neither: the teams, users and apps of bypass_actors must exist, and GitHub can reject a value that otterdog accepts.
  • The plan is not computed: whether the changes require secrets, settings only accessible via the GitHub web interface, or remove resources, which prevents their automatic merge, is only reported on the pull request. The Playground of a project shows the changes to the current configuration of the organization, though.
  • The configuration is not compared with the settings on GitHub, like /otterdog check-sync does on the pull request.
  • The default configuration is the one of the Playground: the global Playground validates with the default configuration it evaluates with, the one of the instance or the example of otterdog, which may not be the one of your organization. Use the Playground of your project to validate with its default configuration.
  • Only the configuration of an organization is validated: the button is not shown for a snippet, e.g. creating a repository, and is disabled for a configuration failing to evaluate or having schema errors, which otterdog does not validate further.

items.title: Webhooks
items.text: Webhooks notify external services, e.g. a CI server or a documentation builder, about events. An organization webhook receives the events of all repositories, a repository webhook only those of its repository.

items.title: Configure a secure webhook
items.text:
orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  webhooks+: [
    orgs.newOrgWebhook('https://ci.example.org/github-webhook/') {
      content_type: "json",
      events+: [
        "pull_request",
        "push",
      ],
      secret: "pass:path/to/ci-webhook-secret", // (1)!
    },
  ],
  _repositories+:: [
    orgs.newRepo('my-repo') {
      webhooks+: [
        orgs.newRepoWebhook('https://docs.example.org/hooks/my-repo') {
          content_type: "json",
          events+: [
            "push",
          ],
          secret: "pass:path/to/docs-webhook-secret",
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
}
  1. A reference to a credential provider, see Secrets and variables.

Open in the Playground

Recommendation

Following the best practices for using webhooks:

  • set a secret, so that the receiver can verify that a delivery comes from GitHub
  • keep SSL verification enabled (insecure_ssl: "0", the default) and use an https URL
  • subscribe only to the events that the service needs

items.title: Change the URL of a webhook
items.text:
The URL identifies a webhook: changing it in the configuration deletes the webhook and creates a new one. To update the existing webhook instead, list the previous URL in aliases, see Renaming of Resources:

orgs.newOrg('my-project', 'my-org') {
  webhooks+: [
    orgs.newOrgWebhook('https://ci.example.org/hooks/github') {
      aliases: [
        "https://ci.example.org/github-webhook/", // (1)!
      ],
      content_type: "json",
      events+: [
        "pull_request",
        "push",
      ],
      secret: "pass:path/to/ci-webhook-secret",
    },
  ],
}
  1. The previous URL: the existing webhook keeps its deliveries and settings, and only its URL is updated. The alias can be removed once the change has been applied.

Open in the Playground

items.title: Pause a webhook
items.text: To stop the deliveries temporarily, e.g. while the receiving service is migrated, set active: false instead of removing the webhook: its URL, events and secret are kept, and deliveries resume once it is active again.

items.title: Secrets after an import
items.text: After an import, the secret of a webhook is ******** and the webhook is skipped until the value is replaced by a reference to a credential provider. A rotated secret must be sent again explicitly. Both are described in SecretValue.

items.title: Remove webhooks that are not used anymore
items.text:
Webhooks often outlive the service they were created for. A webhook pointing to a service that no longer exists fails on every delivery and sends the events of your repositories to a domain that you might not control anymore. Check the recent deliveries of webhooks in the GitHub web interface and remove the webhooks that are not used anymore from the configuration.

Note

Integrations that serve many repositories are often better implemented as GitHub Apps, which receive events through their own webhook and request only the permissions they need. The installation of GitHub Apps cannot be managed with otterdog, see Unsupported Features.
